title: 500-year-old freeze-dried potato snacks discovered in Inca storage room in Peru

reason: 秘鲁海岸出土的五百年前 chuño，证明印加把安第斯山的主粮送到了几百公里外。

cover.caption: Chuño is a snack made of potatoes that are freeze-dried. Archeologists recently found a 500-year-old sample of chuño in Peru.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: 500-year-old freeze-dried potato snacks discovered in Inca storage room in Peru
levels.body:
Two lumps of potato were found in an Inca storage room in Peru. But these were't ordinary potatoes. They were 500-year-old freeze-dried potatoes.

The Inca were an indigenous people who once ruled an empire. Their empire was in and around the Andes Mountains in South America during the 15th and 16th centuries. Today that area is the countries of Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina and Colombia.

These freeze-dried potatoes are known as chuño. They were once eaten across the Inca Empire. They are so fragile that they are almost never found today.

It is only the second time chuño has been found at an Inca site. This discovery was made just a few miles from the Pacific Ocean. But chuño was made in the mountains. This discovery proves that the empire transported chuño from the mountains all the way down to the Ocean.

Making The Snack

Chuño is made by leaving potatoes out for days. Instead of rotting, the potatoes freeze at night. Then they bake in the sun until nearly all water in the potatoes is gone. What is left behind is light and lasts a long time. It doesn't go bad for many years. This technique works because of the Andes Mountains. In the Andes, the temperature drops at night. This creates frost—a thin layer of ice crystals. During the day, the sun shines intensely. So chuño had to be produced in the mountains. It was then transported over hundreds of miles to feed people all over the empire.

The Inca used the same drying method to preserve meat. They made a product called "charki". Today we call it "jerky" in English.

The new study was written by achaeologists Lidio Valdez and Katrina Bettcher.

The discovery happened in 2024 at Tambo Viejo in Peru. The area is about 15 miles from the ocean. It had been part of the Inca Empire.

Inside a small storage room, the team found a clay pot in the dirt floor. Researchers scooped soil out of the pot. Then they reached its bottom.

"Almost at the base of the vessel, the two samples of freeze-dried potatoes were found," Valdez said. "They showed me without knowing what they were, and right away I said: chuño!"

No Rot

Potatoes usually go bad within a week in warm areas. Since there was no refrigeration at the time, the potatoes would have gone bad on long journeys. Valdez said the method of freeze-drying probably happened by accident. Some potatoes may have frozen in the mountains and dried out over days. An adventurous eater might have tasted them and realized they were still good!

Chuño can be made only in the mountains. But Tambo Viejo is by the sea. The potatoes must have traveled down from the mountains.

The two freeze-dried potatoes survived thanks to the extremely dry conditions of Tambo Viejo. The hot, dry weather help preserve food that would otherwise decay.

The ancient preservation method has lessons for today too. "We still have so much to learn from the people of the past," Valdez said. "…even in our times; yet we waste food, perhaps more than at any time in human history."

Valdez thinks more evidence of chuño will be discovered as archaeologists keep digging.

Chuño is made by leaving potatoes out for days. Instead of rotting, the potatoes freeze at night and then bake in the daytime sun until nearly all their moisture has evaporated. What is left behind is a lightweight, long-lasting vegetable that can be stored for decades. This technique works because of the towering Andes Mountains. At high elevations, like in the Andes, hard frost occurs regularly. At night, the temperatures drop, creating a thin layer of ice crystals. During the day, the sun shines intensely. So chuño had to be produced in the mountains. It was then transported using llama caravans over hundreds of miles to feed people living in other parts of the empire.

The study was published in May in a scientific journal. It was co-authored by archaeologists Lidio Valdez and Katrina Bettcher. They reported that the chuño was found alongside a piece of Inca pottery and a broken spindle whorl, a tool used to spin fibers, like wool, into yarn or thread.

The discovery happened in 2024 at Tambo Viejo, an archaeological site in modern-day Peru. The area, about 15 miles from the ocean, had been part of the Inca Empire. Inside a small storage room, the team uncovered a clay pot in the dirt floor. It's top half was gone, and as researchers scooped soil out of the pot, they reached its bottom.

"Almost at the base of the vessel, the two samples of freeze-dried potatoes were found," Valdez said. "They showed me without knowing what they were, and right away I said: chuño!"

No Rot

Potatoes usually rot within a week in warmer areas. So transporting them over long-distance in a time before refrigeration would not have turned out well. Valdez said freeze-drying was likely discovered long before the 15th century. It might have happened by accident when some potatoes may have been exposed to frost at a high elevation and became dried out. An adventurous eater might have tasted them and realized they were still edible.

Chuño can be made only at very high elevations—above roughly 11,800 feet. But since Tambo Viejo is almost at sea-level, the samples must have traveled down from the mountains. They were most likely transported via a llama caravan along the Inca road network, Valdez said.

"Chuño being a light product probably also made its transportation easier," he added.

The two freeze-dried potatoes survived thanks to the extremely dry conditions of the Acarí Valley, where Tambo Viejo is located. The hot, dry weather help preserve organic remains that would otherwise decay.

Beyond its archaeological importance, the ancient preservation method has lessons for today. "We still have so much to learn from the people of the past," Valdez said. "Food security is a main concern, even in our times; yet we waste food, perhaps more than at any time in human history."

Relatively few Inca sites along Peru's coast have been systematically excavated. But Valdez expects more evidence of chuño to surface as archaeologists keep digging.

The discovery, made along Peru's south coast, is only the second time chuño has been recovered from an Inca site. They are concrete evidence that the empire transported one of its most important foods hundreds of miles from the Andes, down to the Pacific Ocean.

Making The Snack

Chuño is made by repeatedly exposing potatoes to freezing night-time temperatures and daytime sun until nearly all their moisture has evaporated. What is left behind is a lightweight, long-lasting vegetable that can be stored for decades. This technique works because of the towering Andes Mountains. At high elevations like in the Andes, hard frost occurs regularly. At night, the temperatures drop, creating a thin layer of ice crystals. During the day, the sun shines intensely. So chuño had to be produced in the mountains. It was then transported using llama caravans, often hundreds of miles, to feed people living elsewhere in the empire.

The Inca used the same drying method to preserve meat. They made a product called "charki" — the source of the English word "jerky."

The discovery happened in 2024 at Tambo Viejo, an archaeological site in modern-day Peru about 15 miles from the ocean, which had been part of the Inca Empire. Inside a small storage room, the team uncovered a clay pot sunk into the dirt floor, its top half long gone. As researchers scooped soil out of the broken pot, they reached its bottom.

"Almost at the base of the vessel, the two samples of freeze-dried potatoes were found," Valdez said. "They showed me without knowing what they were, and right away I said: chuño!"

No Rot

Potatoes are roughly 80% water, and they typically rot within a week at lower, warmer elevations — making them a poor food choice for long-distance storage. Valdez said freeze-drying was likely discovered long before the 15th century, and might have happened by accident, perhaps when some potatoes had been exposed to frost at a high elevation and became dried out. An adventurous eater then may have tasted them and realized they were edible.

Chuño can be made only above roughly 11,800 feet. But since Tambo Viejo is almost at sea-level, the samples must have traveled down from the highlands. They were most likely transported via a llama caravan along the Inca road network, Valdez said.

"Chuño being a light product probably also made its transportation easier," he added.

The two freeze-dried potatoes survived thanks to the hot and dry conditions of the Acarí Valley, where Tambo Viejo is located. Hot, dry weather helps to preserve organic remains that would otherwise decay essentially by dehydration—the same process that resulted in the chuño in the first place.

Beyond its archaeological importance, the ancient preservation method has lessons for today. "We still have so much to learn from the people of the past," Valdez said. "Food security is a main concern, even in our times; yet we waste food, perhaps more than at any time in human history."

Relatively few Inca sites along Peru's coast have been systematically excavated, but Valdez expects more evidence of chuño to surface as archaeologists keep digging.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: 500-year-old freeze-dried potato snacks discovered in Inca storage room in Peru
levels.body:
Two lumps of potato discovered in a roughly 500-year-old Inca storage room in Peru are a rare find: freeze-dried potatoes predating the Spanish invasion, a new study finds.

These freeze-dried potatoes, known as chuño, were once a backbone of the Inca Empire's food supply and a product so fragile that they almost never turn up at archaeological sites.

The new discovery, made along Peru's arid south coast, is only the second time chuño has been recovered from an Inca site, researchers reported in the new study. It is concrete evidence that the empire directed one of its most important food sources hundreds of miles from the Andes, down to the Pacific Ocean.

Chuño is made by repeatedly exposing potatoes to nighttime frost and daytime sun until nearly all their moisture has evaporated, leaving a lightweight, long-lasting vegetable that can be stored for decades. This technique works only at high elevations where hard frost occurs regularly, so chuño had to be produced in the mountains and then transported using llama caravans, often hundreds of kilometers, to feed people living elsewhere in the empire.

The Inca used the same drying method to preserve meat, producing a product called "charki" — the source of the English word "jerky," study principal investigator Lidio Valdez, an adjunct professor in the Department of Anthropology and Archaeology at the University of Calgary, told Live Science in an email.

In the new study, published May 1 in the Journal of Field Archaeology, Valdez and study co-author Katrina Bettcher, an independent archaeologist, reported that the chuño was found alongside an Inca pottery fragment and a broken spindle whorl, a tool used to spin fibers, such as raw wool, into yarn or thread.

The discovery happened during the 2024 field season at Tambo Viejo, an Inca provincial center in the Acarí Valley, where an archaeological team had worked for several years. Inside a small storage room, the team uncovered a clay pot sunk into the dirt floor, its top half long gone. As researchers scooped soil out of the broken pot, they reached its bottom.

"Almost at the base of the vessel, the two samples of freeze-dried potatoes were found," Valdez said. "They showed me without knowing what they were, and right away I said: chuño!"

Potatoes are roughly 80% water, and they typically rot within a week at lower, warmer elevations — making them a poor food choice for long-distance storage. Valdez said freeze-drying was likely discovered long before the Inca rose to power in the 15th century, perhaps when potatoes that were accidentally exposed to frost at a high elevation became dried out and people realized the result was still edible.

Because chuño can be made only above roughly 11,800 feet (3,600 meters), the samples at Tambo Viejo must have traveled down from the highlands, most likely via a llama caravan along the Inca road network, Valdez said.

"Chuño being a light product probably also made its transportation easier," he added.

The two freeze-dried potatoes survived thanks to the Acarí Valley's extremely dry conditions, which help preserve organic remains that would otherwise decay — the same conditions that have previously yielded naturally mummified guinea pigs (Cavia porcellus) in Valdez's previous work at the site.

Beyond its archaeological importance, the ancient preservation method has lessons for today. "We still have so much to learn from the people of the past," Valdez said. "Food security is a main concern, even in our times; yet we waste food, perhaps more than at any time in human history."

Relatively few Inca sites along Peru's coast have been systematically excavated, and Valdez expects more evidence of chuño — and the long supply lines that carried it — to surface as archaeologists keep digging.

title: A 14-year-old used his lasso to save a man drowning in the Yellowstone River
zhTitle: 十四岁少年用套索救起落水者
reason: 黄石河上一次翻船事故，以及一个牧场少年在几分钟里做的判断。

cover.caption: Jory Thomas helps his family on the ranch they live on in Big Timber, Montana.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: A 14-year-old used his lasso to save a man drowning in the Yellowstone River
levels.body:
Jory Thomas was camping with his family in Greycliff, Montana. Jory is 14. For a while, the camping seemed normal. Then, all of a sudden, Jory heard cries for help! They were coming from the Yellowstone River.

Jory looked out to the river. He saw that a small boat had turned over after striking a bridge.

Three people were swimming toward shore. But one man was going downstream. He was desperately holding onto a cooler.

Jory sprang into action. He sprinted across the riverbank with his lariat in hand. A lariat is a long rope with a loop on one end. It can also be called a lasso. Jory's father called 911 to get help.

Jory ran into chest-deep water. When he was about 10 feet from the drowning man, he stopped. He circled his lariat above his head. Then, he tossed it toward the man.

Jory quickly got the rope around the man's head and arm.

Jory tied the rope around his belt buckle. Then he started walking backward to pull the man from the water.

Soon after, emergency help arrived. But by then, the man was out of the water.

Alan Ronneberg is the local sheriff. Ronneberg praised Jory. If not for Jory, he said, his men might have been "looking for a body."

Instead, nobody was badly hurt.

A Life-Saving Skill

For the past year, Jory has been practicing his lassoing. He practices in his backyard.

Jory and his family live on a ranch. Recently, Jory began helping his family rope cattle.

The rescue happened on July 5. Jory was visiting a campsite where his grandparents were staying. He brought his 20-foot- long lariat with him. He figured he might practice with it.

Jory is amazed his lariat saved someone's life.

"I really didn't think I could actually use it and help humans," he said. "I thought I could just use it for ranch life."

Hero At Home

Jory soon became famous. Montana news station KTVQ reported on his rescue. The local Sheriff's Office awarded him a certificate. And Senator Steve Daines named Jory the "Montanan of the Month."

Robin Thomas is Jory's mom. She says he's always ready to help people. She is very proud of him.

levels.title: A 14-year-old used his lasso to save a man drowning in the Yellowstone River
levels.body:
Jory Thomas was with his family at a campsite in Greycliff, Montana. Suddenly, the 14-year-old heard cries for help. They were coming from the Yellowstone River.

When Jory heard the cries, he looked up. He saw that a small boat and paddleboard had turned over after striking a bridge.

Three people were swimming toward shore, but one man was drifting downstream. He was desperately clinging to a gray cooler.

Before he had a chance to think, Jory sprinted across the riverbank with his lariat in hand. A lariat, or lasso, is a long rope with a sliding loop on one end. Meanwhile, his father called 911 to get help.

Jory ran into chest-deep water, soaking his boots, jeans and shirt. When he was about 10 feet from the drowning man, Jory circled his lariat above his head and tossed it toward him.

On his first try, Jory caught the man around his head and arm.

Jory tied the lariat around his belt buckle and started walking backward to pull the man from the water onto the shore. The water at that stretch of the river is about 10 feet deep.

Emergency help arrived about 10 minutes after Jory's father, Jase, first called. By then, the man was out of the water.

Alan Ronneberg is the sheriff of Sweet Grass County. If not for Jory, Ronneberg said, "It's a really good possibility that search and rescue would've been looking for a body by that time."

Instead, he said, nobody was badly injured.

After the rescue, Jory's clothes were drenched. He wrapped himself in a blanket and told his parents, "I think I just saved somebody."

Practice Pays Off

For the past year, Jory has been practicing his lassoing. For the most part, he has been practicing in his backyard with a model of a cattle head. He built the model himself out of wood and plastic.

He and his family live on a ranch in Big Timber, Montana. Recently, Jory began helping his family rope hundreds of cattle. He and his older brothers — Jayden, 19, and Jaxon, 17 — playfully practice their skills by roping one another's legs.

On the afternoon of the rescue, July 5, Jory was visiting a campsite where his grandparents were staying. He brought his 20-foot-long lariat in case he wanted to practice.

After the rescue, Jory's parents drove him home. He sat in a hot tub and thought about the fact that he might've saved someone's life.

"I really didn't think I could actually use it and help humans," Jory said about his lariat. "I thought I could just use it for ranch life."

Honored at Home

Jory became famous locally in the following weeks after a Montana news station, KTVQ, reported on his rescue. The Sweet Grass County Sheriff's Office awarded him a certificate. And Senator Steve Daines named Jory the "Montanan of the Month."

While Jory says the praise has been nice to get, he has other things on his mind. He starts high school soon and is looking forward to the winter basketball season.

Robin Thomas is Jory's mom. She says he's the kind of kid who's always ready to help people. She regularly sees him helping older neighbors pack and carry their groceries at the store.

"Jory is a strong believer of if somebody needs help, you're going to do everything you can," Robin said.

Before he had a chance to think, Jory sprinted across the riverbank with his lariat in hand while his father called 911.

Jory ran into chest-deep water, soaking his boots, jeans and shirt. When he was about 10 feet from the drowning man, Jory circled his lariat above his head and tossed it toward him.

On his first try, Jory said, he caught the man around his head and arm.

Jory said he tied the lariat around his belt buckle and started walking backward to pull the man from the water — which was about 10 feet deep — to shore.

First responders arrived about 10 minutes after Jory's father, Jase, first called. By then, the man, whom authorities declined to identify, was out of the water.

"It's a really good possibility that search and rescue would've been looking for a body by that time," Sweet Grass County Sheriff Alan Ronneberg said.

Instead, Ronneberg said, nobody was badly injured.

His clothes drenched, Jory wrapped himself in a blanket and told his parents, "I think I just saved somebody," according to his mother, Robin Thomas.

For the past year, Jory had been practicing his lassoing, mainly on a model of a cattle head he built in his backyard with timber and plastic.

He and his family live on a ranch in Big Timber, Montana, where Jory recently began helping his family rope hundreds of cattle. He and his older brothers — Jayden, 19, and Jaxon, 17 — playfully practice their skills by roping one another's legs.

On the afternoon of the rescue, July 5, Jory was visiting a campsite where his grandparents were staying. He brought his roughly 20-foot long lariat in case he wanted to practice.

After the rescue, Jory's parents drove him home, where he sat in a hot tub and wrapped his mind around the fact that he might've saved someone's life.

"I really didn't think I could actually use it and help humans and stuff," Jory said about his lariat. "I thought I could just use it for ranch life."

Jory became a local celebrity in the following weeks after Montana news station KTVQ reported on his rescue. The Sweet Grass County Sheriff's Office awarded him a certificate, and Sen. Steve Daines named Jory the "Montanan of the Month."

While Jory said the praise has been gratifying, he has other things on his mind. He starts high school near the end of August and is looking forward to the winter basketball season.

His mom said she's not surprised he's taking it all in stride; she regularly sees him helping older neighbors pack and carry their groceries at the store.

"Jory is a strong believer of if somebody needs help, you're going to do everything you can," Robin said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: A geometric pattern lurks in Chinese money plant leaves
levels.body:
Geometry is a type of math. It deals with shapes and figures. Geometry can be found in beautiful shapes and patterns. These are all around us, even in plants.

The leaves of the Chinese money plant hide one of these geometric patterns. It is called a Voronoi diagram. This pattern might form as the plant grows. A hormone spreads across the leaf to create veins. Water moves across the leaf through these veins. The hormone creates the veins in the shape of a Voronoi diagram. It might happen in other plant leaves, too.

Researchers shared these findings in May in a scientific journal.

This is a "beautiful" example of how plant veins form to move water in the most efficient way, says Lawren Sack. He studies plant biology. He was not part of the research group.

Lurking In Leaves

Leaves of the Chinese money plant have many small holes, called pores. They release water. Each one is fenced in by veins to form a mosaic. In geometry, a mosaic is a pattern made of flat shapes that cover a surface.

While in high school, Elijah Blum discovered an interesting pattern in those leaf veins. He noticed it while plant-sitting for his sister. Today he is in college at New York University. But at the time, Blum was an intern at a lab. He shared what he had found with his internship supervisor, computer scientist Saket Navlakha.

Blum showed Navlakha the veins on the leaf. They held the leaf up to the light. That's when they saw the Voronoi diagram.

In a Voronoi diagram, a surface is divided into zones, and each zone contains a point. Every spot in a zone must be closer to that zone's point than any other.

People who design cities use the same idea to decide which fire station a house should be assigned to. This helps each house in a city be closer to the fire station in its area than any other station. This helps firefighters get to fires faster.

You can find patterns that look like Voronoi diagrams in nature. The tiles on giraffe fur and the scales of dragonfly wings are two examples. But in a true Voronoi diagram, the mosaic must form around a set of points. In the Chinese money plant, the pores are those points.

Making The Mosaic

Blum and the others were curious how this pattern might form.

Computer models showed them what happens as the Chinese money plant leaves form. Waves of a hormone spread out from each pore. Those waves crash into one another. That forms ridges. Those ridges become the veins of the leaf.

CiCi Zheng studies the math of living things. She was part of the research group. The Voronoi diagram might be useful for plants, she says. The leaf's major veins move water. This pattern keeps those veins moving water as far as possible from their pores, which leak water. "You might want to place the veins not directly close to any of those locations where water evaporates super-fast," Zheng says.

Past studies of leaf veins have been very useful. They have helped experts better distribute resources such as water and energy, Sack says. Solar panels, electronic circuits and irrigation systems work much like leaves do. Studies of leaf veins have also helped scientists improve these technologies.

title: AI can be a helpful math tutor if used right — and harmful if not
zhTitle: AI 当数学家教的正确用法
reason: 1300 名高中生的调查结果：哪几种用法帮得上忙，哪几种反而拖后腿。

cover.caption: A recent survey revealed student and teacher attitudes toward using AI for help with math homework.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: AI can be a helpful math tutor if used right — and harmful if not
levels.body:
Should you use artificial intelligence for math help? Yes — and no. That's based on a new survey of students and teachers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is computer systems. It can do difficult work usually done by humans. It can make decisions or be creative. There is no one definition of AI because it can do so many different things.

This survey found that AI can help students learn new material. But only if it is used in certain ways.

The data come from a poll of 1,300 top high school students.

The study found that AI can be a good math tutor. Students can use AI to explain things in different ways. It can also check homework and answer "why" questions. AI can find out what students don't know. Using AI as a tutor could even make students less worried about doing math.

But there are downsides to using AI as a tutor. AI was made to make things easier and faster. But learning is hard work. You have to work through things and come up with your own answers. That's how you learn.

Survey Says

About half of the students in the survey said AI could help with math if used the right way. More than six in every 10 teachers said that an AI tutor could be useful. But they warned that AI might not help if used the wrong way.

Almost two-thirds of students surveyed (63 percent) said they would always try a math problem on their own before asking AI for help. If they had trouble, most students would ask a teacher first (58 percent). Then they would ask classmates (50 percent). Others said they'd keep trying on their own (48 percent). Others say they would look for tutorials on the internet (46 percent). That leaves AI in fifth place at 39 percent.

This study shows that students mostly use AI after getting help other ways. Most students (67 percent) and teachers (62 percent) suggested doing regular practice problems to get better at math.

About half of the students said they think AI can be useful for learning math. But they also said AI is best used along with help from their teacher.

How To Use AI For Homework Wisely

More than half of the teachers (55 percent) said AI's biggest help is that it can explain how to solve a problem. But almost three out of every four teachers worry that students can rely on AI too much.

Amanda Brown is a teacher. She says that AI might help students with homework. But students take tests without AI, so they need to know the material without help from it.

She suggests asking AI very specific questions, then add: "Don't give me the answer."

Another issue is that AI can often be wrong, since its job is to predict the most likely answer. But that answer isn't always right.

Beyond Homework

AI can be useful, though. It can help you prepare for tests by giving you sample problems and making flash cards. It might also help you catch up on topics you missed.

But AI can give you a lot of information. That can be overwhelming. YouTube videos done by teachers might be more helpful.

The Long Game

Learning takes work. If you're using AI for help with math and you don't feel challenged, try a different source.

You can use AI tools like Mathos and Wolfram|Alpha. These only answer math questions.

Using AI to understand math better can be great. But remember this from the teacher survey: "It's critical for students to arrive at the correct answers themselves." Use AI to learn big ideas, not just to get answers.

Is it a good idea to use artificial intelligence (AI) for math help? Yes — and no. That's based on the results of a new survey of students and teachers.

AI is computer systems that can do complicated tasks usually done by humans, such as decision- making and creating. There is no one definition of AI because AI tools can do many things.

This survey found that AI can be great for helping students learn new material. But only if used in certain ways.

The data come from a poll of 1,300 high school students from the United States, England and Wales. Some top math students were surveyed to identify their habits.

The study found that AI has many strengths as a math tutor. Students can use AI to explain things in different ways. It can also be used to check homework and to answer "why" questions. AI can also find gaps in knowledge. Some students said that using AI as a tutor could even reduce math anxiety.

But there are downsides to AI tutoring, notes Robbie Torney from Common Sense Media. It's a nonprofit that works on making the digital world safer for kids and teens. AI was designed to reduce friction. In other words, it aims to do things quickly and efficiently. But learning "requires friction," says Torney, who was not involved in the survey. You have to work through things that feel hard and come up with your own answers, he added.

Survey Says

The teens in the study had all taken part in an international math contest. Afterward, they gave their opinions on whether AI could be a good math tutor. About half said yes — if AI was used in specific ways. More than 200 math teachers also took part. More than six in every 10 teachers agreed that an AI tutor could be helpful. But AI could also decrease learning if used the wrong way, they noted.

Almost two-thirds of students surveyed (63 percent) said they would always try a math problem on their own before asking for help from AI. If they were struggling, most students recommended first asking teachers (58 percent). Then they would ask classmates (50 percent). Others said they'd keep trying on their own (48 percent) or look for tutorials on the internet (46 percent), or use AI (39 percent).

The survey results show that most people suggest using AI only after trying other sources of help. The number one suggestion was to do regular practice problems, according to both students (67 percent) and teachers (62 percent).

Overall, about half of the students said they believe AI has a place in math education, but that it is best used along with help from their classroom teacher.

How To Use AI For Homework Wisely

More than half of the teachers in the study (55 percent) said AI's biggest benefit is its ability to explain how to solve a problem.

Almost three in every four teachers surveyed said their biggest concern was that AI can quickly become a crutch.

Amanda Brown, a teacher, says that AI might help students do well on homework. But in the end, "You're gonna have to take the test [without AI]." And that's when it comes out: Do you know the material or not?

Amelie suggests asking AI very specific questions, such as: "What are different ways I could solve this?" Amelie also suggests adding to your prompt: "Don't give me the answer."

Another issue is that AI can often be wrong. This is called a "hallucination." It predicts the most likely answer, but that answer isn't always correct.

Beyond Homework

AI can be useful, though. It can help you prepare for tests by giving you sample problems and making flash cards. It might also help you catch up on topics you missed.

But AI can give you a lot of information. That can be overwhelming. YouTube videos done by teachers that AI references might be more helpful.

The Long Game

The bottom line is that learning takes work. If you're using AI for help with math and you don't feel like you're being challenged, change the source of your help.

Torney suggests using AI platforms such as Mathos and Wolfram|Alpha, which answer math-only questions, while Khanmigo focuses on education.

Using AI to help you understand math better can be a great thing. But keep in mind this mantra from the teacher survey: "It's critical for students to arrive at the correct answers themselves." Use AI to learn general concepts, not to get specific answers.

AI was designed to reduce friction — meaning it aims to do things quickly and efficiently, but learning "requires friction," says Torney, who was not involved in the survey. You have to work through things that feel hard and come up with your own answers, he added.

Tiago C.P., a Colorado high school senior who did not take part in the survey, says the most important thing is "trying the problem first." This is where students struggle, he adds, but "that's when you get the learning down." Tiago says, "I won't use AI before I've fully attempted a problem."

The teens in the study had all taken part in an international math contest. Afterward, they gave their take on whether AI could be an effective math tutor. About half said yes — if the AI was used in specific ways. More than 200 math teachers also took part, with more than six in every 10 agreeing that an AI tutor could be beneficial. But AI could also decrease learning if used improperly, they noted.

Almost two-thirds of students surveyed (63 percent) said they would always try a math problem on their own before getting help from AI. If they were struggling, most students recommended first asking teachers (58 percent), followed by classmates (50 percent). Others said they'd continue to try on their own (48 percent) or look for tutorials online (46 percent), leaving AI in fifth place at 39 percent.

The survey results show that most people suggest using AI after trying most other sources of help. The number one suggestion for doing well in math was to do regular practice problems, according to both students (67 percent) and teachers (62 percent).

Overall, about half of the students said they believe AI has a place in math education. But they added that it is best used along with — not in place of — help from their classroom teacher.

How To Use AI For Homework Wisely

More than half of the teachers in the study (55 percent) said AI's biggest benefit is its ability to explain — step by step — how to solve a problem.

Almost three in every four teachers surveyed said their biggest concern was that AI can quickly become a crutch.

Amanda Brown teaches math at Broomfield High School in Colorado, and she says that AI might help students ace the homework, but in the end, "You're gonna have to take the test [without AI]." And that's when it comes out: Do you know the material or not?

Amelie suggests asking AI very specific questions, such as: "What are different ways I could solve this?" Amelie also suggests adding to your prompt: "Don't give me the answer."

Another issue is AI "hallucinations." Sometimes AI "hallucinates," or makes errors, because AI doesn't actually know the answer, but rather predicts what the most likely answer is from the data it has ingested.

Beyond Homework

AI can help you prepare for tests by generating sample problems, creating flashcards or drilling you on core concepts. AI might also help you catch up on topics you missed if you were sick. The surveyed teachers suggested letting AI assist you with finding gaps in your knowledge.

But AI can give you a lot of information, which can be overwhelming, says Amelie M., another Colorado senior who did not participate in the survey. YouTube instructional videos that AI references might be more helpful, she says, since such videos show an instructor actually teaching you.

The Long Game

The bottom line is that learning takes work. "When it's easy," Torney says, "learning is probably not happening." If you're using AI for assistance with math and you don't feel like you're being challenged, change the source of your help.

Torney suggests using AI platforms such as Mathos and Wolfram|Alpha, which answer math-only questions, and Khanmigo, which focuses on education.

Using AI to help you understand math better can be a great thing if you keep in mind this mantra from the teacher survey: "It's critical for students to arrive at the correct answers themselves." Use AI to learn general concepts, not to obtain specific answers.

For one thing, "It's hard to get AI to teach you the same way your teacher would," says Amelie M., another Colorado senior (who did not participate in the survey).

How To Use AI For Homework Wisely

More than half of the teachers in the study (55 percent) said AI's biggest benefit is its ability to explain — step by step — how to solve a problem.

Amanda Brown teaches math at Broomfield High School in Colorado, and when learning something new, you can use AI for help, she says, but as you become more familiar with the subject, studies show, you should turn to AI less and less.

"At least a quarter of the time," Tiago says, "I can catch a mistake it's made."

Remember that you can also work on problems with classmates, and teachers are likely your best source for homework assistance. "Learning has always been a social task," Torney points out — "something that we do with other people."

Beyond Homework

AI can be a valuable supplementary tool as you prepare for tests, Tiago finds, since it can generate sample problems, create flash cards or drill you on core concepts. Or, if you were out sick for a few days, AI might help you catch up on topics you missed.

But AI will "pull from so many things," says Amelie, that it can return "long, long paragraphs" of info. This "might actually be more overwhelming" than helpful, she points out. What might prove more beneficial are YouTube instructional videos that AI references, she says, since such videos show an instructor actually teaching you.

A math hack: You can also ask AI to tell you about your own thinking and learning. The surveyed teachers suggested letting AI assist you with finding gaps in your knowledge, and students recommended asking AI "why" questions about math, since these could make you a better learner.

The Long Game

Math is a bit like learning a sport, since you have to learn certain procedural skills and in a certain sequence. Consider ice hockey— until you learn how to skate — and how to stop — you'll have a difficult time mastering a slap shot.

In math, if you don't learn factoring, you'll have trouble in algebra, and if you don't learn algebra well, calculus will be exceedingly demanding. This is why Torney advises that you "keep your eye on the long game."

And learning takes work. "When it's easy," Torney says, "learning is probably not happening." If you're using AI for assistance with math and don't feel like you're being challenged, change the source of your help.

Because utilization of general-use systems for math can lead to relying on them for social advice or emotional support—which can result in secondary psychological dependency in some people— systems focused on a unilateral topic, Torney says, "tend to be less risky for kids and teens."

Using AI to help you understand math better can be a great thing, if you keep in mind this mantra from the teacher survey: "It's critical for students to arrive at the correct answers themselves." Use AI to learn overall general concepts, not to obtain specific answers.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Aid groups scramble to help as Israel-Hamas war intensifies
levels.body:
Aid groups are scrambling to help people caught in the war between Israel and Hamas. Israel is a country in the Middle East. Hamas is an armed Palestinian group. Palestine is a state in the Middle East. Israel and Hamas are fighting in and around Gaza by the Mediterranean Sea. Gaza is home to 2.3 million people. It is Palestine's largest city. The aid groups have to decide on how to get help to people safely.

Hamas fighters took the world by surprise on October 7, 2023. They made surprise attacks against Israel. Israel fought back. The country's soldiers sent planes to strike targets in Gaza. Israel also stopped food and other supplies from going into Gaza.

Hundreds Killed and Wounded On Both Sides

The United Nations (U.N.) and aid groups are worried about working in the area. Hundreds of people have been killed. Thousands have been wounded on both sides. Aid groups say there are needs both in Gaza and Israel. They are begging to be allowed into Gaza to help Palestinians stuck in the middle of the fighting.

The Egyptian Red Crescent is one aid group. It sent more than 2 tons (2,000 pounds) of supplies to Gaza. Efforts to organize food and other deliveries are underway. The U.N. and other aid agencies were talking with Egypt about how to send aid to Gaza. The area is surrounded by armed forces. The groups were looking at a crossing point between the strip and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt.

Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said its supplies have already been used up in seven hospitals in Gaza. It was working on getting funds. It would buy more supplies from local markets.

Sharing Medical Supplies

Doctors Without Borders is still working in Gaza. The aid group has to depend on medical supplies it already has in Gaza. It can't bring any more supplies in.

Doctors Without Borders says it runs programs in Palestine because Israel has strong emergency and health services. The group is helping patients in Gaza and giving supplies to other hospitals. The hospitals have become overcrowded with patients. They are running out of medicine.

Doctors Without Borders said it may run out of supplies. These supplies are used to operate on wounded patients.

EU Weighs In On Conflict

Governments have also been weighing how to respond. The European Union (EU) is a 27-nation group. On October 9 it said it might stop aid for Palestine in the wake of Hamas' attacks on Israel. Germany and Austria are two countries in Europe. They also said they were stopping aid for Palestine.

Meanwhile, some groups are stepping up aid work in Israel. Many people have left their homes because of the war.

Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, is an aid group. It said its center is treating wounded Israeli soldiers and other people. About 90 percent of the patients in the center are soldiers. The center also accepts anyone who's wounded or injured.

Palestine Children's Relief Fund helps children who need to travel to the U.S. for medical care. Because of the war, the group will help in other ways. It will provide food, medication, clothing and other types of aid.

levels.body:
On October 10, 2023, aid groups were scrambling to assist people caught in the war between Israel and Hamas. They are determining what aid operations are safe to continue. Efforts are being complicated by an intensified Israeli blockade of Gaza and continued fighting.

Hamas fighters went on an attack that took the world by surprise on October 7. They attacked Israel without warning. They killed and wounded many Israeli people and took some captive. Israel responded by ordering airstrikes on Gaza. It also cut off food, fuel and other supplies from going into the territory. The United Nations (U.N.) and aid groups operating in the area became concerned about these moves. Gaza is home to 2.3 million people. Hamas, in turn, pledged to kill Israelis it took captive if the country's military bombs targeted people in Gaza without warning.

Hundreds Killed On Both Sides Of Conflict

Hundreds of people have been killed and thousands wounded on both sides. Aid groups operating in the region say there are needs both in Gaza and Israel. More than 2 tons (2,000 pounds) of medical supplies from the Egyptian Red Crescent have been sent to Gaza. Similar to the Red Cross, the Red Crescent is a humanitarian aid society. Efforts are underway to organize food and other deliveries, said an Egyptian military official. But the United Nations and other aid groups are pleading for more access to Palestinians who find themselves in the middle of intense fighting.

The U.N. and other aid agencies were working with Egypt to send aid to the besieged Gaza, said an Egyptian official and aid worker on October 10. It would be through a crossing point between the strip and Egypt's Sinai Peninsula. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization said its medical supplies in seven hospitals in Gaza had already been used up. It was shifting funds to purchase more from local markets.

Doctors Without Borders is still operating in Gaza. It has to rely on supplies it already has inside the territory because it can't bring more in, said Emmanuel Massart. He's a deputy desk coordinator with the organization.

The group says it only runs programs in Palestinian areas because Israel has strong emergency and health services. It reported on October 9 that it provided treatments to more than 50 people following airstrikes north of Gaza City. The group said it is helping patients in Gaza and donating medical supplies to other clinics and hospitals. The centers have become overcrowded with patients. There are also shortages of drugs and fuel that can be used for generators.

If Doctors Without Borders is not able to resupply quickly, Massart said, it will run out of supplies to operate on wounded patients. He also said the organization's centers are running on generators due to the low supply of electricity. Cutting off fuel will present a "huge problem," he said.

"Looks Like It's Going To Get Worse"

Mercy Corps' work has also been disturbed by the war. It has been providing people in Gaza with food and water. Right now, the group said the team on the ground is trying to find a scenario that would enable them to get back to work. The blockade of food and other supplies into Gaza is a major worry.

"We are very concerned with the way things are going at this point because it looks like it's going to get worse — very soon," said Arnaud Quemin. He's the Middle East regional director for the organization. The sealing of Gaza, he said, will increase the need for aid "very quickly."

Governments have also been weighing how to respond. As the fighting intensified, the European Union (EU), a 27-nation group, announced on October 9 that it would review the assistance it provides in the wake of Hamas' attacks on Israel. Germany and Austria said they were suspending development aid for Palestinian areas.

Helping Those In Need

Meanwhile, some organizations are stepping up aid efforts in Israel.

Hadassah, The Women's Zionist Organization of America, said its center in Jerusalem is treating wounded Israeli soldiers and citizens. About 90 percent of the patients in the center are soldiers. They are typically the first to be brought in for traumatic injuries. The center also accepts anyone who is wounded or injured.

The American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee said on October 8 that it was activating its emergency response team in Israel. It runs programs to support people with disabilities, the elderly and children and families who've been affected by the war and prior conflicts. The organization said it was working with its partners, including the Israeli government, to address what it called an emergency never seen before.

One organization that helps Palestinian children is shifting its focus, too. Palestine Children's Relief Fund is a U.S.-based charity that helps children in need travel to the U.S. for medical treatment. Given the war, the fund is shifting from long-term programs toward more urgent needs for food, medication, clothing and other types of aid. The group noted the blockade and security risks to its Gaza staff make it more challenging to do that.

"There are no areas of security, there are no safe havens," said Steve Sosebee, the president of Palestine Children's Relief Fund. "And therefore, it's very difficult for us to be out in the field."

title: As Chipotle opens in Mexico, there are fans and skeptics
zhTitle: Chipotle 开进墨西哥
reason: 一家美式墨西哥快餐回到墨西哥开店，本地食客对「正宗」的两种判断。

cover.caption: A customer eats inside the newly opened Chipotle in San Pedro Garza García, part of the Monterrey metropolitan area in Mexico.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: As Chipotle opens in Mexico, there are fans and skeptics
levels.body:
Javier Gámiz remembers the first time he tried Chipotle. It was ten years ago in Texas. He wanted fast food but didn't like how it made him feel. Then he tried a Chipotle bowl.

"It's fast food," Gámiz said. "But it's real food."

Since then, every time he visited the U.S., he went to Chipotle.

Now, Chipotle is doing something new. The American restaurant is selling its food in Mexico. The first Chipotle opened last month in a mall in Monterrey. This idea might seem strange. Some say it's "like bringing ice to the Arctic." That joke was used when Taco Bell tried to open in Mexico.

Gámiz lives in Monterrey. He was very happy that Chipotle opened in his city. Gámiz ate there more than twelve times in two weeks. Each time, there were many people in line and no empty tables.

Monterrey is a rich city. People there make more money than in other parts of Mexico. The city is close to the United States. Many people speak English, and there are many American stores. Chipotle is in a mall with other American places like Chuck E. Cheese and KFC. There's also a Chili's and a 7-Eleven.

Pablo de Brito is the director of Chipotle in Mexico. He said Monterrey has lots of money and young people. He said more people in Monterrey know about Chipotle. Chipotle is doing better than Taco Bell did. Taco Bell tried to open in Mexico before but closed both times.

Marco Fragoso is an office worker. He said Taco Bell's food was not good.

"They're not tacos," said Fragoso. "They're folded tostadas. They're very ugly."

People wonder whether Chipotle can reach beyond Mexico's rich. Daniel Jiménez Morales works in construction. He said he had never heard of Chipotle and wasn't interested.

Chipotle is focusing on Mexico's wealthiest areas. "People with extra money have traveled to the United States," De Brito said. People with more money are more likely to know Chipotle, he said.

Nearby, in the mall's food court, was El Bocadito. It serves traditional Mexican food. It doesn't target rich Mexicans. But Felicitas Martínez Hernández, the cook for over twenty years, said everything is made with love, and that's what brings people back. "My mother always said, 'If you cook from your heart, the people will like it,'" she said. "If you're going to cook, you need to cook as if the people were part of your family."

That, to her, is Mexican food. She said she wasn't worried about Chipotle. El Bocadito has been around for many years, and she expects it to be around for many more. She wished Chipotle well.

figures.credit: Photo: Cesar Rodriguez/For The Washington Post

figures.caption: Customers have been showing up in droves at the newly opened Chipotle in Monterrey.
figures.credit: Photo: Cesar Rodriguez/For The Washington Post

"I was so happy," said Gámiz, who has eaten there more than twelve times in two weeks. Every time, he saw no empty tables and long lines. Many Mexicans were eating Mexican food, kind of.

Monterrey is a very rich city. It is different from other parts of Mexico. It has many large companies and tech jobs. People there make more money than in other places in Mexico. Monterrey is close to the United States. Texas is just a three- hour drive away. Many people speak English, and there are many American stores. Chipotle is in a shopping mall with other American places like Chuck E. Cheese and KFC. There is also a Chili's and a 7-Eleven.

Pablo de Brito is the director of Chipotle in Mexico. He said Monterrey has "money, young people, college students," and is close to the United States. He said this means more people know about Chipotle and have eaten there before. Chipotle is doing better than Taco Bell. Taco Bell tried to open in Mexico in 1992 and 2007 but closed both times.

Marco Fragoso, an office worker, said Taco Bell's food was not good.

"They're not tacos," said Fragoso. "They're folded tostadas. They're very ugly."

But no one had come to Chipotle for tacos — they'd come for bowls and burritos.

A big question is if Chipotle can reach beyond Mexico's richest people. Daniel Jiménez Morales is a construction worker. He said he had never heard of Chipotle and wasn't interested.

Chipotle is focusing on Mexico's wealthiest areas. "People with higher purchasing power have traveled to the United States," De Brito said. "People with higher purchasing power know Chipotle and they give greater importance to the quality of ingredients and healthier food."

Nearby, in the mall's food court, was El Bocadito, which serves a buffet of traditional Mexican food. It was nothing fancy. The target wasn't Mexicans with extra money. But Felicitas Martínez Hernández, the restaurant's cook for over twenty years, said everything is made with love, and that's what brings people back.

"My mother always said, 'If you cook from your heart, the people will like it,'" she said. "If you're going to cook, you need to cook as if the people were part of your family."

That, to her, is Mexican food.

She said she didn't feel threatened by Chipotle. El Bocadito has been inside Plaza Fiesta San Agustín for decades, and she expects it to be around for many years. She wished Chipotle well. "Everyone has their own touch," she said. "As my mother said, 'The sun comes out for us all.'"

levels.title: As Chipotle opens in Mexico, there are fans and skeptics
levels.body:
SAN PEDRO GARZA GARCÍA, Mexico - Javier Gámiz will never forget the first time he tried Chipotle - a decade ago, while visiting family in Texas. He craved the convenience of fast food but hated how it made him feel. Until he had a Chipotle bowl.

"It's fast food," Gámiz said. "But it's real food."

Since then, every time Gámiz visited the United States, he made a beeline for Chipotle's "Mexican Grill," becoming what he called a "real Chipotle-man."

Recently, the burrito broke his way. Chipotle, the American chain that popularized the fast-casual concept and has more than 4,000 locations in the United States, has launched its most daring move: selling its "Mexican" food in Mexico.

The first of what executives hope could be as many as 200 Chipotles opened last month at the base of a large shopping mall in the Monterrey metropolitan area, bringing to life what might seem an absurd proposition - one that Taco Bell attempted, and failed at, twice.

"Like bringing ice to the Arctic," went a famous quip about Taco Bell's doomed forays into Mexico.

But Gámiz, who grew up eating his mother's traditional cooking, was delighted nearly beyond words. Here, at last, was Chipotle - not just in Mexico but in his Monterrey.

"I was so happy," said Gámiz, who has eaten at the restaurant more than a dozen times in two weeks. Every time, he has found the same scene: Not a single table available. Lines snaking along the windowed-walls. Everywhere, Mexicans eating Mexican food, kind of.

It's difficult to extrapolate from Chipotle's early success. Perhaps Mexico, with its celebrated cuisine, a country where Michelin stars adorn eateries from food stands to chic restaurants, is listo - ready to embrace this populist U.S. take on its gastronomy.

Or perhaps Chipotle chose its first location very wisely.

By virtually every measure, greater Monterrey - one of Latin America's wealthiest cities - is unlike the rest of Mexico. Home to many of Mexico's largest companies and its tech sector, per capita income is twice the national average.

More importantly, it has a far tighter relationship with the United States, especially to Texas, which is just a three-hour drive away. English is frequently spoken here. American chains and brands are omnipresent.

Put another way, Chipotle, in this Monterrey shopping mall, has chose a home alongside a venerable collection of its American brethren: Chuck E. Cheese, KFC and Hooters.

While visiting for this story, a Washington Post reporter ate lunch at Chipotle, went for dinner at Chili's, slept at a Wyndham Hotel and bought toothpaste at a 7-Eleven.

"Money, youth, college kids and proximity to the United States," Pablo de Brito, director of Chipotle Mexico, said of Monterrey. "So there's a much greater chance they've traveled to the United States, a much greater chance they know Chipotle, and a much greater chance that they've eaten at Chipotle."

Regardless of what the future portends, Chipotle appears to be off to a stronger start than Taco Bell.

Taco Bell's first try was in 1992, when it opened a food cart in Mexico City to sell soft-shell tacos and nachos. But in a country where tacos are literally fast food - served within minutes at street stands - Taco Bell folded faster than a Burrito Supreme.

Its next attempt, in 2007, met the same result.

"They're not tacos," Marco Fragoso, an office worker, told the Associated Press, seeming to speak for the entire country. "They're folded tostadas. They're very ugly."

But Chipotle might have more success, said Jeffrey Pilcher, a taco historian at the University of Toronto. He said Chipotle and Taco Bell may belong to the same food genus, but they've branched out in completely different directions.

Taco Bell, Pilcher said, is unabashed "junk food," while Chipotle has branded itself as a health- conscientious alternative, with fresh ingredients prepared in full view of the consumer. Chipotle's menu, which derives from the Mission burrito in San Francisco, may have been inspired by Mexican cuisine, he said, but isn't trying to imitate it.

"It's a San Francisco thing," Pilcher said. "It's not Mexican Mexican."

That was a distinction many diners drew at the Monterrey Chipotle on July 30. Few said they were eating Mexican food. They were eating American food, made from Mexican ingredients.

"The taco is inherently Mexican," said Rodrigo Oyarzun, 24. "For it to be a taco, it has to be made here in Mexico. That's a fact."

But neither Oyarzun, nor anyone else in view, had come to Chipotle for tacos. They'd come for bowls and burritos.

"Burritos are from over there," Oyarzun said. "The concept of the burrito is completely American."

Gabriela Ramos, 21, eating a Chipotle salad, agreed: "People aren't going to order tacos here because people don't come here for tacos."

A bigger question is if Chipotle can reach beyond Mexico's upper and upwardly mobile classes. Daniel Jiménez Morales, a construction worker who was laying cement outside, said he'd never heard of Chipotle and had no interest.

"It's gringo food for gringos," he said.

It was also unclear if Chipotle would ever try. De Brito said the early focus is entirely on Mexico's wealthiest pockets.

"People with higher purchasing power have traveled to the United States," he said. "People with higher purchasing power know Chipotle and they give greater importance to the quality of ingredients and healthier food."

A short walk away, at a post in the mall's food court, was El Bocadito, which serves a buffet of traditional Mexican options. It was nothing fancy. The target wasn't Mexicans of higher purchasing power.

But Felicitas Martínez Hernández, the restaurant's cook for more than two decades, said everything is made with love - and that's what brings people back.

"My mother always said, 'If you cook from your heart, the people will like it,'" she said. "If you're going to cook, you need to cook as if the people were part of your family."

That, to her, is Mexican food.

She said she didn't feel threatened by Chipotle. El Bocadito has been inside Plaza Fiesta San Agustín for decades and she expects it to be around for decades more. She wished Chipotle well.

"Everyone has their own touch," she said. "As my mother said, 'The sun comes out for us all.'"

levels.title: Asian Games offer a few sports you may not recognize, like kabaddi and wushu
levels.body:
The Asian Games started on September 23, 2023. They are being held in Hangzhou, China.

About 12,500 athletes participate in the games. That's more than the number of participants in the Olympic games. The Asian Games highlight sports that are more popular in Asia. Read on to learn more about them.

Kabaddi

Kabaddi is pronounced kuh-bud-DEE. It started in India and is very popular there. It draws millions of viewers. The sport does not use clubs or rackets. There are no goals. There is not even a ball.

Here's how it is played. Two teams have seven players each. They play on a small court. A single player on the offense is called a "raider." The raider crosses the centerline and tries to touch as many players as possible on the other side. They only have 30 seconds to do so. Then, they have to return across the centerline without being tackled. The game is played in two 20-minute periods. Points are earned by tagging opponents or by stopping the raider.

Sepaktakraw

Sepaktakraw started in Malaysia. The sport is like volleyball. But players can't use their hands. Players are on each side of a 5-foot-high net. The ball is kicked back and forth over the net. The goal is to get the ball to hit the ground on the opponent's side of the net. The sport has also been known as "kick volleyball" in the United States. The ball is smaller than a volleyball, though. It's closer to the size of a large melon.

Wushu

Wushu has been part of the Asian Games since 1990. It is the Chinese term for "martial arts." Wushu competition takes place in two distinct areas.

One area of competition is performing routines. Athletes show off different ways to attack and defend. The other area of Wushu competition is the full-contact version of the sport. It is often called Chinese kickboxing.

China won 10 gold medals in wushu at the 2018 Asian Games. Iran, Indonesia and Macau also won medals in the sport. Macau is part of China. China won gold medals in both the men's and women's finals this year.

Kurash

Kurash is a form of wrestling. It started in Central Asia. The sport is thousands of years old. It was first introduced into the Asian Games five years ago. At the time, Uzbekistan won a gold medal in the sport. Iran, Mongolia, Taiwan and India also won multiple medals in 2018.

title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in the Milky Way
zhTitle: 银河系已知最快的恒星
reason: 绕中心黑洞每秒 25000 公里，望远镜如何测出这个速度。

cover.caption: A black hole is a region of spacetime with gravity so strong that not even light can escape. Today, scientists are still discovering how these gravitational giants shape our universe.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in the Milky Way
levels.body:
Scientists have just made a big discovery. They have found the fastest star in the galaxy. A galaxy is a giant group of billions of stars, gas and dust. Our galaxy is called the Milky Way. Earth and the sun are part of the Milky Way. This fast star is racing around something called a supermassive black hole. There are supermassive black holes at the center of almost every galaxy, including ours. Black holes are not actually holes. They are huge concentrations of matter in very small spaces. Matter is anything that has weight and takes up space. Supermassive black holes have very strong gravity. That's the invisible force that pulls objects toward each other. A black hole's gravity is so powerful that not even light can escape. So it's very hard for scientists to know what's inside a black hole.

This fast star orbits, or follows a circular path, around the black hole. It reaches speeds of about 15,534 miles per second. That's 100,000 times faster than an airplane.

"That star is really, extremely fast," said astronomer Stefan Gillessen. He is a scientist who studies space and the objects in it.

This fast star gets really close to the black hole. It gets closer than scientists have ever seen a star get. The star uses the black hole's gravity to orbit the black hole very fast. It takes 8.7 years for this star to go all the way around the black hole.

The Discovery

Gillessen and his team found the star by using the Very Large Telescope. Telescopes are special tools that allow scientists to look deep into space. This one is actually four big telescopes. It is in the Atacama Desert in Chile, where the sky is very clear.

There are several hundred stars that closely orbit this supermassive black hole. They are also affected by the black hole's gravity. But this fast star is much closer to the black hole than the others. That means it is also affected by the black hole's rotation. Scientists think black holes spin, or rotate. Most objects in the universe rotate. Earth does one rotation in 24 hours. That's one full day. So scientists think black holes rotate too. But they don't know a lot about how that works. Fortunately, this fast star is helping them know more. That's because a spinning black hole affects the orbits of stars around it. This fast star gets so close to the black hole that it is helping scientists study the black hole's spin.

More To Learn

Studying stars like this one could help scientists better understand the mysteries of black holes. Powerful telescopes are helping to find stars that are even farther away. So there could be even speedier stars out there waiting to be found.

levels.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in the Milky Way
levels.body:
Scientists have found the fastest known star in our galaxy racing around a supermassive black hole. There are supermassive black holes at the center of almost every large galaxy, including our galaxy called the Milky Way. There are several types of black holes, but none of them are actually holes at all. Supermassive black holes are huge concentrations of matter in very small spaces. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Supermassive black holes have very strong gravity—the invisible force that pulls objects toward each other. In fact, a black hole's gravity is so powerful that not even light can escape. So it's very difficult for scientists to know what's going on inside a black hole.

This star orbits, or follows a circular path, around the black hole. It reaches speeds of about 15,534 miles per second—that's 100,000 times faster than an airplane.

"That star is really, extremely fast," said astronomer Stefan Gillessen. He studies space and the objects in it at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics in Germany.

The newly discovered star orbits the black hole closer than scientists have ever seen before. It takes just 8.7 years to complete one orbit.

The star uses the black hole's gravity to orbit the black hole very fast without falling in. It comes from one direction, gaining speed, then makes a sharp turn around the black hole. Then it flies back out again and slows down until it's at its farthest point. Then it speeds up and begins the orbit all over again.

The Discovery

Gillessen and his team found the star by using the Very Large Telescope in the Atacama Desert in Chile. The Very Large Telescope is actually four big telescopes. Telescopes are special tools that allow scientists to look deep into space.

There are several hundred stars that closely orbit this supermassive black hole and are also affected by its gravity. Scientists have mapped the orbits of about 50 of them. But this star is 10 times closer than the previous record holder. That means it is also affected by the black hole's rotation. Scientists think black holes spin, or rotate, just like most everything else in the universe. A spinning black hole affects the orbits of stars around it. This star gets so close to this supermassive black hole that it is helping scientists study the black hole's spin. This is something scientists know little about.

More To Learn

Studying stars like this one could help scientists better understand the mysteries of black holes. Powerful telescopes are helping to find stars that are farther away. So there could be even speedier stars waiting to be found.

Tuan Do is an astronomer at the University of California. He was not involved in the study, but said: "This is just the tip of the iceberg …there should be many more stars like this."

levels.title: Astronomers detect fastest known star in the Milky Way
levels.body:
A telescope has found the fastest known star in our galaxy, the Milky Way, racing around a supermassive black hole. There are supermassive black holes lurking in the center of almost every large galaxy, including ours. There are several types of black holes, but none of them are actually holes at all. Supermassive black holes are huge concentrations of matter in very small spaces. Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Supermassive black holes have very strong gravity—the invisible force that pulls objects toward each other. In fact, a black hole's gravity is so powerful that not even light can escape. So it's very difficult for scientists to figure out what's going on inside a black hole.

This star, called S301, zips around the black hole. It reaches speeds of about 15,534 miles per second—that's 100,000 times faster than a commercial plane.

"That star is really, extremely fast," said astronomer Stefan Gillessen. He studies space and the objects in it at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics in Germany.

The newly discovered star orbits, or goes around, the black hole at closer range than scientists have ever seen before. It takes just 8.7 years to complete one orbit.

The star uses the black hole's gravity to orbit the black hole very fast without falling in, coming from one direction, gaining speed, then making a sharp turn around the black hole, then flying back out again and slowing down until it's at its farthest point. Then it speeds up and begins the orbit all over again.

The Discovery

Gillessen and his colleagues uncovered the star in data collected by the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in Chile's Atacama Desert. Their findings were published Wednesday, August 19, in the journal Nature.

There are several hundred stars that closely orbit this supermassive black hole and are sensitive to its gravity. Scientists have mapped the orbits of around 50 of them. But S301 is 10 times closer than the previous record holder, which means it also feels the effects of the black hole's rotation. Scientists think black holes spin, or rotate, just like most everything else in the universe, and a spinning black hole affects the orbits of stars around it. S301 gets so close to this supermassive black hole that it is helping scientists study the black hole's spin—something scientists know little about.

More To Learn

Studying stars like this one could help scientists better understand the mysteries of black holes, including how fast the supermassive black hole spins. Advanced telescopes are helping to pinpoint stars that are farther away, which scientists could not previously see. So there could be even speedier ones waiting to be found.

"This is just the tip of the iceberg," said astronomer Tuan Do with the University of California, Los Angeles, who had no role in the study. "…there should be many more stars like this."

title: Barbie "chooses" Women in Sports for Career of the Year
zhTitle: 芭比把「体育行业女性」选为年度职业
reason: 一次玩具公司的选择，对应着女性在职业体育管理岗上的真实比例。

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Barbie "chooses" Women in Sports for Career of the Year
levels.body:
This year, Mattel's Barbie put the spotlight on Women in Sports. The company chose this for its Career of the Year.

Jen Welter was blown away.

"As a little girl, I didn't have this," she said. Welter was the first female coach in the National Football League. The Arizona Cardinals hired her in 2015.

Welter never imagined herself coaching football. "There was no one who looked like me," she said.

Some jobs hire more men than women. But that does not have to be true in the future. Mattel is the company that makes Barbie. It hopes the dolls in this collection will help girls to dream big.

This year's collection highlights four sports careers: general manager, coach, referee and sports reporter.

The First Female General Manager In Baseball

A report came out in 2021. It looked at the number of women in sports writing careers. Only a small number worked in sports writing.

Even fewer women are sports team managers. In 2020, Kim Ng was hired by the Miami Marlins. They are a baseball team. Ng was the first female general manager in Major League Baseball. There still aren't any in football, basketball or hockey.

"Every first was impossible until it wasn't," Welter said. Her dad helped her become confident. He taught her to fish. He trusted her to reel in the biggest fish.

Later, Welter started playing football. She became a running back on a professional men's team. She was the first woman to do that, too.

A Role Model For Women Coaches

Wendell Davis encouraged her to become a coach. Davis played for the Dallas Cowboys. "I [without thinking] said, 'No, girls don't coach football,'" Welter said.

But Davis knew what to do. He told the team that Welter would coach.

Welter became a great role model. More women have become coaches because of her. There were 15 female coaches in the NFL in 2022. There were also three female referees last season.

Welter said that dreaming is the first step. "Once you have that dream, you can do the work. You're driven to do the same things that the guys are doing."

Jen Welter, a former defensive specialist coach for the Atlanta Legends, walks the field before a game at the Georgia State stadium in 2019. She reflects on her career in football after finding out about Barbie's 2023 Career of the Year doll line.
Kim Ng also breaks boundaries as the first female general manager in MLB. She holds the position of general manager of the Miami Marlins.

levels.body:
"As a little girl, I didn't have this," Jen Welter said. She was blown away after finding out Mattel's Barbie had chosen Women in Sports for her Career of the Year.

Welter was the first female coach in the National Football League (NFL). The Arizona Cardinals hired her in 2015. She said that she didn't imagine herself coaching football.

"There was no one who looked like me," said Welter. She was also the first woman to play running back on a professional men's team. "Football was the first place in the world that somebody told me that girls and boys did different things."

The Barbie collection highlights four sports careers: general manager, coach, referee and sports reporter. Mattel hopes to encourage girls to get involved in sports.

Mattel has highlighted more than 250 careers with Barbie. The company wants to inspire girls to get jobs in fields where women often don't work.

The First Female General Manager In Baseball

In 2021, Associated Press Sports Editors released a report on women in sports careers. It showed how few women there are in sports journalism. A little over 16 percent of sports editors, reporters and column writers are women.

In 2020, the Miami Marlins hired Kim Ng. That made her the first female general manager in Major League Baseball. However, there are currently no female general managers in football, basketball or hockey. Women have been hired in assistant manager roles, though.

"Every first was impossible until it wasn't," Welter said. She said that her dad helped her gain confidence as a child. She credited him for her belief that things should be decided on ability, not tradition.

"He let me go fishing with the boys. It wasn't like he only let me take the rod when it was a small fish. He believed if it was your fish, you took it, and you either caught it, or you didn't. When I finally got an opportunity to try out for my first football team, it was the same thing."

"After I played in pro football, he told me I had to coach," Welter said. She was referring to former Dallas Cowboy Wendell Davis. "I [without thinking] said, 'No, girls don't coach football.' Thankfully, he took the job on my behalf and told me about it later."

Paving A Path For Future Women

Davis told Welter that her choice was bigger than she was. If she quit, "the entire [story] surrounding women coaching in men's pro football would be about how there once had been a woman, but she quit."

She didn't quit. Instead, Welter paved a path for future women on the sidelines. By the 2022 season, there were 15 female coaches in the NFL. There were three female game officials last season. The college all-star game the Hula Bowl even had an all-female officiating crew in 2023.

Welter said that her presence on the sidelines provides a visible example of what girls can become. "Girls could say, 'That looks cool. I want to do that.' Now you have a brand like Barbie, with a big giant corporation like Mattel, saying they want to change this for girls. This is how we're going to start. That doesn't mean it's a finish. It's a start."

She said that the permission to dream is the first step toward imagining what you can become. "Once you have that dream, you can do the work. You're driven to do the same things that the guys are doing. But if we don't have that early idea, then where does that same permission come from?"

Barbie commits to empowering the next generation of female leaders in sports. To do so, Barbie is partnering with VOICEINSPORT. This group connects and inspires girls through sports.
