title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
zhTitle: 美国气候队
reason: 一项就业计划如何同时服务气候目标，以及它绕开国会的方式。

cover.caption: Climate activists rallied outside the White House in Washington, D.C., urging President Joe Biden to declare a climate emergency on July 4, 2023.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
The United States government is trying to fight climate change. This is the significant change in the climate of Earth. It happens over a long period of time. Climate change can happen naturally. Today, human activities largely cause climate change.

The U.S created a major program. The program is called the American Climate Corps.

This climate corps will create jobs for more than 20,000 people. They will all work on protecting the environment. President Joe Biden approved this program.

First Tried As A Law

Many people have wanted a climate corps for years. These people include activists and some lawmakers. They have been asking Biden to make it possible.

Some lawmakers wrote him a letter. In it, they wrote about storms, heat waves and fires in this past year. They said that the government needed to do something big.

Then Biden approved the creation of the climate corps. It is modeled after a program from the 1930s. That was called the Civilian Conservation Corps. President Franklin D. Roosevelt created it. That program created many jobs, too. It helped the country during the Great Depression.

Many Jobs With One Purpose

Many people are happy about the climate corps. Not everyone thinks it is a good idea, though. Some lawmakers think the climate corps is a waste of money.

The White House did not say how much the program will cost. It also did not say how it will be paid for.

Workers in the climate corps will do all kinds of jobs. Some will help protect coasts from storms and high water. Some will plant trees. Others will work on sun and wind power. They will do many other jobs, too.

Everyone will have one thing in common, though. They will be working on protecting the environment and the people who live in it.

At the United Nations in New York, President Joe Biden met with government officials to discuss plans for the environment on September 19, 2023.
Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts threw his support behind the climate corps initiative on September 6, 2023.

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
The United States government is about to create a major program to fight climate change. It is called the American Climate Corps. Climate change is the significant change in the climate of Earth over a long period of time. It can happen naturally, but today, climate change is largely caused by human activities.

President Joe Biden approved this program in September 2023. It will train a huge work force to do jobs related to conservation, or protecting the environment.

The White House says the program will create jobs for more than 20,000 people. For example, some of these people will build trails and plant trees. Others will help install solar panels, devices that change energy from the sun into electricity.

First Tried As A Law

U.S. lawmakers had considered creating a climate corps before. However, lawmakers could not agree on it. Members of the Democratic Party wanted the plan to succeed, but members of the Republican Party strongly opposed it. They were concerned about the cost. As a result, the idea never went forward.

Democrats and environmental groups never gave up, though. They pushed Biden to issue an executive order allowing the creation of the climate corps. An executive order is a rule that the president can issue without the approval of Congress.

The Sunrise Movement is an environmental group that led the push for a climate corps. Its leader, Varshini Prakash, celebrated the announcement.

She said, "The path toward a Green New Deal is beginning to become visible." The Green New Deal is a plan for taking on climate change and creating new jobs. Many activists support the Green New Deal, but Republicans ridicule it. They say it would raise taxes and cost too much money.

"Young People Nationwide Are Excited"

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Biden uses executive power to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps
levels.body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — After being thwarted by Congress, President Joe Biden will use his executive authority to create a New Deal-style American Climate Corps that will serve as a major green jobs training program.

In an announcement on September 20, 2023, the White House said the program will employ more than 20,000 young adults who will build trails, plant trees, help install solar panels and do other work to boost conservation and help prevent catastrophic wildfires.

The climate corps had been proposed in early versions of the sweeping climate law approved in 2022, but was jettisoned amid strong opposition from Republicans and concerns about cost.

Democrats and environmental advocacy groups never gave up on the plan and pushed Biden in recent weeks to issue an executive order authorizing what the White House now calls the American Climate Corps.

"After years of demonstrating and fighting for a climate corps, we turned a generational rallying cry into a real jobs program that will put a new generation to work stopping the climate crisis,″ said Varshini Prakash, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, an environmental group that has led the push for a climate corps.

With the new corps "and the historic climate investments won by our broader movement, the path toward a Green New Deal is beginning to become visible,″ Prakash said, referring to a comprehensive jobs-and-climate plan supported by many activists and some Democrats but ridiculed by Republicans as a socialist nightmare that would raise taxes and hamper the economy.

Prakash, a frequent Biden critic, participated in a White House call on September 9 promoting the new job corps, which comes as Biden tries to strengthen his appeal to young voters in the 2024 presidential campaign.

The Sunrise Movement and other climate activists, including many young adults, were outraged this spring after Biden approved the huge Willow oil-drilling project in Alaska. Opponents say the project and others approved by Biden put his climate legacy at risk and are a breach of his 2020 campaign promise to stop new oil drilling on federal lands.

Those concerns were put aside, for now, as environmental activists hailed the new jobs program, which is modeled after the Civilian Conservation Corps, created in the 1930s by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, a Democrat, as part of the New Deal.

"Young people nationwide are excited to see the launch of the American Climate Corps, enhancing career pathways in clean energy, conservation and climate resilience,″ said Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, president of NextGen America, an organization that promotes education, registration and mobilization for voters age 18 to 35.

"Young people are fighting for climate justice every day in their community, and now they have even more opportunity to continue this fight in their careers,″ Ramirez said.

More than 50 Democratic lawmakers, including Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey and New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, had also encouraged Biden to create a climate corps, saying in a letter on September 18 that, "The climate crisis demands a whole-of-government response at an unprecedented scale.″

The lawmakers cited deadly heat waves in the Southwest and across the nation, as well as dangerous floods in New England and devastating wildfires on the Hawaiian island of Maui, among recent examples of climate-related disasters.

Democrats called the creation of the climate corps "historic" and a key step toward fulfilling the vision of the Green New Deal.

"Today President Biden listened to the (environmental) movement, and he delivered with an American Climate Corps,″ a beaming Markey said at a celebratory news conference outside the Capitol.

"We are starting to turn the green dream into a green reality,″ added Ocasio-Cortez, who co-sponsored the Green New Deal legislation with Markey four years ago.

"You all are changing the world,″ she told young activists.

The White House declined to say how much the program will cost or how it will be paid for, but Markey and other Democrats said money from the climate law and the 2021 infrastructure law would serve as a "down payment" for thousands of jobs.

Republicans have largely dismissed the climate corps as a do-gooder proposal that would waste money and could even take jobs away from other workers displaced by the COVID-19 pandemic.

"We don't need another FDR program, and the idea that this is going to help land management is a false idea as well," Arkansas Representative Bruce Westerman, chairman of the House Natural Resources Committee, said in 2021.

Representative Joe Neguse, a Colorado Democrat, said the program should pay "a living wage" while offering health care coverage and other benefits.

A key distinction between the original Civilian Conservation Corps and the new climate contingent is that, unlike the 1930s, the U.S. economy is not in an economic depression. The U.S. unemployment rate was 3.8 percent in August, low by historical measures.

The new corps is also likely to be far more diverse than the largely white and male force created 90 years ago.

White House climate adviser Ali Zaidi said the administration will work with at least six federal agencies to create the climate corps and will pair with at least 10 states. California, Colorado, Maine, Michigan and Washington have already begun similar programs, while five more are launching their own climate corps, Zaidi said: Arizona, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina and Utah.

The initiative will provide job training and service opportunities to work on a wide range of projects, including restoring coastal wetlands to protect communities from storm surges and flooding; clean energy projects such as wind and solar power; managing forests to prevent catastrophic wildfires; and energy-efficient solutions to cut energy bills for consumers, the White House said.

The creation of the climate corps comes as the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) launches a $4.6 billion grant competition for states, municipalities and tribes to cut climate pollution and advance environmental justice. The Climate Pollution Reduction Grants are funded by the 2022 climate law and are intended to drive community-driven solutions to slow climate change.

EPA Administrator Michael Regan said the grants will help "communities so they can chart their own paths toward the clean energy future."

The deadline for states and municipalities to apply is April 1, 2024, with grants expected in late 2024. Tribes and territories must apply by May 1, with grants expected by early 2025.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Replacing Dianne Feinstein: Laphonza Butler sworn in as California's newest U.S. senator
levels.body:
Laphonza Butler is California's newest senator. She had a historic swearing-in ceremony with Vice President Kamala Harris in the U.S. Capitol. It took place on October 3, 2023.

Butler raised her right hand to take the oath of office. On either side of her stood California Senator Alex Padilla and Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer. They are both Democrats.

Butler signed her name, and the Senate chamber broke out in applause. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky shook her hand. He is a Republican.

Butler replaces Senator Dianne Feinstein, who recently died. California Governor Gavin Newsom asked Butler to replace Feinstein on October 1. He had previously promised to name a Black woman to the Senate. The Democrats will keep their one-seat majority in the Senate.

Background

Butler is 44 years old. She was never a public official but has worked behind the scenes for Democrats for many years. She worked for Service Employees International Union Local 2015 for more than 10 years. In 2018 she was appointed by then-Governor Jerry Brown to the University of California board. She left in 2021. That same year she became president of Emily's List. The political action committee helps elect Democratic women who support abortion rights.

Butler also worked with Harris during her 2020 bid for president. She did the same for Hillary Clinton in 2016. More recently, she served as an official at Airbnb.

Butler is the first Black woman to serve in the Senate since Harris became vice president. Newsom appointed Padilla to fill Harris's seat. At the time, Padilla was the California Secretary of State. Newsom promised that the next person he appointed would be a Black woman.

Milestones

Butler will be the nation's 12th Black senator. She'll be the third Black woman senator. She is also the first openly gay person of color to serve in the Senate. Moreover, she's the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent California.

Some Californians wanted Newsom to pick a different Black woman as senator. Supporters and lawmakers wanted U.S. Representative Barbara Lee.

Lee is the only well-known Black woman running to replace Feinstein. Surveys show that she is behind two white Democrats who are campaigning for the Senate seat. They are U.S. Representatives Adam B. Schiff of Burbank and Katie Porter of Irvine.

In September, Newsom avoided pressure to name Lee. He said the role would be for a limited time. Voters will decide the next senator in the primary. "It would be completely unfair to the Democrats that have worked their tail off," Newsom said. "That primary is just a matter of months away. I don't want to tip the balance of that."

Shortly before the announcement, however, Newsom made his view clearer. He said that Butler could be a candidate for Senate. Many people began talking about the possibility that Butler might run for the Senate.

Will Butler Run For Senate?

Butler said she is still undecided.

"I have no idea. I genuinely don't know," Butler said after her appointment.

Lee was asked about the possibility that Butler might run. She said it was up to Butler to decide.

In a tweet, Lee said that she wished Butler well. Lee wrote that she is looking "forward to working closely with her to deliver for the Golden State."

Lee wrote that she is focused on winning the election for the Senate. She said California deserves an experienced senator who will deliver on issues. "That's exactly what I'm running to do."

levels.name: 高阶
levels.title: Replacing Dianne Feinstein: Laphonza Butler sworn in as California's newest U.S. senator
levels.body:
Laphonza Butler became California's newest senator, following a historic swearing-in ceremony with Vice President Kamala Harris.

On October 3, 2023, in the U.S. Capitol, Butler raised her right hand to take the oath of office. Butler was joined by California Senator Alex Padilla and Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, both Democrats.

The Senate chamber erupted in applause as Butler signed her name. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, a Republican from Kentucky, shook her hand as Butler walked off the Senate floor.

California Governor Gavin Newsom tapped Butler on October 1 to replace the late Senator Dianne Feinstein. This fulfilled his promise to name a Black woman to the Senate. The appointment ensures that Democrats keep their one-seat majority in the upper chamber.

Background

Butler is 44 years old. She has never served as a public official but has worked behind the scenes for Democrats and their causes for decades. She worked for Service Employees International Union Local 2015 for more than a decade. In 2018 she was appointed by then-Governor Jerry Brown to the University of California governing board for a 12-year term. She left the position in 2021, the same year she became president of Emily's List, a political action committee that helps elect Democratic women who support abortion rights.

Butler served as an adviser to Harris's 2020 presidential campaign and also to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's 2016 bid for the White House. She also recently served as Airbnb's public policy and campaigns director.

No Black woman has served in the chamber since Harris left to become vice president. Newsom appointed then-California Secretary of State Padilla to fill Harris's seat and promised that his next Senate appointment would be a Black woman.

First Openly Gay Person Of Color In Senate

Butler will be the nation's 12th Black senator and the third Black woman senator. She is also the first openly gay person of color to serve in the Senate, and the first openly LGBTQ+ person to represent California in the chamber.

Some Californians wanted Newsom to pick a different Black woman for the role.

After Feinstein's death, supporters and lawmakers pressed Newsom to name U.S. Representative Barbara Lee as the state's next senator.

Lee is the only well-known Black woman running to replace Feinstein. Polls show that she is trailing two white Democrats who are also running for the seat, U.S. Representatives Adam B. Schiff of Burbank and Katie Porter of Irvine.

Last month Newsom sidestepped pressure to name Lee, saying the role would be temporary. "It would be completely unfair to the Democrats that have worked their tail off," Newsom said in September. "That primary is just a matter of months away. I don't want to tip the balance of that."

Shortly before the announcement, however, Newsom said that the new senator could be a candidate, leading to speculation that Butler might throw her hat into the ring.

Butler Wants To Honor Feinstein's Career

Butler said that she is undecided if she will join the hotly contested Senate race.

"I have no idea. I genuinely don't know," Butler said in her first interview since her appointment. She added that she wants to be focused on honoring Feinstein's career. "I want to devote my time and energy to serving the people of California. And I want to carry her baton with the honor that it deserves and so I genuinely have no idea."

When asked by reporters about the possibility of Butler running, Lee replied, "That's her decision."

In a tweet, Lee said that she wished Butler well. Lee said she looks "forward to working closely with her to deliver for the Golden State."

Lee also wrote that she is solely focused on winning her campaign for Senate. California, she wrote, "deserves an experienced Senator who will deliver on progressive priorities. That's exactly what I'm running to do."

title: California camp combines math and dance for middle schoolers
zhTitle: 把数学和舞蹈放在一起的暑期营
reason: 加州 SHINE 项目面向零基础的六到八年级女生，课程怎么排。

cover.caption: Middle school girls attended a recent camp in Bakersfield, California, that focused on math and dance.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: California camp combines math and dance for middle schoolers
levels.body:
Do you like to dance? If so, have you ever thought about how much math is in dance?

A group in California has a math and dance camp. It is called the Kern Dance Alliance. The camp was at a high school in Bakersfield, California. It happened this past July.

Mayah Smallwood was a camper in 2025. "I love doing dance," she says. After camp, she said, "I'm getting a lot better in math." Also, "you get to meet new people, you get to make new friends, you dance," She said. But you also learn math. "And they explain it in a way that is understandable," she says.

Algebra And Choreography

The free camp ran for one week in July. It was open to middle school girls in the Bakersfield area. It was ok if this was their first dance class.

Andrea Hansen is in charge of the Kern Dance Alliance. She says the program is all about trying something new. You are not "expected to be the best person in the room. That's perfectly ok," she says.

Each day had a schedule. The girls had dance sessions and math tutoring sessions. There was also time for snacks and bonding.

Students covered elementary math. This included fractions and decimals. And they covered middle school math. This included percents and probability. (Percents are a fraction where the whole is 100. Probability is the chance that something will happen.)

Wendy Wisheropp-Brice is a math teacher in Bakersfield, California. She is also a former professional dancer. She leads the program. She created math lessons for the camp. For example, she created algebra lessons. That's a branch of math that uses numbers, mathematical symbols, and variables (unknown quantities) to solve problems.

The students wrote algebraic equations. Those are math sentences. They have a variable, such as x or y. The variable stands for an unknown value. In this case, "each variable represents a dance move," says Wisheropp-Brice. Then the girls solved their equation. Then they had a dance routine.

Each day included a special guest. They were women who worked in science and math. They told the girls about their careers.

Finally, the week ends with a big performance. Family, friends and teachers went to watch.

Growing Numbers

Almost 300 students have done the camp. That is because of program directors like Wendy Wisheropp-Brice.

What they do "in those classrooms is incredible," she said. Also important are the mentors. Those are girls in high school or college. They went to the camp too. Aubrey Baldoz was a mentor in 2025. "I just want the girls to feel confident in themselves," she says. "So I try really hard," she says.

Andrea Hansen is in charge of the Kern Dance Alliance. She says the program is all about trying something new. levels.name: 进阶
levels.title: California camp combines math and dance for middle schoolers
levels.body:
Sometimes the hardest part about learning a subject in school is relating it to the real world.

For girls in California's Kern County, that's where the Kern Dance Alliance comes in. The nonprofit organization offers community programs. They use dance to encourage learning, healthy living, and tolerance in the community. And this past summer, a group of middle school girls spent a week learning dance and math together. It was part of the SHINE program at Garces Memorial High School in Bakersfield, California.

Mayah Smallwood was a camper in 2025. "I love doing dance," she says. And after a week in the SHINE program, she said, "I'm getting a lot better in math. You get to meet new people, you get to make new friends, you dance, you learn math, and they explain it in a way that is understandable," she says.

Algebra And Choreography

The free camp ran for one week in July. It was open to middle school girls in the Bakersfield area. Unlike other dance schools and programs, SHINE is made to meet girls at their level of experience, even if they have none.

Andrea Hansen is the executive director of the Kern Dance Alliance. She says the program is all about trying something new. "We want to show the students in the program that it's OK to not have a dance background." It's ok to "feel yourself stretched in a way that you aren't normally stretching yourself," she says. You are not "expected to be the best person in the room. That's perfectly ok," she says.

Daily sessions include snacks and bonding, hands-on math activities through movement, dance technique and choreography, and small-group tutoring.

"Every day is a little bit different in terms of the math subjects they're learning," Hansen said. "It could range from fractions and decimals and percentages to order of operations to statistics and probability, geometry, algebra. They get a little bit of almost everything from sixth- to eighth-grade curriculum."

The day balances dance lessons with small-group tutoring sessions. Wendy Wisheropp-Brice is a math teacher at Liberty High School in Bakersfield, California. She is also a former professional dancer. She leads the SHINE program and helped to create math lessons for the camp. For example, she created algebra lessons. That's a branch of math that uses numbers, mathematical symbols, and variables (unknown quantities) in mathematical expressions and equations.

"We take those tutoring sessions and turn them into activities that blend the world of dance," she says. So the students wrote algebra equations where "each variable represents a dance move," says Wisheropp-Brice. Then the girls solved their equation and they had a dance routine.

Along with small group tutoring and big group math activities, each day includes warm-ups and choreography, snacks, and a special guest. Hansen said, "Every day features a professional woman in STEM," Hansen said. They are "coming in and speaking to the girls about what they do in their field."

The week ends with a celebratory performance. Family, friends and teachers attended.

Growing Numbers

Almost 300 students have finished the program over its 10 years in existence. Hansen says much of the success is because of program directors Jessica Johnson and Wendy Wisheropp-Brice.

"What Jessica and Wendy do in those classrooms is incredible," she said, and "they are the ones in charge of ensuring the mentors are doing what they need to do. … They are communicating with the parents. They're right there on site for the students that need something."

Johnson said in a news release, "SHINE for Girls is the program I wished I could've been a part of as a young teen! Through mentorship and tutoring we show girls what it looks like to be a woman in STEM, and how they can get there too! We also use dance as a way to reinforce their math skills and help build the confidence to put themselves out there and SHINE both on stage and in the classroom."

Mentors were local high school and college women with strong math skills, tutoring experience, dance training, and a passion for helping girls. Many mentors were former students who have continued to study in STEM fields. Like Aubrey Baldoz, who was in her third year of mentoring when she worked at the camp in 2025. "Whether it's through dance or math, I just want the girls to feel confident in themselves. I just really see myself in some of them, so I try really hard to lead them and guide them to the best of my ability," she says.

title: Contiguous US breaks its record for hottest month ever
zhTitle: 美国本土有记录以来最热的一个月
reason: NOAA 的月度均温、1936 年沙尘暴那次的对照，以及记录只能回溯到 1895 年这件事。

cover.caption: Eleven-year-old Ruth gets a splash of cold water to beat the heat during the Great American State Fair in Washington, D.C. on July 2.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Contiguous US breaks its record for hottest month ever
levels.body:
July was the hottest month ever for most of the United States. July averaged 76.89 degrees Fahrenheit across the contiguous U.S. Those are the 48 states on the mainland. They don't include Alaska or Hawaii. They are also known as the Lower 48 states. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced this new record. NOAA is the government agency that studies the weather.

This new record beats the one set in July 1936 by an eighth of a degree. But 1936 was not an normal year. It was during the Dust Bowl. In this period in American history, heavy farming in the Great Plains left the land very dry. This, along with natural cycles of the ocean, led to dust storms and very hot temperatures.

Jeff Masters is a meteorologist. As a scientist who studies the weather and its affects on the planet, he is worried. "If we're exceeding records from the Dust Bowl, that says that we're in deep trouble," says Masters. The dust storms and failed crops during the Dust Bowl led to food shortages. Tens of millions of people left the Great Plains.

It was unusually cool in Alaska in July. But the Lower 48 saw very hot temperatures. It was especially hot in the Mountain West, Southwest, Northern Plains and Southeast. The Lower 48 states was at least 1 degree Fahrenheit warmer than the 20th century average, said Russ Vose from NOAA. To get an average, you add up all the numbers in the group. Then you divide that total by how many numbers you added. This let's you know the center of data. Looking at averages over a long period lets scientists see how Earth's temperatures have changed over time.

Contributions

Scientists said that what's happening now is due to the burning of coal, oil and gas. These are fossil fuels. Burning fossil fuels includes using oil for cars, for example. Climate change is the significant change in Earth's climate over a long period of time. It can happen naturally. But today data shows that climate change is mostly caused by human activities. This includes the burning of fossil fuels and the clearing of forests. Carbon dioxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. This traps heat in Earth's atmosphere. And that makes temperatures go up.

Katharine Jacobs is a climate scientist. She says that high temperatures, drought and wildfires are all signs of climate change.

Hotter nights are also a sign of human-caused climate change. July's nighttime temperatures beat the old record by 0.7 degrees.

Nighttime heat is also dangerous. If your body doesn't cool off at night, your body doesn't have time to get used to the heat. This can lead to a rise in the body's core temperature. And that can be dangerous. Studies show that as nights become hotter, more people lose sleep and even die.

Masters said that we need "to stop burning so many fossil fuels. We also need to be spending money to adapt to the new climate that we've put in place."

In this period in American history, over-ploughing in the Great Plains left the land very try. This, along with natural oceanic cycles, played a role in droughts, dust storms and soaring temperatures.

"It's not good when you're breaking records from the Dust Bowl, which we are in this case," said meteorologist Jeff Masters. As a scientist who studies the weather and its affects on the planet, he is concerned. The dust storms and failed crops during the Dust Bowl led to food shortages. Tens of millions of people left the Great Plains. "If we're exceeding records from The Dust Bowl, that says that we're in deep trouble," says Masters.

Although it was unusually cool in Alaska in July, the Lower 48 were very hot. The most excessive heat was in the Mountain West, Southwest, Northern Plains and Southeast. The heat was so widespread that all the Lower 48 states was at least 1 degree Fahrenheit warmer than the 20th century average, said Russ Vose from NOAA. To get an average, you add up all the numbers in the group. Then you divide that total by how many numbers you added. This let's you know the center of data. Looking at averages over a long period of time lets scientists see how Earth's temperatures have changed over time.

Contributions

Scientists said that what's happening now is due to the burning of coal, oil and gas—fossil fuels. Climate change is the signifiant change in Earth's climate over a long period of time. It can happen naturally. But today data shows that climate change is mostly caused by human activities. This includes the burning of fossil fuels—such as oil for cars—and clearing of forests. Carbon dioxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. This traps heat in Earth's atmosphere. And that makes temperatures go up.

The very high temperatures, intense drought and wildfires are all signals of climate change, said Katharine Jacobs. She is a climate scientist at the University of Arizona.

Hotter nights are also a sign of human-caused climate change. July's nighttime temperatures beat the old record by 0.7 degrees.

"If you're talking heat waves, that nighttime low is incredibly important for determining total heat stress," Masters said. If your body doesn't cool off at night, your body doesn't have time to get used to the heat. This can lead to a rise in the body's core temperature. And that can be dangerous.

Studies show that as nights become hotter, more people lose sleep and even die.

What's needed, Masters said, is "to stop burning so many fossil fuels. We also need to be spending money to adapt to the new climate that we've put in place."

title: Cut the number of choices you make each day. Your brain will thank you
zhTitle: 减少每天要做的选择
reason: 选项变多为什么反而降低满意度，行为科学给出的机制与三条做法。

cover.caption: Drowning in options? Reducing the number of decisions you make each day can boost your focus and peace of mind.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Cut the number of choices you make each day. Your brain will thank you
levels.body:
People make choices every day. They choose clothes. How to style their hair. Who to be friends with.

Scientists have done hundreds of studies on choices. And research shows that having too many choices is not a good thing. In fact, you should make less choices, said Barry Schwartz. He used to teach psychology.

Limit the number of choices you make every day, he said. Your brain will thank you.

More Is Often More Confusing

Schwartz gave a few examples of decision-making studies.

Some companies help workers save money for the future. They offer money-saving plans. One popular plan is a 401(k). But when a company offers many plans, fewer workers sign up.

The same thing happens with less important choices. One study looked at how people buy jam. Some customers had six different jam options. Others had 24 options. People bought more jam when they only had six choices.

Schwartz said that too many choices can make people feel stuck.

People might also make worse decisions. More options mean a greater chance of making a bad choice.

Not all people are like this all the time, Schwartz said. Car enthusiasts love cars. They will happily review every detail of a car when buying a new one.

But most people don't do this for jam.

The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

Daniel Willingham is also a psychology professor. He said our brain tries not to think too much.

Solving problems is harder for the brain. It uses more energy than remembering. This behavior comes from how humans survived long ago. When we have a goal, the brain first remembers what worked before. This came from our ancestors reacting to danger or finding a place to stay. The brain solves problems only when it has to.

This is why people often do the same thing without thinking about it. They could take a new path to work, for example. But they usually take the same one every day.

Schwartz also gave an example with jeans. If you have two options for jeans, they probably won't fit everyone perfectly. But what if there are 2,000 jean companies? "Now," Schwartz said, "You do expect your jeans to fit perfectly."

Limit Your Choices And Move On

David Epstein says he limits his opportunities to make choices. Once, he bought 10 of the same T- shirt in different colors.

He followed Herbert Simon's example. Simon was a famous thinker. He only had three sets of clothes. He ate almost the same thing every day. Simon created the word "satisficing." It means picking something that is good enough and moving on.

Epstein sets satisficing rules for himself when shopping online. He doesn't read reviews, for example.

Willingham and Schwartz suggest looking to people in real life to help, too. If you need a new phone, ask a friend who likes theirs.

Changing how you make choices is hard, but it helps. "Over time … you find it easier to make decisions," Schwartz said. "You end up more satisfied with the decisions you make." And, he added, you get more free time.

"When all you've got to choose from is Lee's and Levi's, nobody expects the jeans they buy to fit perfectly," he said. "When there are 2,000 options, well, now, you do expect your jeans to fit perfectly."

Limit Your Choices And Move On

David Epstein said that after researching his book, "Inside the Box: How Constraints Make Us Better," he began to shift away from his maximalist tendencies. Now, he limits his opportunities for making choices, such as when he bought 10 of the same well-fitting T-shirts in different colors.

He was following the example of Herbert Simon, a psychologist and 1978 Nobel laureate in economics, who had three sets of clothes and ate nearly the same thing every day. Simon introduced the term "satisficing," a combination of satisfying and sufficing that means setting good-enough criteria for decisions and moving on.

Epstein sets satisficing rules for himself when shopping online by first focusing on the purpose of the purchase.

"When I find one that does that, I'm buying it, instead of reading all the reviews and getting sucked into, 'Well, this one has all these other features.'"

Willingham and Schwartz suggested farming out some decisions. If you're looking for a new phone, find a friend who is happy with theirs and buy that one.

For larger decisions like financial planning, you'll be happier if you rely on someone else's professional expertise, Willingham said.

"If you're thinking, 'Well, I'm a clever guy, I can figure that out,' I think 9 times out of 10, you're fooling yourself," he said.

Schwartz acknowledged that for people who have trouble making decisions, changing is difficult. But it's worth it.

"What happens over time is you find it easier to make decisions, you end up more satisfied with the decisions you make, and all of a sudden, you've got an extra two hours in every day," he said.

levels.body:
Dianne Feinstein was a U.S. lawmaker. She died at age 90.

Feinstein was in the U.S. Senate. She was a Democrat. She was from California, but she died at her home in Washington, D.C. That was on September 28, 2023. On September 29, lawmakers spoke about her. Senator Chuck Schumer said that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

President Joe Biden worked with Feinstein in the Senate. He called her a leader and a friend.

Feinstein was the oldest senator in office. She pushed to protect the environment and limit gun sales. She also reached out to Republicans and found middle ground.

Her death came after health problems kept her away from the Senate. She was out for more than two months earlier in the year.

Praise For Feinstein's Work

On September 29, lawmakers remembered her. The California members of the House of Representatives visited the Senate.

Mitch McConnell is a senator. He is one of the Republicans who praised Feinstein. California and the country are better because of her work, he said.

Biden said, "Dianne made her mark on everything" from the environment to protecting civil rights. The country will see her work for years, he said.

Barack Obama is a former president. He also praised Feinstein as a leader. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion of civil rights and environmental protection.

She was elected to a San Francisco board of leaders in 1969. San Francisco is in California. She was the first woman to be its board president in 1978. That year, Mayor George Moscone was shot and killed.

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

After Moscone died, Feinstein became the first woman to be the city's mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two women to serve as the state's senators. She also was a leader in Senate groups.

Feinstein had help passing laws because she was good at working with others.

Still, when someone challenged her, she might have a sharp reply. She lost that edge in her later years. Her health was failing.

In February 2023, she said she would not run for office again.

Some of Feinstein's most important work came in 1994. The Senate approved her measure to stop the sales of some kinds of guns. It was part of a bill that Clinton signed into law.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco. She graduated from Stanford University in 1955. In 1980, she married Richard Blum. He died in February 2022.

Feinstein is survived by her daughter, Katherine, and her granddaughter, Eileen. She also has three stepchildren.

levels.body:
U.S. lawmaker Dianne Feinstein fought for her causes but also found ways to agree with others. She has died at age 90.

Feinstein was a senator and member of the Democratic Party. Representing California, she died at her home in Washington, D.C., on September 28, 2023. Tributes poured in on September 29. Lawmaker Chuck Schumer, a U.S. Senate leader, announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

President Joe Biden served with Feinstein for years in the Senate. He called her "a pioneering American" and a friend.

Feinstein was the oldest sitting U.S. senator. She pushed for causes including environmental protection and gun control. She also was known for reaching out to Republicans and seeking middle ground.

Her death came after health problems sidelined her for more than two months in 2023. Her absence drew frustration, even among her own political group. When she returned to the Senate in May, she voted only occasionally.

Politicians Paid Tribute To Feinstein

On September 29, senators gave tearful tributes. Other lawmakers, the California members of the House of Representatives, stood in the back.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who praised Feinstein. "California and our entire nation are better" because of her service, he said.

Biden said, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties." The country will benefit from her work for years, he said.

Former President Barack Obama also praised her as a pioneer. Former President Bill Clinton called her a champion of rights, environmental protection and strong national security.

San Francisco's First Female Mayor

Feinstein was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1969. She became its first female board president in 1978. That year, San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was shot and killed alongside another city leader, Harvey Milk. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two female senators. She also was the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Feinstein's experiences shaped her outlook throughout her 50 years in government.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she said in 2005.

Feinstein's efforts to work with Republicans helped her get lawmaking wins.

A fierce debater, she was known for her sharp comebacks when challenged on certain issues. She lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health failed and she sometimes became confused. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term in the next year. She had stepped down as the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee after the 2020 elections.

Some of Feinstein's most important lawmaking work came in 1994. The Senate approved her measure to stop the manufacturing and sales of some types of assault weapons. It was part of a crime bill that Clinton signed into law. Though the weapons ban ended 10 years later and wasn't replaced, it was an emotional win.

A Historic U.S. Senate Race

In 1990, Feinstein became the first woman picked to run for California governor by a major political party. Although she lost that race, the stage was set for her election to the Senate in 1992.

Feinstein worked with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S. senator.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco and graduated from college in 1955. In 1980, she married Richard Blum. He died in February 2022.

Feinstein is survived by her daughter, Katherine, and her granddaughter, Eileen. She also has three stepchildren.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who gave tributes to Feinstein. "Her beloved home state of California and our entire nation are better" because of her service, he said.

Feinstein was elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in 1969 and became its first female board president in 1978. That year, San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was gunned down alongside Supervisor Harvey Milk at City Hall by a disgruntled former supervisor. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. Later, she was one of California's first two female senators, the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Senate Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Feinstein's experiences colored her outlook throughout her five decades in politics.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she said in 2005.

Feinstein's efforts to work with Republicans helped her notch legislative wins throughout her career.

A fierce debater, the California senator was known for her sharp comebacks when challenged on issues she cared about. She lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health declined and she sometimes became confused when speaking publicly. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term the next year. She had stepped down as the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee after the 2020 elections.

A Historic U.S. Senate Race

One of Feinstein's most significant legislative accomplishments was early in her career. The Senate approved her amendment to ban the manufacturing and sales of certain types of assault weapons. It was part of a crime bill that Clinton signed into law in 1994. Though the assault weapons ban ended 10 years later and wasn't renewed, it was an emotional win after her experience with gun violence.

In 1990, she won the Democratic nomination for California governor and was the first female major-party nominee for the office.

Although she lost the election to Republican Pete Wilson, the stage was set for her election to the Senate.

Feinstein campaigned with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S. senator.

During Donald Trump's presidency, Feinstein became the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee in 2016 and led her party's messaging through three U.S. Supreme Court nominations.

Confirmation Hearings Caused Controversy

Feinstein closed out confirmation hearings for Justice Amy Coney Barrett by hugging and thanking Judiciary Committee Chair Lindsey Graham. He is a Republican from South Carolina. She called the hearings some of the best she's participated in.

Liberal groups opposed having Barrett replace the late liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Barrett is considered conservative, with Republicans supporting her. Some called for Feinstein to step down from committee leadership. Later, she announced she would remain on the committee, but step down as the top Democrat.

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco and graduated from Stanford University in 1955, with a bachelor's degree in history. In 1980, she married Richard Blum, who died in February 2022.

In addition to her daughter, Feinstein has a granddaughter, Eileen, and three stepchildren.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: A "true trailblazer": Senator Dianne Feinstein of California dies at age 90
levels.body:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Senator Dianne Feinstein of California, a centrist Democrat and champion of liberal causes who was elected to the Senate in 1992 and broke gender barriers throughout her long career in local and national politics, has died. She was 90.

Feinstein died on September 28, 2023, at her home in Washington, D.C., her office said on September 29. Tributes poured in all day. Opening the Senate floor, Majority Leader Chuck Schumer announced that "we lost a giant in the Senate."

"As the nation mourns this tremendous loss, we know how many lives she impacted and how many glass ceilings she shattered along the way," Schumer said, his voice cracking.

President Joe Biden, who served with Feinstein for years in the Senate, called her "a pioneering American," a "true trailblazer" and a "cherished friend."

Feinstein, the oldest sitting U.S. senator, was a passionate advocate for liberal priorities important to her state — including environmental protection, reproductive rights and gun control — but was also known as a pragmatic lawmaker who reached out to Republicans and sought middle ground.

Her death came after a bout of shingles sidelined her for more than two months earlier this year — an absence that drew frustration from her most liberal critics and launched an unsuccessful attempt by Democrats to temporarily replace her on the Senate Judiciary Committee. When she returned to the Senate in May, she was frail and using a wheelchair, voting only occasionally.

On September 29, her Senate desk was draped in black and topped with a vase of white roses. Senators gave tearful tributes as members of the California House delegation stood in the back of the chamber and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi sat in the gallery with Feinstein's daughter, Katherine.

Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell was one of several Republicans who gave tributes to the Democratic icon, calling her his friend. "Dianne was a trailblazer, and her beloved home state of California and our entire nation are better for her dogged advocacy and diligent service," McConnell said.

Biden said in a statement, "Dianne made her mark on everything from national security to the environment to protecting civil liberties. "Our country will benefit from her legacy for generations."

Former President Barack Obama also saluted her as "a trailblazer," and former President Bill Clinton called her a champion "of civil rights and civil liberties, environmental protection and strong national security."

She was elected to the San Francisco (California) Board of Supervisors in 1969 and became its first female board president in 1978, the year San Francisco Mayor George Moscone was gunned down alongside Supervisor Harvey Milk at City Hall by Dan White, a disgruntled former supervisor. Feinstein found Milk's body.

After Moscone's death, Feinstein became San Francisco's first female mayor. In the Senate, she was one of California's first two female senators, the first woman to head the Senate Intelligence Committee and the first woman to serve as the Judiciary Committee's top Democrat.

Although Feinstein was not always embraced by the feminist movement, her experiences colored her outlook throughout her five decades in politics.

"I recognize that women have had to fight for everything they have gotten, every right," she told The Associated Press in 2005, as the Judiciary Committee prepared to hold hearings on President George W. Bush's nomination of John Roberts to replace Sandra Day O'Connor on the U.S. Supreme Court.

"So I must tell you, I try to look out for women's rights. I also try to solve problems as I perceive them, with legislation, and reaching out where I can, and working across the aisle," she said.

Feinstein's bipartisan efforts helped her notch legislative wins throughout her career. But it also proved to be a liability in her later years in Congress, as her state became more liberal and as the Senate and the electorate became increasingly polarized.

A fierce debater who did not suffer fools, the California senator was long known for her verbal zingers and sharp comebacks when challenged on the issues about which she was most fervent. But she lost that edge in her later years in the Senate, as her health visibly declined and she sometimes became confused when answering questions or speaking publicly. In February 2023, she said she would not run for a sixth term the next year. And within weeks of that announcement, she was absent from the Senate for more than two months as she recovered from a bout of shingles.

Amid the concerns about her health, Feinstein stepped down as the top Democrat on the judiciary panel after the 2020 elections, just as her party was about to take the majority. In 2023, she said she would not serve as the Senate president pro tempore, or the most senior member of the majority party, even though she was in line to do so. The president pro tempore opens the Senate every day and holds other ceremonial duties.

One of Feinstein's most significant legislative accomplishments was early in her career, when the Senate approved her amendment to ban the manufacturing and sales of certain types of assault weapons as part of a crime bill that former President Clinton signed into law in 1994. Though the assault weapons ban expired 10 years later and was never renewed or replaced, it was a poignant win after her career had been significantly shaped by gun violence.

Feinstein became mayor of San Francisco after the 1978 slayings of Moscone and Milk, leading the city during one of the most turbulent periods in its history. Even her critics credited Feinstein with a calming influence, and she won reelection on her own to two four-year terms.

With her success and growing recognition statewide came visibility on the national political stage.

In 1984, Feinstein was viewed as a vice presidential possibility for Walter Mondale, but faced questions about the business dealings of her husband, Richard Blum. In 1990, she used news footage of her announcement of the assassinations of Moscone and Milk in a television ad that helped her win the Democratic nomination for California governor, making her the first female major-party gubernatorial nominee in the state's history.

Although she narrowly lost the general election to Republican Pete Wilson, the stage was set for her election to the Senate two years later to fill the Senate seat Wilson had vacated to run for governor.

Feinstein campaigned jointly with Barbara Boxer, who was running for the state's other U.S. Senate seat, and both won, benefiting from positive news coverage and excitement over their historic race. California had never had a female U.S.

senator, and female candidates and voters had been galvanized by the U.S. Supreme Court hearings in which the all-male Senate Judiciary Committee questioned Anita Hill about her sexual harassment allegations against nominee Clarence Thomas.

Feinstein was appointed to the judiciary panel and eventually the Senate Intelligence Committee, becoming the chairperson in 2009. She was the first woman to lead the intelligence panel, a high-profile perch that gave her a central oversight role over U.S. intelligence controversies, setbacks and triumphs, from the killing of Osama bin Laden to leaks about National Security Agency surveillance.

Under Feinstein's leadership, the intelligence committee conducted a wide-ranging, five-year investigation into CIA interrogation techniques during President George W. Bush's administration, including waterboarding of terrorism suspects at secret overseas prisons. The resulting 6,300-page "torture report" concluded among other things that waterboarding and other "enhanced interrogation techniques" did not provide key evidence in the hunt for bin Laden. A 525-page executive summary was released in late 2014, but the rest of the report has remained classified.

The Senate investigation was full of intrigue at the time, including documents that mysteriously disappeared and accusations traded between the Senate and the CIA that the other was stealing information. The drama was captured in a 2019 movie about the investigation called "The Report," and actor Annette Bening was nominated for a Golden Globe for her portrayal of Feinstein.

In the years since, Feinstein has continued to push aggressively for eventual declassification of the report.

"It's my very strong belief that one day this report should be declassified," Feinstein said. "This must be a lesson learned: that torture doesn't work."

During Donald Trump's presidency, Feinstein became the top Democrat on the judiciary panel in 2016 and led her party's messaging through three U.S. Supreme Court nominations.

Feinstein closed out confirmation hearings for Justice Amy Coney Barrett with an embrace of Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Lindsey Graham, a Republican from South Carolina, and a public thanks to him for a job well done. "This has been one of the best set of hearings that I've participated in," Feinstein said at the end of the hearings.

Liberal advocacy groups that had fiercely opposed Barrett's nomination to replace the late liberal icon Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg were furious and called for her to step down from the committee leadership.

A month later, Feinstein announced she would remain on the committee, but step down as the top Democrat. The senator, then 87 years old, did not say why. In a statement, she said she would "continue to do my utmost to bring about positive change in the coming years."

Feinstein was born on June 22, 1933, in San Francisco. She graduated from Stanford University in 1955, with a bachelor's degree in history. In 1980, she married investment banker Richard Blum, and thanks to his wealth, she was one of the richest members of the Senate. He died in February 2022.

In addition to her daughter, Feinstein has a granddaughter, Eileen, and three stepchildren.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Dolly Parton's contributions to literacy will outlive the star, just like she planned
levels.body:
Dolly Parton was a country music legend. But she was also proud to just be "the book lady."

In 1995, Parton created the Imagination Library. This program has given over 330 million books to kids everywhere.

A Literary Legacy

Parton died on Tuesday, August 25. She was 80 years old. Parton earned many awards in her career, including 10 Grammys. But she cared the most about helping young readers get books.

In 2023, the American Library Association recognized her work. They gave her a lifetime membership.

The Imagination Library mails free books to young children. They get a book every month until they turn 5.

Growing Up Dolly

Parton grew up in the town of Sevierville, Tennessee. She was the fourth of 12 kids. Her family lived in a one-room cabin with no electricity. Her father was a farmer and couldn't read or write. The only book they had was a Bible.

Parton's childhood made her want to start the Imagination Library. With her dad's help, she began close to home. She helped kids in her town love reading. She thought reading was the start of dreaming. Dreaming, she said, is the first step to success.

By 2000, the program spread across the country. By 2003, it had sent one million books to kids. Then the program launched in Canada in 2006, England in 2007, Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.

Melanie Florence is a writer from Canada. Her book, "Sarabeth's Garage," was picked by the Imagination Library. She grew up in a small town without a bookstore. She knows how special it is for a child to own a book.

Creating A Lasting Impact

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Dolly Parton's contributions to literacy will outlive the star, just like she planned
levels.body:
"Everywhere I go, the kids call me 'the book lady.'"

Dolly Parton wore the moniker like a badge of honor, and she earned it too. Through her Imagination Library program, launched by the Dollywood Foundation in 1995, she put more than 330 million books into the hands of children across America, Canada, the U.K., Australia and the Republic of Ireland.

The program is rooted in a childhood of poverty and illiteracy — roots that those who knew Parton said she never denied or abandoned.

A Literary Legacy

Parton, 80, died Tuesday after a brief battle with cancer. And although the country western superstar collected accolades — including 10 Grammy Awards, a National Medal of the Arts and two Academy Award nominations — across her storied career, Parton said her contributions to children's literacy were most precious to her.

In 2023, the American Library Association awarded the singer-songwriter, book lady and philanthropist its highest honor — lifetime membership — to recognize her lasting impact on literacy and inspiring a love of reading in children.

"Dolly Parton represented the very best of America," ALA President Maria McCauley told The Times on Tuesday, adding that, like people all over the world, she's been playing Parton's music since news of her death broke, particularly the song "I Can See the Light of a Clear Blue Morning."

"That song has so much resonance right now," she said, noting its lyrics capture a theme of resilience and faith in overcoming dark times.

"We want to make sure that Dolly's vision, that reading is for everyone, becomes a reality. That's something that we can all carry forward in memory of Dolly."

Parton's Imagination Library gifts a book a month to children signed up for the program from the time they are born until they are 5 years old. Parton described the program best when speaking with librarian Carla Hayden in 2018. "We send the book in the mail with their name on it. It's not in the care of Mom and Dad — it's got their little name on it, and they love to think, 'This is mine.' They wait at the mailbox. They get their little books, and to them, it's personal."

Growing Up Dolly

Parton understood the novelty of owning your very own book. Growing up in the Great Smoky Mountains town of Sevierville in east Tennessee, Parton was the fourth of 12 kids. Her father, a tobacco sharecropper, couldn't read or write, and the family lived in a one-room cabin with no electricity. There were no books in the home, aside from the Bible.

The singer's upbringing, particularly her father's illiteracy and his shame around what he considered a shortcoming, was what inspired her to launch the Imagination Library. With the help of her dad, they set out to foster a love of reading in the kids of Sevier County. Reading, she believed, was the gateway to dreaming, and dreaming, the first step in the path toward success.

By 2000, the program had expanded beyond the Smoky Mountains and into a nationwide movement. By 2003, the Imagination Library had mailed 1 million books to budding readers. After the United States, the gifting initiative launched in Canada in 2006, then the U.K. in 2007, Australia in 2013 and the Republic of Ireland in 2019.

The program operates on a shared funding model split between the Dollywood Foundation — which manages the central overhead, administration, and global book-selection strategy of the Imagination Library — and local community partners including businesses, school districts, small or large organizations, or individuals who share in the mission.

Selina Brown, a U.K. author whose book "My Rice Is Best" was selected by the Imagination Library this year, said that 14,000 copies had been distributed across the U.K. to children in underprivileged areas. "To know that my book has gone into the hands of young children across the U.K. is absolutely incredible," she told The Times.

Brown said that public figures often make shallow promises and vanity moves, but "with Dolly Parton, you can actually see her work manifest, and it really makes an impact. In the U.K. alone, there are children who do not have books in their house, and because of Dolly Parton, they now have their own library."

Canadian author Melanie Florence, who penned "Sarabeth's Garage" — another of Imagination Library's picks — also grew up in a small town, with no bookstore, during a time with no online retailers. "If that had existed when I was a kid, being gifted a book that you get to keep, it's a big thing, especially for a kid like I was, who just lived to read," Florence told The Times.

"I think that's such a beautiful legacy," Florence said, "her music and this spirit of generosity."

Creating A Lasting Impact

But it's also a working legacy that Parton built to last, according to Dollywood Foundation's president, Jeff Conyers.

"Dolly's legacy was never meant to be something we simply preserve or look back upon," Conyers said. "She built things that could keep doing good in the world."

Conyers said the foundation was set to "make certain the love at the heart of her work continues reaching children, families and communities long into the future."

Although the foundation is heartbroken after Parton's death, he said, "the mission she gave us is as clear today as it has ever been, and we will carry it forward for generations to come."

Washington, D.C., Councilmember Charles Allen said he was visiting family in east Tennessee more than decade ago when his 2-year-old niece went tottering off toward the mailbox. When her parents brought her back in, she was holding a book with her name on it. Allen said his brother had signed her up for Parton's Imagination Library at the hospital just after she was born — "right then and there."

Allen said he was inspired by "the joy on my own niece's face when she opened up a book with her name on it" to write a D.C. law called "Books From Birth."

"We basically borrowed that program and then partnered with them," he said. "And now every child in D.C. from the time they're born 'til they're 5 years old gets a free book delivered."

Allen said that the program is now 10 years old, and 4 million books have been distributed to about 100,000 kids: "It's made a big impact."

Allen met with Parton years ago and said she never forgot her roots.

"Watching her own parents struggle with literacy and kind of hiding it, she realized very quickly the power that she had as this just massive cultural and musical star," he said, adding that she was going to use that power for something that would outlast her. "It'll outlast me. It'll outlast everybody."

Children of D.C. "they know Dolly Parton," he added. "They know she's the lady that delivered the books. I have all the confidence in the world that she is smiling somewhere, knowing that so many people think of her as the book lady. That she was going to battle illiteracy, one kid, one family, one household at a time."

In 2018, Parton donated her 100 millionth book to the Library of Congress.

During the ceremony Hayden, the librarian, asked the country star if she ever thought she'd be known so widely as "the book lady."

Parton responded with her signature self-deprecating wit and wisdom: "I never thought about being the book lady — the painted lady, yes. The overexaggerated, overdressed lady — yes. But that just goes to show you that you can't judge a book by looking at the cover, right? Or even a 100 millionth book by looking at the cover."

In September, 336,004,951 books will have been distributed through Imagination Library. More than 3.6 million families have been registered globally.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Drone footage shows rare bird's-eye view of stingrays off New York coast
levels.body:
Video of a large group of stingrays has captivated people. The video was taken by a drone camera off the coast of Long Island, New York. It offers a rare bird's-eye view of the animals. Though scientists say rays have visited the area for decades.

The footage was taken on August 7 by Joanna Steidle. She is a professional drone pilot based in the area. She is known for her aerial ocean shots. The footage shows a large group of cownose rays gliding through the water.

Steidle said: "While filming these I can feel my heartbeat and breathing align with their wings flapping....it is in these moments I feel completely connected and present."

A Fever Of Rays

The video appears to show hundreds of cownose rays. A group of rays is sometimes called a fever. Rays are a large migratory fish. These rays are named for their heads, which look like a cow's nose. They have a large wingspan, stretching up to 3 feet. They are shy creatures that eat mostly clams and other bottom-dwelling animals. Stingrays are related to sharks. Like sharks, rays do not have bones. Instead, they have cartilage. That's the same material that you feel inside the tip of your nose.

Long Island is a narrow island off the coast of New York City. The rays usually arrive in the warmer months. They follow water temperatures that are right for them as they migrate north from warmer waters farther south.

Ocean temperatures are rising rapidly around the world. This is driven largely by climate change, scientists say. Warmer waters could be behind the changes to the rays' migration. Climate change is the significant change in Earth's climate over a long period of time. It can happen naturally. But today data shows that climate change is largely caused by human activities. This includes the burning of fossil fuels—such as oil for cars—and the clearing of forests. Carbon dioxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. It traps heat in Earth's atmosphere. This makes temperatures rise, both on land and in the ocean.

Dean Grubbs is a marine biologist. He says that warmer ocean temperatures may be allowing the rays to travel farther north. "Now, as ocean temperatures warm, the northern migrations of a lot of species are shifting further and further north."

Not New To The Area

Cownose rays, however, are not new to Long Island.

For the last 25 years, large groups of cownose rays have traveled to the waters off New York and New Jersey. That's according to Thomas Grothues, another marine biologist. He added that people often think rays are sharks. The rays' wingtips stick out of the water, like a shark's fin.

Matthew Ajemian is a scientist. He said cownose rays have been documented in New York's waters since the 1800s. He added that drones have changed the way wildlife is observed. It's much easier to take pictures and video of animals in the wild today.

Researchers say drones are especially helpful for studying cownose rays. Drones can help scientists estimate cownose ray populations. The fish spend a lot of time near the surface. This makes it easier to see them by drone.

Describing the rays from an earlier video, Steidle said on Instagram: "While filming these I can feel my heartbeat and breathing align with their wings flapping....it is in these moments I feel completely connected and present."

A Fever Of Rays

The video appears to show hundreds of cownose rays swimming in a group, which is sometimes called a fever. Rays are a large migratory fish. These rays are named for their heads, which look like a cow's nose. With wingspans stretching up to 3 feet, the shy and non-aggressive cownose ray feeds mostly on clams and other bottom-dwelling creatures. Stingrays are related to sharks. Like sharks, rays do not have bones. Instead, they have cartilage, the same material that you feel inside the tip of your nose.

Long Island is a narrow island off the southeast coast of New York City. The rays typically arrive in its coastal waters during the warmer months. They follow water temperatures that suit them as they migrate north from waters farther south.

Ocean temperatures are rising rapidly around the world, driven largely by climate change, scientists say. Warmer waters could be behind the changes in the timing and range of the rays' migration. Climate change is the significant change in Earth's climate over a long period of time. It can happen naturally. But today data shows that climate change is largely caused by human activities. This includes the burning of fossil fuels—such as oil for cars—and the clearing of forests. Carbon dioxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. It acts as a greenhouse gas, trapping heat in Earth's atmosphere. This makes temperatures rise, both on land and in the ocean.

Dean Grubbs is a marine biologist at Florida State University. He says that the sighting was probably due to the rays traveling farther north as ocean temperatures warm. "Now, as ocean temperatures warm, the northern migrations of a lot of species are shifting further and further north."

Ryan Wallace is a professor at Adelphi University in New York. He said cownose rays generally prefer water temperatures between 70 and 79 Fahrenheit. As water in New York reaches those temperatures earlier in the spring and stays warm longer, the rays could migrate north earlier and remain in the region longer.

Not New To The Area

Cownose rays, however, are not new to Long Island.

For the last 25 years, large groups of cownose rays have traveled to the waters off New York and New Jersey. That's according to Thomas Grothues, a marine biologist at Rutgers University. "They are 'newly' discovered by beachgoers every year and are frequently mistaken for sharks because their wingtips protrude."

Matthew Ajemian is a professor at Florida Atlantic University. He said cownose rays have been documented in New York's waters since the 1800s. He added that drones have changed the way wildlife is observed.

People are capturing more photos and videos of everything everywhere, including animals in the wild. But just because we have more photos and videos of certain animals doesn't necessarily mean there are more of them in an area.

Kevin Weng is a marine biologist at the College of William & Mary in Virginia. He said drones are particularly valuable for observing cownose rays from above. But researchers need to account for where and how often those observations are made.

"Drones, amazing. What we need to understand is the distribution of observation effort," he said.

Researchers say drones are helpful for studying cownose rays. That's especially true when it comes to estimating their size and movement.

"Drones are definitely giving us views and a perspective we haven't seen before for a lot of species," Grubbs said. He added that aerial drones are especially useful for estimating cownose ray populations. The fish spend a lot of time near the surface. This makes it easier to see them by drone.

With wingspans stretching up to 3 feet, the shy and non-aggressive cownose ray feeds mostly on clams and other bottom-dwelling creatures. Stingrays are related to sharks, and like sharks, rays do not have bones. Instead, they have cartilage, the same material that you feel inside the tip of your nose.

Long Island is a narrow island that appears to jut off the southeast coast of New York City. The rays typically arrive in its coastal waters during the warmer months. They follow water temperatures that suit them as they migrate north from waters farther south.

Ocean temperatures are rising rapidly around the world, driven largely by climate change, scientists say. Warmer waters could be contributing to changes in the timing and range of the rays' migration. Climate change is the significant change in Earth's climate over a long period of time. It can happen naturally, but today data shows that climate change is largely caused by human activities. This includes the burning of fossil fuels—such as oil for cars—and the clearing of forests. Carbon dioxide is released when fossil fuels are burned, and traps heat in Earth's atmosphere. This makes temperatures rise, both on land and in the ocean.

Dean Grubbs is a marine biologist at Florida State University. He says that the sighting was probably due to the rays shifting their migration farther north as ocean temperatures warm. "Now, as ocean temperatures warm, the northern migrations of a lot of species are shifting further and further north."

Blacktip sharks are an example of another species moving north, according to Grubbs. While that species was rarely seen north of North Carolina in the 1970s, he said, it had become common in Virginia and Delaware by the 1990s. Now it is frequently found even farther north, in New England, during warm summers.

Ryan Wallace is a professor at Adelphi University in New York. He said cownose rays generally prefer water temperatures between 70 and 79 Fahrenheit. As those preferred temperatures reach New York earlier in the spring and last longer, the rays could migrate north earlier and remain in the region longer.

Not New To The Area

Cownose rays, however, are not new to Long Island.

For the last 25 years, large groups of cownose rays have frequented the waters off the coasts of Long Island, New York and Long Beach Island, New Jersey. That's according to Thomas Grothues, a marine biologist at Rutgers University, in New Jersey. "They are 'newly' discovered by beachgoers every year and are frequently mistaken for sharks because their wingtips protrude."

Matthew Ajemian is a professor at Florida Atlantic University. He said cownose rays have been documented in New York's waters since the 1800s. He added that researchers must also consider how advances in drone technology have changed the way wildlife is observed by the general public and experts alike.

"People are seeing them, I think, more frequently [in real life and online]. We also have to be aware of our observer bias too, because it's so much easier for us to capture these types of things [nowadays]," Ajemian said. Meaning, just because we have more footage of certain animals, it doesn't necessarily mean there are more of them in an area.

Kevin Weng is a marine biologist at the College of William & Mary in Virginia. He said drones are particularly valuable for observing cownose rays from above. But researchers need to account for where and how often those observations are made.

"Drones, amazing. What we need to understand is the distribution of observation effort," he said.

Researchers say drones offer a valuable new tool for studying cownose rays. That's especially true when it comes to estimating their size and movement.

"Drones are definitely giving us views and a perspective we haven't seen before for a lot of species. Estimating population abundances for cownose rays is particularly difficult because they travel in such large schools," Grubbs said. He added that aerial drones are especially useful for estimating cownose ray populations because the fish spend so much time near the surface.

Drone footage of dozens of stingrays in the ocean off New York has captivated beachgoers and marine enthusiasts, offering a rare bird's-eye view of a species that scientists say has visited the area for decades.
