The sighting raises the possibility that the species is migrating farther north and appearing in the area more consistently as ocean temperatures rise, or could simply indicate that increased drone use is making everyday wildlife activity more visible to the public, various experts said.

A Fever Of Rays

The video appears to show hundreds of cownose rays swimming in a group that some refer to by the collective noun "fever", as in a fever of rays. The species is a large, migratory elasmobranch, a subclass of cartilaginous fish, named for their distinctive high-lobed head resembling a cow's nose. With wingspans stretching up to 3ft (1 meter), the shy and non-aggressive cownose ray feeds mostly on bivalves, including clams and other bottom-dwelling prey.

The rays typically arrive in Long Island waters in the warmer months, following water temperatures that suit them as they migrate north from the Chesapeake Bay, the mid-Atlantic estuary, and other waters farther south.

As ocean temperatures rise rapidly around the world, driven largely by climate change, scientists say, warmer waters could be contributing to changes in the timing and range of the rays' migration.

Speaking about the sighting, Dean Grubbs, associate director of research at Florida State University's coastal and marine laboratory, said: "This occurrence probably does represent a northern shift in the migration due to temperature. Historically, there would be some cownose rays that would make it up to Cape Cod or so in small numbers during warm years, but the big schools would terminate the northern migration around Chesapeake Bay. Now, as ocean temperatures warm, the northern migrations of a lot of species are shifting further and further north."

Grubbs pointed to blacktip sharks as a precedent for a northward shift. While that species was rarely seen north of North Carolina in the 1970s, he said, it had become common in Virginia and Delaware by the 1990s and is now frequently found in New England during warm summers.

Ryan Wallace, an assistant professor of environmental studies and sciences at Adelphi University, said cownose rays generally prefer water temperatures 70-79F (approximately 21-26C), meaning New York's warm, coastal waters could drive them to migrate north earlier in the spring and remain in the region longer.

"Water temperature kind of dictates that timing, and so that can then trigger – as the drone footage had captured – these large fevers, which can be hundreds, even thousands in some cases," Wallace said.

Not New To The Area

Cownose rays, however, are not new to Long Island.

"The cownose rays are very common, often in very large groups, along beaches of Long Island, New York and Long Beach Island, New Jersey, in the surf and also in the quiet bay waters behind the barrier islands for at least the last 25 years," said Thomas Grothues, associate research professor at Rutgers University, in New Jersey. "They are 'newly' discovered by beachgoers every year and are frequently mistaken for sharks because their wingtips protrude."

Matthew Ajemian, associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute, said cownose rays have been documented in New York's waters since the 1800s. While there may be more public sightings, he said, researchers must also consider how advances in drone technology have changed the way wildlife is observed by the general public and experts alike.

"People are seeing them, I think, more frequently [in real life and online]. We also have to be aware of our observer bias too, because it's so much easier for us to capture these types of things [nowadays]," Ajemian said, adding: "We have drone technology, which really helps with some of the capacity to see things that are relatively rare, although I guess the correct term for its abundance within New York is 'uncommon'."

Echoing Ajemian, Kevin Weng, an associate professor at College of William & Mary Virginia Institute of Marine Science, said drones are particularly valuable for observing cownose rays from above, but researchers need to account for where and how often those observations are made.

"Drones, amazing. What we need to understand is the distribution of observation effort," he said.

Still, researchers say drones offer a valuable new tool for studying cownose rays, especially when it comes to estimating their size and movement.

"Drones are definitely giving us views and a perspective we haven't seen before for a lot of species. Estimating population abundances for cownose rays is particularly difficult because they travel in such large schools. I think aerial drones may be a useful tool for estimating abundances of species like cownose rays that do spend a substantial amount of time near the surface," Grubbs said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Farmers bring 100-year-old heirloom okra to Toronto, Canada
levels.body:
Nicole Austin grew up in Canada. Her family was from Jamaica. But in Canada, they couldn't find many foods from back home, like okra. Her grandmother grew some plants from home in the backyard if she had the right seeds.

Today Austin is growing a very old type of okra on a rooftop in Toronto, Canada. Okra is a vegetable. The most common kind is green. Austin is growing a type of okra called white velvet. It has been passed down from person to person for years.

Joining A Rooftop Farm

In 2021, Austin started working on a rooftop farm in the city of Toronto. She also started a program that helps Black residents in the city grow foods that are important to them and help them stay healthy.

Austin wanted to grow foods from from African and from people whose family come from Africa but who now live all over the world. Okra probably came from Africa. It is used in West African and Jamaican stews or soups. It is a main ingredient in the stew gumbo, enjoyed in the U.S.. Fried okra is a popular dish in southern and soul foods.

Okra comes in many colors and forms. Some okra is red, some is green or purplish. They come in different shapes and sizes as well. These differences can occur in nature as the plant changes over time to fit certain conditions, like weather or nutrients in the soil. This is called natural selection. Or it may happen as humans grow the plant. They pick and choose the traits they want. Then they use those plants to make new plants with those traits. This is called artificial selection.

Green okra is the most common type of okra in stores today. But it is less common in Canada, which has a small Black community. Okra grows in warmer parts of the world. So it's also not usually found in colder places, like Canada.

Many plants that like warm weather cannot often survive in cold temperatures. Freezing weather can turn the water inside the plant into ice. This breaks the plant's cell walls and ruins the plant's tissue. The plant then can no longer take in water or nutrients and dies.

But Austin's okra is doing well.

A Story Of Strength

"I was really drawn to and really inspired by the history of this heirloom," Austin said. Heirloom seeds are open-pollinated plants. These plants grow when pollen is moved by the wind or by insects. They look the same as their parent plants. In other words, they don't change. They can look the same as ones that were grown decades, or even a hundred years, ago.

White velvet okra was once popular in parts of the American South. But about fifty years ago, big farms starting taking over many small farms. These big farms grew strong crops that made more money. By 2015, white velvet okra was barely grown or sold in the United States, unlike green okra.

Sharing Seeds, Sharing History

The white velvet okra Austin will grow this year comes from seeds she saved from last year's crop. Growing seeds is like magic, she said. The seeds, once picked, are dormant. It's almost like they are asleep.

They are waiting for the right time to start growing. This stops the seed from growing at the wrong time, like when it is too cold. But during this dormant time, the plant is still alive. Even in cold Toronto, those same seeds can grow many more white velvet okra plants. And they will.

levels.body:
When Nicole Austin was growing up in Oshawa, Canada, her Jamaican family couldn't find foods from back home, like okra. Her grandmother grew some plants in the backyard if she had the right seeds.

Today Austin is growing a very old variety of okra on rooftop in Toronto, Canada. This okra is called white velvet okra. It has been passed down from person to person. It connects the farm with many generations of growers around the world. Thanks to Austin and seed growers, this vegetable has traveled about 1,000 miles and 100 years.

Joining A Rooftop Farm

In 2021, Austin joined the rooftop Urban Farm at Toronto Metropolitan University. She started the Black Food Sovereignty Initiative. This program helps Black people in the community grow foods that are important to their culture, build their community and stay healthy.

Austin wanted to start by growing five crops with roots in the African diaspora—people of African descent who live around the world. She knew okra should be on the farm's list. The vegetable probably came from Africa. Okra is used in West African and Jamaican stews or soups. It is a main ingredient in gumbo. Fried okra is a popular dish in southern and soul foods.

Okra comes in many colors and forms: red, green or purplish; with spines or without; long pods or shorter, stubby ones. Varieties like these can occur in nature as the plant responds slowly over many years to conditions, such as climate or nutrients in the soil. This is called natural selection. Or it may occur through cultivation as humans pick and choose the traits they want, and use those plants to produce new plants with those desired traits. This is called artificial selection, because humans help the process.

Green okra varieties have become the most common. But this vegetable is very diverse. It's less common in Canada, which has a small Black community. Okra grows in warmer climates, so it's also not usually found in colder places, like Canada.

Many plants that like warm weather often cannot handle cold temperatures. Freezing climates can turn the water inside the plant into ice. This breaks open the plant's cell walls—the parts that give the cell support—and ruins the plant's tissue. The plant then can no longer take in water or nutrients, and dies.

But Austin's okra is doing well.

A Story Of Strength

"I was really drawn to and really inspired by the history of this heirloom," Austin said. Heirloom seeds are "open-pollinated seed varieties that have been in existence and saved continuously since usually pre-World War II," said Chris Smith, author a book about okra.

Open-pollinated plants reproduce when pollen is moved naturally, like by the wind or insects. These plants have traits that are passed from one generation to the next. This means the offspring look just like their parents. An open-pollinated plant can look the same as one that was grown decades, or even a hundred years, before.

In the past, white velvet okra was grown around Mississippi, Louisiana, Georgia, and Alabama. It was so popular that people wanted it to be planted and shared more widely.

But despite how prized it once was, the unique, fuzzy white velvet okra was cast aside for more traditional green varieties. This happened because regional food plants were being replaced by global farming. Over the last 50 years, big farms took over smaller, local farms. They planted strong crops that made more money. This led to more crops being grown, but it also destroyed many traditional local crops. It also reduced biodiversity, or variety of living things. With less variety in traits, crops might be more at risk from diseases, pests or changes in the environment.

By 2015, white velvet okra was barely grown and sold in the United States, unlike green okra.

Sharing Seeds, Sharing History

The white velvet okra Austin will grow this year comes from seeds she saved from last year's crop. Growing and preserving seeds is like magic, she said. The seeds, once harvested, are dormant. They may look as if they're not doing anything, but they are waiting patiently for the right conditions, like enough water and warmer temperatures.

Then they will start to sprout. This prevents the seed from sprouting at the wrong time, like when the weather is still too cold, and dying. But during this dormant period the plant is still alive. Even in chilly Toronto, those same seeds can grow many more white velvet okra plants. And they will.

levels.title: Farmers bring 100-year-old heirloom okra to Toronto, Canada
levels.body:
When Nicole Austin was growing up in Oshawa, Canada, her Jamaican family couldn't find the foods they enjoyed back on the island. No callaloo, garden eggs or okra. Austin's grandmother grew certain things in her backyard, but only if she had the necessary seeds.

"It's often small-scale farmers, farmers of color, Black farmers that make sure that these foods that are culturally significant to us are available, that we grow them, that we share them," Austin said. "It wasn't until I'm in these spaces now that I realized how important the place is of farmers of color and Black farmers to make sure that these food histories are maintained and celebrated and shared."

She had planned to become a registered dietitian after getting a degree in geology but, while working part-time at the Toronto Metropolitan University's (TMU) Centre for Studies in Food Security, Austin realized that she was most drawn to food justice, security and advocacy.

Today, Austin is one of those small-scale farmers of color, something she never expected.

And she's growing a very old variety of okra on a downtown Toronto rooftop, connecting Africa, the Caribbean, Canada and the American south. As an heirloom passed from person to person, white velvet okra connected the farm with generations of growers around the world. Thanks to Austin and seed growers, this variety has made a long journey across space and time, traveling about 1,000 miles and a 100 years, to be cultivated and enjoyed in Toronto.

Joining A Rooftop Farm

In 2021, Austin joined TMU's Urban Farm to develop the Black Food Sovereignty Initiative and its Harvest Collective and Learning Circle programs. Part of the initiative's mission is to foster self- determination, community and good health in Black residents via the cultivation of culturally relevant foods. The programs engage both the TMU and greater Toronto area's Black communities through sharing farm-to-table foods.

Austin wanted to start by growing five culturally significant crops with roots in the African diaspora. She knew okra should be on the farm's list. The vegetable probably originated or was domesticated somewhere in Africa. It stars in many west African and Jamaican stews or soups, and it is an essential ingredient in their American cousin, gumbo. Its fried form is a staple on southern and soul food menus.

Okra comes in many colors and forms: red, green or purplish; with spines or without; long pods or shorter, stubby ones. Green okra varieties have come to dominate the market, but there is a world of diversity within this vegetable that's very prized by many African and Asian diaspora communities.

It's less common in Canada, which has a smaller Black community (some 4% compared to about 14% in the US) and a colder climate that's not a natural fit for this warm-weather plant. But a University of Guelph study found it tops the list of the 13 most sought-after vegetables for the three largest ethnic groups in the Toronto metropolitan area.

Every season, Austin buys seeds from Truelove Seeds, a US-based seed company that curates an African diaspora seed collection. Through its site, she found white velvet okra, named for its fuzzy pods and a lack of spines common to many varieties of the vegetable.

A Story Of Resilience

"I was really drawn to and really inspired by the history of this heirloom," Austin said, "[which] is carrying the genetic makeup of the generations before it."

Heirlooms are "open-pollinated seed varieties that have been in existence and saved continuously since usually pre-World War II", said Chris Smith, author of The Whole Okra.

"When [people] talk about heirlooms or think about heirlooms, it's something that has maybe a people or a place attached to it and has, in some ways, survived the test of time in that they're still around today," he said.

Historically, according to the Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity, white velvet okra was cultivated around Mississippi, Louisiana, Georgia and Alabama. It was so popular that citizens called for its commercial cultivation.

Austin sees white velvet okra as a way to "reach out across time and space". She's not from the American south nor is she Black American, but the plant connects her to those parts of the African diaspora. Initially introduced in 1890 by Peter Henderson & Company of New York, white velvet okra is a distinctly southern vegetable, grown and consumed by many people in the region.

But, despite how prized it once was, the unique, fuzzy white velvet okra was cast aside for more traditional green varieties, following a trend of regional food plants being pushed out by globalized agriculture.

By 2015, white velvet okra was not commercially produced in the United States, never having been grown on as large a scale as its green cousins.

"White velvet okra is fuzzy. It's tender. It's delicious. To me, it's a variety that's worth celebrating, saving and telling the story of our people's resiliency in food sovereignty, sharing knowledge," Austin said. "I like what this food item can symbolize in terms of resiliency, in terms of celebrating heritage."

The variety, whose notable characteristics made it a beloved vegetable in deep southern states, has been added to the Ark of Taste, which, since 1996, has operated as a "living catalogue" of foods facing extinction.

The seeds are now available through a number of small US-based specialty growers, like Truelove Seeds and Sistah Seeds, where founder Amirah Mitchell grows the crop.

Mitchell also likes the unique texture of white velvet okra's pod and its flavor, which she said "is maybe a touch less vegetal than some of the green okras".

She has grown the variety for several years, since she ran a seedkeeping program in which students identified and grew a crop or variety they connected to their heritage. White velvet okra made the cut.

"Okra is one of the African vegetables that has survived, that has kept a cultural connection to African-descended peoples that survived the Middle Passage," she said. "There were a lot of crops that were not able to adapt to the climate of North America and were not able to thrive here and, therefore, were lost to the diets of African people who were brought here. Those crops that were able to survive that journey and were able to survive in cultural memory and cuisine and continue to be part of the diets and the food culture of African Americans are really quite special."

Sharing Seeds, Sharing History

Preserving and sharing the seeds is engaging in a way of "practicing our living history", Austin said. She is committed to making sure that others have the chance to grow the crop, something that is both a cultural and scientific mission.

"A big, big part of food sovereignty is actually saving seeds and sharing seeds across our community," she said. "There's only about four companies that basically have propriety over about 80% of commercially available seeds, which is insane. The fact that you can even put a patent and own seed production is bizarre to me. It's part of that broken food system."

Okra is also a crop that is near-essential for cultural reconnection work, given its significant history in the US south, African diasporic communities, and also in south-east Asia and India.

"People are in a moment of trying to reconnect with the foods of their cultures, and okra belongs to a lot of people," said Smith. He's sent okra seeds to growers in Scotland, England and the American west coast.

The white velvet okra Austin will grow this year comes from seeds she saved from last year's crop. Growing and preserving seeds is like magic, she said. The seeds, once harvested, are dormant; they may look as if they're not doing anything.

But ultimately everything about the plant, from the fruit to the seeds, is living. Even all the way up in Toronto, those same seeds can grow many more white velvet okra plants.

And they will.

"I brought [these seeds] up from people that grow them in the American south. I was able to grow them in Toronto. And now I'm able to share those seeds to my network," Austin said. "They can then do that in turn. It's just one component of building a food sovereignty movement, but I really love what white velvet okra symbolizes for history, heritage, resiliency and self-determination."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Four young mathematicians awarded the 2026 Fields Medals
levels.body:
The Fields Medal is an important prize in math. It awards mathematicians who are doing important work. This year, four mathematicians won. They are Hong Wang, Yu Deng, John Pardon, and Jacob Tsimerman. They work at different universities in New York, Illinois and Ontario, Canada.

Wang is only the third woman to win. The first two women were Maryam Mirzakhani and Maryna Viazovska. Wang and Deng are only the second and third winners born in China.

The award is named for John Charles Fields, a Canadian mathematician. He wanted to bring mathematicians from around the world together. The Fields Medals are given out every four years.

They are for researchers under 40 years old. These mathematicians work on very advanced math. But it builds on the math they first learned in grade school.

Hong Wang

Hong Wang is 34 years old. She has made important contributions to algebra and geometry. She studies groups of wavelike equations. She used them to explore how shapes fill space.

Wang remembers when Mirzakhani won the medal in 2014. She was very excited that Mirzakhani was the first woman to win.

Yu Deng

Deng received an award for his work on how fluids move. Mathematicians had tried to understand how fluids could act in two different ways. Deng's award is for showing that the math equations for fluids at different sizes are actually the same.

With this award, there are three times more Chinese-born Fields Medal winners. China has spent many years making math education better. Today, there are talented young mathematicians from China at top universities.

John Pardon

Pardon won his award for his work on knot theory. In math, a knot is a loop of rope that cannot be untangled without cutting it. There are many ways to tie a piece of string, with the two ends glued together afterward. These forms are hard to tell apart. Pardon showed that no loops, even if very tangled, could fit in a certain bendy shape.

Jacob Tsimerman

Tsimerman loved math from a very young age. His grandfather would give him simple math puzzles to solve. His mother gave him her high school math textbook to read.

In 2021, he and two friends solved a big math problem called the André-Oort conjecture. This problem is about finding answers to math questions where all the numbers are whole numbers. This is very advanced math. But it is important.

The Fields Medal is a 14-karat gold medal. The award comes with 15,000 Canadian dollars (about 10,000 US dollars). Receiving the award is a huge achievement. It is very respected. Tsimerman wants to use his award to focus on a new area: artificial intelligence. "I think that there are big changes coming to our world, and I want people to focus on that," he says.

levels.title: Four young mathematicians awarded the 2026 Fields Medals
levels.body:
Math's most important prizes were announced on July 23: the Fields Medal, which recognizes achievements by mathematicians. This year, four prizes were awarded.

The winners were Hong Wang, Yu Deng, John Pardon, and Jacob Tsimerman. They work at different universities in New York, Illinois and Ontario, Canada.

Wang is only the third woman to win, after mathematicians Maryam Mirzakhani and Maryna Viazovska in 2014 and 2022. Wang and Deng are only the second and third Chinese-born winners.

The awards are named for John Charles Fields. He was a Canadian mathematician who pushed to create the awards in the 1920s to bring the international math community together. The Fields are awarded only every four years. They only go to researchers who are under 40 years old. These mathematicians work on very advanced math. But it is theoretical work that builds on the math they first learned in grade school.

Hong Wang

At 34 years old, Hong Wang has made important contributions to algebra and geometry. She was awarded for her work with Joshua Zahl on the Kakeya conjecture.

The Kakeya conjecture is the answer to a math problem. It involves swirling a pencil around in the air so that it points in every direction once while using as little space as possible. Wang and Zahl showed the smallest space needed for this.

Wang remembers being excited when Mirzakhani became the first woman to win a Fields medal in 2014.

Yu Deng

Deng received an award for his work on how fluids move. A fluid is any a substance that can flow from place to place and through holes or gaps in containers. It contains many molecules (groups of atoms stuck together) bouncing off one another like tiny balls. But a fluid also moves as one continuous whole. Mathematicians had tried to understand how fluids could move in these two different ways. Deng's award is for showing that the math equations for fluids at different sizes are actually the same.

With this year's awards, Deng and Wang have now tripled the total number of Chinese-born Fields Medal winners. China has spent many years improving math education. This has led to a group of talented young mathematicians at top universities.

John Pardon

Pardon received his award for his work on knot theory. In math, a knot is a loop of rope that cannot be untangled without cutting the rope. There are many ways to tie a piece of string, with the two ends glued together afterward. These forms are hard to sort out. Two knotted strings might look very different, but they can be made to match, so mathematicians try to find ways to tell them apart. Pardon proved that no loops, no matter how tangled, could fit within a certain measure of how bendy the loop was.

Jacob Tsimerman

Tsimerman loved math from a very young age. "My parents recognized, by the time I was three, that I was super into it," he says. "I never really considered not being a mathematician." His grandfather would give him simple math puzzles to solve. When his mother noticed his early interest in negative numbers, she offered him her high school math textbook to explore. "It just became like recreation for me, long before it was a career," Tsimerman says.

In 2021, he and two collaborators proved the André-Oort conjecture, which involves finding solutions to equations where all the variables are whole numbers. (Equations are mathematical sentences with an equal sign. Variables are symbols that stand for an unknown quantity in an equation.) This is advanced, theoretical math, but it is very important in mathematics today.

The Fields Medal itself is 14-karat gold, and the award comes with 15,000 Canadian dollars (about 10,000 US dollars). But it is incredibly prestigious. Tsimerman wants to use his share to focus on a new area: artificial intelligence. "I think that there are big changes coming to our world, and I want people to focus on that," he says. "One of the many scary things about AI is that we don't really understand the system very well." Tsimerman hopes pure mathematics can change that.

levels.title: Four young mathematicians awarded the 2026 Fields Medals
levels.body:
Math's most prestigious prizes were announced on July 23: the Fields Medal, which recognizes achievements by mathematicians. This year, four prizes were awarded to mathematicians for work ranging from the theory of knots to the motion of fluids.

The winners were Hong Wang of New York University and France's Institute of Advanced Scientific Studies. They also included Yu Deng of the University of Chicago, in Illinois and John Pardon of Stony Brook University in New York. And they included Jacob Tsimerman of the University of Toronto in Ontario, Canada.

In the awards' 90-year history, Wang is only the third woman to win one, after mathematicians Maryam Mirzakhani and Maryna Viazovska in 2014 and 2022. Wang and Deng are only the second and third Chinese-born recipients.

The awards, often referred to as math's Nobel Prizes, are named for John Charles Fields. He was a Canadian mathematician who led the push to create the awards in the 1920s to bring the international math community together. But unlike the Nobels, the Fields are awarded only every four years and, starting in 1966, only go to researchers who are under 40 years old. These mathematicians work on math at the highest level. But it is theoretical work that builds on the math that these experts first learned in grade school.

Hong Wang

At age 34, Hong Wang's work in both algebra and geometry had already transformed both subjects. She explored collections of wavelike equations and used them to explore how shapes fill space. In particular, a 2025 proof (an argument in mathematical terms) of the Kakeya conjecture that she co- authored with mathematician Joshua Zahl.

The Kakeya conjecture is the answer to a mathematical game: swirl your pencil around in the air so that it points in every direction exactly once while also swiveling it through as little space as possible. Wang and Zahl showed the smallest space needed for this.

Wang remembers being excited when Mirzakhani became the first woman to win a Fields medal in 2014.

Yu Deng

In 2024 and 2025, he and his co-authors published a series of papers that marked a huge achievement in math and physics. The motion of fluids has always seemed contradictory. A fluid is a chaotic jumble of molecules bouncing off one another like billiard balls. But a fluid also follows laws of motion as if it were one continuous whole.

Mathematicians had tried — and largely failed — for more than a century to understand how fluids could behave in these two different ways. Deng and his collaborators proved that the equations describing fluids at different scales are actually the same.

With this year's awards, Deng and Wang have now tripled the total number of Chinese-born Fields Medalists. China has spent decades investing in math education. That has led to a group of talented young mathematicians at the top universities. "I'm working mostly just as myself," Deng says, "but I'm also happy that I'm one of the first of this new generation to get this recognition."

John Pardon

Pardon's was awarded for his work on knot theory. A knot, in the mathematical sense, is as a loop of rope that cannot be untangled without cutting the rope. There are many different ways a piece of string can be tied, with the two loose strands glued together afterward. These many forms are difficult to sort. Two knotted-up strings might look totally different yet, through elaborate manipulations, be made to match. So mathematicians try to develop methods to tell them apart. Pardon proved that no loops, no matter how tangled, could fit within a certain measure of how bendy the loop was.

Jacob Tsimerman

Tsimerman loved math from an age at which most children are barely aware it even exists. "My parents recognized, by the time I was three, that I was super into it," he says. "I never really considered not being a mathematician." His grandfather would give him simple mathematical puzzles to work with, and when his mother noticed his early fascination with negative numbers, she offered him her high school math textbook to thumb through. "It just became like recreation for me, long before it was a career," Tsimerman says.

In 2021, he and two collaborators proved the André-Oort conjecture, which involves solutions to equations for which all the variables are whole numbers. (Equations are mathematical sentences with an equal sign. Variables are symbols that stand for an unknown quantity in an equation.) This is high-level, theoretical stuff, but it is hugely important in math today.

"Jacob is a brilliant mathematician," says his longtime collaborator Jonathan Pila of the University of Oxford. "I have seen his brilliance and resourcefulness at first hand — he is also a very easygoing character."

The Fields Medal itself is 14-karat gold, and the award comes with 15,000 Canadian dollars (about 10,000 US dollars). But it is incredibly prestigious. Tsimerman wants to use his share to direct more attention to a new area: artificial intelligence. "I think that there are big changes coming to our world, and I want people to focus on that," he says. "One of the many scary things about AI is that we don't really understand the system very well." Tsimerman hopes pure mathematics can change that.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Four young mathematicians awarded the 2026 Fields Medals
levels.body:
Math's most prestigious prizes were announced July 23 at the International Congress of Mathematicians. Following a lively brass-band performance by the West Philadelphia Orchestra in a massive auditorium at the Pennsylvania Convention Center, the president of the International Mathematical Union bestowed the prizes to four mathematicians for work ranging from the theory of knots to the motion of fluids.

The Fields Medals went to Hong Wang of New York University and France's Institute of Advanced Scientific Studies (IHES), Yu Deng of the University of Chicago, John Pardon of Stony Brook University and Jacob Tsimerman of the University of Toronto.

In the awards' 90-year history, Wang is only the third woman to win one, after mathematicians Maryam Mirzakhani and Maryna Viazovska in 2014 and 2022, respectively. Wang and Deng represent the prizes' only Chinese-born recipients besides mathematician Shing-Tung Yau, who won a Fields Medal in 1982.

The awards, often referred to as math's Nobel Prizes, are named for John Charles Fields, a Canadian mathematician who led the push for their creation in the 1920s as a way to bring the international math community together. But unlike the Nobels, they are only bestowed every four years and, starting in 1966, only go to researchers who are less than 40 years old.

Hong Wang

When Wang rose to speak during a symposium at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J., this past February, she opened with a characteristic note of humility. "Thank you for having me; it's a great honor," she said. "Especially when I saw the speaker list, I thought, 'Maybe I shouldn't speak.'"

But no one in the rapt audience shared Wang's opinion. At age 34, her work at the interface of two mathematical fields — taking collections of wavelike equations and using them to explore how shapes fill space — had already transformed both subjects. In particular, a 2025 proof of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture that she co-authored with mathematician Joshua Zahl marked a triumphant end to what had been a fervent, field-defining 50-year search.

Now Wang possesses the ultimate qualification for any list of mathematical greats: a Fields Medal.

The Kakeya conjecture is the answer to a mathematical game: swirl your pencil around in the air so that it points in every direction exactly once while also swiveling it through as little space as possible. Wang and Zahl proved a fundamental limit to how small that space can possibly be.

"She solved the 'holy grail' problem," says Nets Katz, a mathematician at Rice University, adding that this is only one of the accomplishments that "has made her a central figure" in the area. Wang's Fields Medal, he says, "is well deserved."

Wang remembers being excited when Mirzakhani became the first woman to win a Fields medal in 2014. But like it was for the late Mirzakhani, who was a reticent public figure, this aspect of the achievement is somewhat secondary to Wang. "I didn't think too much about it," she says.

Yu Deng

Informed quietly in January that he'd won a Fields medal, Deng fled his University of Chicago office, spending the next few days walking the shores of Lake Michigan to calm his nerves. But then he went back to work. "You just act as if nothing happened," he says.

In 2024 and 2025 he and his co-authors released a series of gargantuan papers that amounted to an unprecedented achievement in math and physics. The motion of fluids has always seemed contradictory. Microscopically, a fluid is a chaotic jumble of molecules bouncing off one another like billiard balls. But macroscopically, it follows laws of motion as if it was one continuous whole.

Mathematicians had tried — and largely failed — for more than a century to formally reconcile how fluids could behave in these two distinct ways. Deng's award is for changing that. He and his collaborators proved that the equations that describe fluids on different scales are actually one and the same.

"It's a truly spectacular, singular result," says Scott Armstrong, a mathematician at N.Y.U. It's hard to imagine a more deserving recipient, Armstrong adds, and he expects Deng's mathematical run to continue. "It would have been a disaster had he not won."

With today's awards, Deng and Wang have now tripled the total number of Chinese-born Fields Medalists. This reflects China's decades of investment in math education, which has led to a fresh crop of talented young mathematicians populating the top universities. "I'm working mostly just as myself," Deng says, "but I'm also happy that I'm one of the first of this new generation to get this recognition."

John Pardon

If a Fields Medal is an award for the mathematically precocious, it's hard to imagine a better fit than Pardon. In 2010 he was just a 21-year-old undergraduate at Princeton University when his work in knot theory ensured the entire math world learned his name.

Knot theory is about all the different ways a piece of string can be tied up, with its two loose strands glued together after the tying. These myriad forms are famously difficult to sort — two knotted-up strings might look totally different yet, through elaborate manipulations, be made to match. So mathematicians try to come up with foolproof methods for differentiating them.

One of these is "distortion": a way of measuring how difficult a knot is to traverse. It gauges how long it would take an ant, for instance, to crawl from one point along the string to another — compared with a grasshopper that could simply leap between them.

"John showed that, for a certain sequence of knots, the distortion became arbitrarily large," says David Gabai, a mathematician at Princeton. "This simply stated problem attracted much interest among mathematicians during the previous 25 years."

"I was happy about it," Pardon recalls of toppling this mathematical Goliath as a mere equation- slinging undergraduate. But in hindsight, he says, he should've been even happier. "It's hard to know at the time how much significance a given solution will have." This is a sentiment Pardon has experienced many times since: in graduate school and beyond, he went on to conquer other major conjectures covering other areas of geometry.

Jacob Tsimerman

Tsimerman loved math from an age at which most children seem scarcely aware it even exists. "My parents recognized, by the time I was three, that I was super into it," he says. "I never really considered not being a mathematician."

His grandfather would give him simple mathematical puzzles to work with, and when his mother noticed his early fascination with negative numbers, she offered him her high school math textbook to thumb through. "It just became like recreation for me, long before it was a career," Tsimerman says.

In 2021 he and two collaborators proved the André-Oort conjecture, which concerns the field of math that seeks solutions to equations for which all the variables are whole numbers. But this conjecture leaves simple equations and whole numbers behind; it seeks special points on rarified objects called "Shimura varieties," which are sometimes (but not always) solutions to equations. This is esoteric stuff, but Shimura varieties are hugely important in math today, and the conjecture gives mathematicians an unprecedented handle on their elaborate structure.

"Jacob is a brilliant mathematician," says his longtime collaborator Jonathan Pila of the University of Oxford. "I have seen his brilliance and resourcefulness at first hand — he is also a very easygoing character."

The André-Oort conjecture is just one of Tsimerman's mathematical feats. He's also made important contributions in "Hodge theory," an area that relates to one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems — meaning its solution has a $1-million reward.

Although a Fields Medal's monetary value is modest — just the 14-karat-gold medal itself plus 15,000 Canadian dollars — the prestige it bestows is invaluable. Tsimerman wants to use his share to direct more attention to a new area: artificial intelligence. "I think that there are big changes coming to our world, and I want people to focus on that," he says. "One of the many scary things about AI is that we don't really understand the system very well." Tsimerman hopes pure mathematics can change that.

levels.body:
Frank Rubio is a NASA astronaut. He was supposed to spend six months in space. Instead, he stayed for more than a year.

Rubio was living on the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS is a laboratory. It circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

On September 11, Rubio broke a NASA record. He completed the longest single space flight. The previous record was 355 days. On September 27, Rubio touched down on Earth. He logged a total of 371 days on the ISS.

On the ISS, Rubio had problems with his spacecraft. A spacecraft is a vehicle or machine. It is built to work in harsh environments. This includes outer space.

Rubio was only supposed to be in space for six months. But the spacecraft issues forced him to stay longer.

"It was unexpected. In some ways, it's been an incredible challenge," Rubio said. "But in other ways, it's been an incredible blessing."

Coolant Leak Caused Delay

Rubio traveled to the ISS on a Russian spacecraft. It is called the MS-22 Soyuz. He flew with Sergey Prokopyev and Dmitri Petelin. They both work with Roscosmos. This is the Russian space agency.

MS-22 was meant to be their ride home. Then, in December 2022, something happened. The spacecraft lost all of its coolant during a leak. Coolant is a liquid or gas. It is used to remove heat from something.

So Roscosmos shipped up an empty replacement spacecraft. It is called MS-23. It arrived at the ISS in February 2023.

But Rubio and his crewmates still had to wait for a relief crew. The relief crew was supposed to use MS-23. That meant they needed a new spacecraft. They were reassigned to MS-24. Their departure was delayed to September 15.

Finally, on September 27, Rubio and his two crewmates left the ISS. They flew on board the MS- 23. They touched down to Earth safely. They parachuted into Kazakhstan.

Rubio said that the NASA community rallied around him. They made sure his family was doing well while he was in space. NASA recently upgraded the internet on the ISS. So Rubio was able to have video calls with family.

"I spent so many hours looking for that thing," he said. But he never found it.

Only seven astronauts have spent more than a year in space. The other four were Russian astronauts on missions visiting the then-Soviet Mir space station.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: "It was unexpected": NASA astronaut breaks U.S. record for longest single spaceflight
levels.body:
NASA astronaut Frank Rubio celebrated a spaceflight milestone with two former astronauts on Earth.

Rubio spoke with senior NASA management from the International Space Station (ISS) on September 13, 2023, two days after breaking the previous record of 355 days on a single spaceflight.

On September 27, Rubio touched back down to Earth, logging a total of 371 days in orbit, making him the first American to spend more than a year in space on a single mission. More incredibly, it wasn't planned that way; problems with his spacecraft forced an expected six-month orbital stay to double to a year.

"It was unexpected. In some ways, it's been an incredible challenge," Rubio said of the milestone during the livestreamed call on NASA Television, with NASA Administrator Bill Nelson and Deputy Administrator Pam Melroy. "But in other ways, it's been an incredible blessing. I count myself lucky and honored to be able to represent the agency and our country."

Rubio, a Salvadorian American born in Los Angeles, California, added that with his record-breaking stay falling during National Hispanic Heritage Month (which concludes October 15), he finds it "timely" as it "symbolizes the diversity of the wonderful rich fabric of America."

Rubio and his Russian MS-22 Soyuz spacecraft crewmates Sergey Prokopyev and Dmitri Petelin, cosmonauts from Roscosmos, were scheduled to spend a typical six months in space after launching on September 21, 2022. Both Rubio and Petelin were on their first flight.

Halfway through their stay, however, MS-22, also serving as their ride home, dramatically lost all its coolant in a December 2022 leak. After considering options, Roscosmos rapidly shipped up an empty replacement Soyuz, called MS-23, which arrived on February 25, 2023.

The agencies also formulated an emergency escape plan from the ISS before MS-23 arrived, assigning Rubio to a temporary seat (involving tie-down straps on the floor of an already docked SpaceX Crew Dragon). His Russian crewmates were authorized to use MS-22 if absolutely needed, as two humans would not heat up the uncooled spacecraft as rapidly as three. But that plan luckily did not need to be implemented after MS-23 safely docked.

Rubio and his crewmates, however, were needed to stay on board until a relief crew could arrive. That required getting yet another spacecraft (MS-24) ready for spaceflight to send the astronauts. Since NASA astronaut Loral O'Hara and Roscosmos cosmonauts Oleg Kononenko and Nikolai Chub were supposed to use MS-23, that crew's departure date on MS-24 was delayed to no earlier than September 15 for their MS-24 reassignment.

On September 27, Rubio, Petelin and Prokopyev touched down to Earth safely, parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan aboard the MS-23.

"As much as it was a challenge to stay an extra six months, I'm so grateful that the agency was able to say, 'Hey, you know what the safe thing to do would be: To fire up a new spacecraft, and have [my crew] wait and ensure a more safe return,'" Rubio said in the call, adding, "I am looking forward to a return on a more safe and more secure spacecraft."

Nelson and Melroy, both flown astronauts from the space shuttle program, paid tribute to the challenges Rubio had faced in orbit. (Melroy flew three times as a NASA astronaut. Nelson, then a member of the House of Representatives on a space committee, flew on mission STS-61C in 1986 under a program NASA then had for nonprofessionals to reach space.)

"You made all kinds of records up there, and you've had six months that you didn't expect," said Nelson, speaking from NASA's headquarters in Washington, D.C.

Melroy, standing beside Nelson in the view of the video, said Rubio's wife and kids "have been on my mind so much." The former astronaut added she wanted to check in to make sure Rubio was getting the support he needed.

Rubio said that the NASA community had rallied around him, sending people over to the house as needed to help the family. Luckily, upgrades to NASA's internet on station came in during his mission as well, allowing for high-quality video conferences with family at least twice a week, he said.

Rubio joked that his only regret was not eating one of the space-grown Red Robin tomatoes his crew tended, and managed to save from an unexpected humidity drop on ISS at a crucial growth point. Rubio's inch-long tomato unfortunately floated away to a hidden spot before he could take a bite. "I spent so many hours looking for that thing," he quipped. "I'm sure the desiccated tomato will show up at some point and vindicate me, years in the future."

Only seven astronauts have spent more than a year in space. Aside from the trio on MS-22/23, the other four were cosmonauts on missions visiting the then-Soviet Mir space station. Topping the list is Valery Polyakov (437 days), while the others are Sergey Avdeev, Musa Manarov and Vladimir Titov.

Rubio's mark surpasses the 355-day record last set by NASA astronaut Mark Vande Hei. Vande Hei was also expected to spend six months in space, but learned preflight that he might extend to a year due to space station staffing needs (which is what ended up happening).

Vande Hei, speaking with Rubio in early September from NASA's Johnson Space Station in Houston, Texas, said the most memorable part of his own stay was "the people that I got to spend that much time [with] … intensively, both working and playing as much as we possibly can."

title: From "digital detoxes" to flip phones: Gen Z shows signs of turning anti-tech
zhTitle: Z 世代转向反技术
reason: 换成翻盖机之后屏幕时间从九小时降到二十分钟，几名大学生各自的做法。

cover.caption: Brooke Williams, a recent Kent State University graduate, shows off her new flip phone that replaced her smartphone.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: From "digital detoxes" to flip phones: Gen Z shows signs of turning anti-tech
levels.body:
Brooke Williams took a big step this past March: She replaced her iPhone with a flip phone. Her flip phone doesn't connect to the internet.

Williams is 22. After she switched to a flip phone, her screen time dropped greatly. It went from over nine hours a day to just 20 minutes a day.

What made her switch phones? She realized she cared too much about what people thought of her online.

"I was spending hours and hours … playing a person that wasn't me," Williams said. "That wasn't …who I wanted to be."

Williams is not alone. Many young people are trying to reduce their smartphone use.

Williams Broke Her Technology Cycle

Williams knows people can't completely escape phones. But she wants to cut back as much as possible.

Williams said her mind has become much clearer since she reduced her screen time. She has been replacing screen time with reading, studying or talking to people. She stopped bringing her phone into her bedroom or to class.

How Other Students Are Addressing Technology

Joseph Driscoll is a university student. He lives in a fraternity house. A fraternity is a kind of club. Sometimes the members live in a house or building together. Driscoll says he often sees people in the house sitting together on a couch. But they are all on their phones.

"They'll still be talking to each other. But … it's just people doing their own thing next to someone else," Driscoll said. "I prefer to be more involved."

He said he spends around three hours a day on his phone. Mostly, he listens to music. Since reducing his phone use, his life has gotten much better, he said.

Driscoll now focuses more on rock climbing, playing instruments and work. That means he doesn't have much time left for scrolling.

"I'm at a point where I don't really need social media," he said. "Before, I went on it just out of boredom."

Jessica Greene is a 21-year-old student. She, too, has been trying to disconnect from the online world. During class, she takes paper notes and keeps her phone in her bag. And she stays off her phone for the first hour she's awake every morning.

Anti-Tech Student Recommends Phone Audits

Williams says people should go through their apps carefully. They should decide what makes them happy and what doesn't.

When Williams sees other people on their screens, she remembers how smartphones made her feel tired. There was just so much information coming at her all the time.

"It's like standing in an airport all … day and just hearing the … [noise] constantly," Williams said. "It's not healthy. You need to rest."

Brooke Williams made a big change this March: She replaced her iPhone with a flip phone that has no access to the internet.

The 22-year-old Kent State student's screen time dropped steeply to 20 minutes a day, down from over nine hours.

What was the tipping point that led her to switch? She realized she cared more about what people thought of her online than she cared about herself in real life.

"I was spending hours and hours and days of my life curating and playing a person that wasn't me to serve to other people," Williams said. "That wasn't …who I wanted to be."

Williams is not alone. A growing number of young adults are pushing back against what they consider excessive time on smartphones.

In 2025, 46 percent of teens said they are online almost constantly, according to the Pew Research Center. But in another 2024 study, more than a third of teens ages 13 to 17 said they have cut back on their phone screen time. And 72 percent said they feel peaceful when they don't have their smartphone.

Like Williams, 21-year-old Jessica Greene, a University of Akron student, has been trying to disconnect from the online world. She said she doesn't want to rely on technology to live her day- to-day life.

"Every time I look at it, I'm disgusted," she said.

title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
zhTitle: AI 该不该帮学生写大学申请文书

cover.caption: With more students relying on ChatGPT to write their essays, colleges such as Georgia Tech set some guidelines for their applicants.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Many high school seniors are applying to colleges. Some have to write admissions essays. They may get help from ChatGPT.

ChatGPT is a software system. It writes code. It also generates text. It can produce essays and stories. ChatGPT is powered by artificial intelligence (AI). AI is an approach that uses code to teach a machine to spot patterns and make decisions. The company OpenAI created ChatGPT. The company released ChatGPT as a free web-based tool in 2022.

Some professors fear that ChatGPT could lead to cheating. Others think that ChatGPT could help students. Now, college admissions offices must weigh in. Georgia Tech is one of the first schools to issue guidance around AI.

Brainstorming Is OK

Many schools have said nothing about using AI for college applications, said Rick Clark. He works at Georgia Tech. Clark is in charge of undergraduate admissions.

Georgia Tech says applicants can use ChatGPT. They can use it to brainstorm. They can use it for editing. But they shouldn't copy and paste paragraphs. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

Riley Samples goes to Seckinger High School. It is in Buford, Georgia. Samples is a senior there. She is working on 15 admissions essays. She uses AI to check grammar.

She said AI is not good at writing with personality. "It's very flat," she said.

Ethical Concerns

Noelle Halverson is a senior at Seckinger, too. A teacher encouraged her to use ChatGPT for creative writing. Halverson used it to flesh out plot details. But using it for applications feels wrong to her, she said.

Lauren Chiru-Danzer is a junior at Seckinger. She used ChatGPT to research law schools. She thinks it's ethical to use AI as "a way to get ideas started." But copying AI text is plagiarism, she said.

"That's Not Really My Voice"

Many students get stuck on essays. Clark said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." ChatGPT can help students, he said.

"It gets them … started, thinking about things, and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Admissions officers are also using AI. Georgia Tech plans to run its applications through a computer program. They want to see how the program will score them. They will compare the scores from humans to the ones from computers. But people will still decide which students get in.

figures.caption: With more students relying on ChatGPT to write their essays, colleges such as Georgia Tech set some guidelines for their applicants.
Administrators at Georgia Tech face the issue of 2024 applicants using AI to write their admission essays. Other colleges discourage the use of the AI writing tool.
To some, using ChatGPT to brainstorm ideas for an essay is useful and beneficial.

levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Many high school seniors are starting to write college admissions essays. Some may consult ChatGPT for help.

ChatGPT is a software system. It writes code and generates text such as essays and stories. ChatGPT is powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This is an approach that uses code to teach a machine to spot patterns and make decisions. A company called OpenAI created ChatGPT. In 2022, the company released ChatGPT as a free web-based tool.

Some professors fear that ChatGPT could lead to cheating. Other professors are trying to figure out how ChatGPT could help students. Now, college admissions offices must weigh in. Georgia Tech is one of the first schools to issue guidance around AI.

Brainstorming Is OK

Many schools have said nothing about using AI for applications, said Rick Clark. He works at Georgia Tech. He is in charge of undergraduate admissions.

Georgia Tech says applicants can use ChatGPT to help with their essays. They can use it to brainstorm ideas. They can use it to organize their thoughts or for editing. But they shouldn't copy and paste paragraphs. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

The online site Intelligent recently surveyed 750 students. One in 10 said they had used or likely will use ChatGPT to write application essays. Most said the text it produced "required some or a lot of editing."

Riley Samples is a senior at Seckinger High School. It is in Buford, Georgia. Samples is working on 15 essays for seven colleges. She uses AI programs to check grammar.

"I think AI-generated essays cannot really capture who you are as a person," Samples said. "When it writes, it's very flat. It's not very emotion-filled."

Ethical Concerns

Seckinger High School students are used to thinking about the ethical uses of AI. The school incorporates AI into courses.

Noelle Halverson is a senior there. She experimented with ChatGPT for a creative writing assignment. Her teacher encouraged it. Halverson used ChatGPT to flesh out plot details. But using a chatbot for college essays feels wrong to her, she said.

The college search is "a daunting task," said Lauren Chiru-Danzer. She is a junior at Seckinger. She used ChatGPT to research schools with law programs. She thinks it's ethical to use AI as "a way to get ideas started." But she knows that copying AI text is plagiarism.

College counselors can help students brainstorm ideas for essays, edit and proofread. Elaine Rosenblum helps run a counseling business. She said college essays should capture a student's personality.

So far, AI writing can't replicate emotion, said Rosenblum.

"That's Not Really My Voice"

Some students don't have access to college counselors. AI might help make the application process fairer, Clark said.

Clark also points out that essays are not everything. They are a valuable component of an application. But it's rare to admit or deny someone based on those writings alone. Grades, test scores and involvement outside of class are critical.

Still, many students get stuck on essays. Clark said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." That's where ChatGPT can chip in.

"It gets them throwing out some stuff, getting started, thinking about things and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Admissions officers are exploring how AI could work for them, too. This year, Georgia Tech will run applications through a computer program. Officials will check how the program scores submissions compared to humans. But ultimately, people will still decide which students get in.

levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Many high school seniors are tackling college admissions essays. The best writers will respond with authenticity, personality, good grammar and maybe some wit. Some may consult ChatGPT for help.

ChatGPT is a complex software system that writes code and generates text such as essays, stories and summaries. ChatGPT is powered by artificial intelligence (AI). This is an approach that uses code to teach a machine to spot patterns and make decisions. A company called OpenAI created and released ChatGPT as a free web-based tool in late 2022.

When ChatGPT launched last fall, it forced professors to contend with a new cheating threat. They had to figure out how to incorporate it into courses. Now, the disruption is pounding at the admissions office door. Georgia Tech is among the first schools to issue guidance about using artificial intelligence for application essays.

Brainstorming Is OK

Many schools have said nothing about using AI for applications, said Rick Clark. He is Georgia Tech's executive director of undergraduate admission.

Georgia Tech decided to tackle the issue head-on. Georgia Tech applicants can use a chatbot to brainstorm essay ideas, organize their thoughts and edit. But they shouldn't copy and paste AI-authored paragraphs into their applications. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

"We know students are using it in their own academic work in high school, and so if they're going to, let's give them … some guardrails," Clark said.

The online site Intelligent recently surveyed 750 students about ChatGPT. One in 10 high school seniors and incoming college freshmen said they had used or likely will use ChatGPT to write their college application essays. Nearly all students who used AI said the text it produced "required some or a lot of editing."

Riley Samples, a senior at Seckinger High School in Buford, Georgia, is working on 15 essays for seven colleges. The submissions will vary from short statements to 800-word pieces.

Samples thought it was interesting that Georgia Tech didn't ban AI entirely but steered applicants away from plagiarizing. She errs on the side of caution, using such programs only to check grammar.

"I think AI-generated essays cannot really capture who you are as a person," Samples said. "When it writes, it's very flat. It's not very emotion-filled."

Ethical Concerns

Seckinger High School students are accustomed to thinking about the ethical uses of AI. The school incorporates AI into courses.

Noelle Halverson, a senior, experimented with ChatGPT when a teacher encouraged her class to try it on a creative writing assignment. Halverson used it to flesh out plot details.

Using a chatbot to help with college essays, though, doesn't feel right, she said.

The college search is "a daunting task," said Seckinger junior Lauren Chiru-Danzer. She used ChatGPT to research schools with good law programs. But while she thinks it's ethical to use AI as a "brainstorming partner" or "a way to get ideas started," she said that copying and pasting AI text is plagiarism.

College counselors can help students brainstorm ideas for essays, edit and proofread. Elaine Rosenblum helps run a counseling and tutoring business. She said college essays should capture a student's personality and a reader's attention.

So far, AI writing can't replicate nuance and emotion, said Rosenblum. Relying on ChatGPT is "a very dangerous proposition" unless colleges clearly state what's allowed.

"I wouldn't test the waters," she said. "I think it's lazy. It's the opposite of what a college wants you to do. Why risk it?"

"That's Not Really My Voice"

For first-generation students and others who don't have access to college coaching, AI might help make the application process fairer, Clark said.

And while essays are a valuable component of an application, it's rare to admit or deny someone based on those writings alone, Clark said. Grades, test scores and involvement outside of class are critical.

Still, many students get stuck on essays. Clark said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." That's where ChatGPT can chip in.

"It gets them throwing out some stuff, getting started, thinking about things and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Admissions officers are exploring how AI could work for them, too.

Last year, humans read more than 52,000 undergraduate applications to Georgia Tech. This year, the school plans to run applications through a computer program, too. Officials will check how the program scores submissions compared to humans. But ultimately, people will still decide which students get in.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Should AI help Georgia students write college admissions essays?
levels.body:
Thousands of high school seniors applying to one of Georgia's most selective universities are tackling the same admissions essay question: "Why do you want to study your chosen major specifically at Georgia Tech?"

The best writers will respond with authenticity, personality, a solid grasp of grammar and maybe a dash of wit. Some even will consult ChatGPT for help.

And that's just fine with Georgia Tech, to a point. The highly ranked public research school in Atlanta is among the first to issue guidance about how to use artificial intelligence (AI) as the applicants write their essays.

ChatGPT upended classrooms when it launched last fall, forcing professors to contend with a new cheating threat and figure out how to incorporate it into courses. Now, the disruption is pounding at the admissions office door.

There's been "deafening silence" from many schools about the use of AI in college applications, said Rick Clark, Georgia Tech's executive director of undergraduate admission. That was all the more reason to tackle it head on as applications for fall 2024 admission opened August 1, 2023.

Georgia Tech applicants can use a chatbot to brainstorm essay ideas, organize their thoughts and edit. But they shouldn't copy and paste AI-authored paragraphs into their applications. According to Georgia Tech, "Your ultimate submission should be your own."

"We know students are using it in their own academic work in high school, and so if they're going to, let's give them … some guardrails," Clark said.

The AI conundrum adds to the upheaval happening as some competitive colleges adjust policies following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in late June to end race-conscious admissions programs.

Elite institutions have taken varied approaches. The University of Michigan Law School tells applicants to write all drafts and the final product, declaring they "ought not use ChatGPT or other artificial intelligence tools." Duke University pointed to guidelines developed to assist faculty as they think about the use of AI in classrooms, but the recommendations don't specifically address admissions.

The Common Application, accepted by 1,000 schools including roughly two dozen in Georgia, advises colleges "to set reasonable parameters" around the use of AI, said Jenny Rickard, the organization's president and CEO, in a written statement. Just over half of Common App schools don't require an essay.

One in 10 high school seniors and incoming college freshmen used or likely will use ChatGPT to write their college application essays, according to a recent survey of about 750 students by the online site Intelligent. Nearly all students who used AI to write their essays said the text it produced "required some or a lot of editing," the survey found.

Riley Samples, a senior at Seckinger High School in Gwinnett County, is working on 15 essays as she applies to about seven colleges, including Georgia Tech and some in the Ivy League. The submissions will vary from short statements to 800-word pieces.

Samples thought it was interesting Georgia Tech didn't ban AI entirely but steered applicants away from plagiarizing. She errs on the side of caution, using such programs only to check grammar.

"I think AI-generated essays cannot really capture who you are as a person," Samples said. "When it writes, it's very flat. It's not very emotion-filled."

Campus Policies

Georgia Tech, the University of Georgia (UGA) and the private Oglethorpe University in Brookhaven are among those addressing how to use AI in applications.

UGA advises those seeking admission to treat AI programs "like any other form of assistance, whether it is a parent, counselor or friend," but the writing must be the applicant's own.

Oglethorpe recognizes AI as a "powerful and convenient" tool that can assist with "language, grammar and structure" in an essay or application. But, the school stresses, "Ultimately, we want to learn about you from you."

Rebecca Sandidge, Oglethorpe's vice president for enrollment management, said it's too hard to police the use of AI.

"My goal is to not villainize AI," she said. "It is a tool and students have to learn how to use it appropriately."

Detection tools are unreliable, Clark said. Ultimately, the best way to deter students from submitting all-bot essays is to remind them that the writing won't impress admissions readers.

Georgia College & State University hasn't provided applicants with specific guidance regarding AI, a spokeswoman said. Neither has the private Emory University, though a spokeswoman said, "We expect applicants to write their essays themselves."

Spelman College also doesn't have a policy forbidding the use of AI in admissions essays. Ingrid Hayes, senior vice president for enrollment management, said in a statement that if AI-generated text is suspected, it "may raise doubts about the students' academic potential in the holistic application review."

Abby Hyken, a senior at Atlanta's Midtown High School who plans to apply to about a dozen colleges, has used ChatGPT to brainstorm debate team arguments, where it provided a helpful starting point. But the text it generates is emotionless and "not that good." She has not turned to it for the 20 or more college essays on her to-do list.

Hyken's biggest writing challenge is showcasing her personality and how she'd fit into a school "without sounding too cliche."

Ethical Concerns

At Seckinger High School, a school that intertwines artificial intelligence into courses, students are accustomed to thinking about its ethical uses.

Noelle Halverson, a senior, experimented with ChatGPT when a teacher encouraged her class to try it on a creative writing assignment. Halverson used it to flesh out plot details and to look for a period-appropriate name for an 18th century character.

Using a chatbot to help with college essays, though, doesn't feel right, she said. "It wouldn't be me at all."

The college search is "a daunting task," said Seckinger junior Lauren Chiru-Danzer, who has used ChatGPT to research schools in the Northeast with good law programs.

"We are constantly discussing the ethical implications of AI," she said. "We have deemed it ethical to use AI as almost like a brainstorming partner, as a way to get ideas started. But it is not ethical to copy and paste what AI has given to you because it is plagiarism."

College counselors at the Buckhead-based Access Test Prep & Tutoring help students brainstorm ideas for essays, edit and proofread. Co-founder Elaine Rosenblum said teenagers communicate in smartphone "text-speak" and learn formulaic writing in high school. But those skills don't exactly translate into crafting strong college essays, which should capture a student's personality and a reader's attention.

So far, AI writing can't replicate nuance and emotion, said Rosenblum. Relying on ChatGPT is "a very dangerous proposition" unless colleges clearly state what's allowed.

"I wouldn't test the waters," she said. "I think it's lazy. It's the opposite of what a college wants you to do. Why risk it?"

Rosenblum draws a distinction between students who use AI and those who hire advisers to help them apply to college.

"Someone who is doing college counseling that has integrity will not write the essay for the student," she said.

"Paralysis Of The Blinking Cursor"

For first-generation students or those from rural communities who don't have access to college coaching, AI isn't an equalizer, but it might help democratize the application process, Clark said. Georgia Tech's guidance notes that "AI could be a helpful collaborator, particularly when you do not have access to other assistance to help you complete your application."

And while essays are a valuable component of a student's application, it's exceedingly rare to admit or deny someone based on those writings, Clark said. Grades, academic rigor, test scores and involvement outside of class are critical to decision-makers, he said.

Still, many students get stuck on essays. Clark calls it the "paralysis of the blinking cursor" and said admissions departments should do what they can to "de-stress the process." That's where ChatGPT can chip in.

"It gets them throwing out some stuff, getting started, thinking about things and then realizing, 'Well, that's not exactly the way I want to put it. Or, that's not really my voice,'" he said.

Students aren't the only ones figuring out how to use AI. Admissions officers are exploring how it could work for them, too.

Last year, humans read more than 52,000 undergraduate applications to Georgia Tech. They'll do so again this year (2023), but the school is testing the use of AI in its own process. The school plans to run applications through a computer program at the end of the admissions cycle. Officials will check how the program scores submissions compared to humans, who will still decide who gets in, Clark said.

"We have to find ways to learn and to be more efficient and to spend our time on what really matters," he said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Giant metal roosters spread autism acceptance in Maine after town law spat
levels.body:
Metal roosters are popping up all over a town in Maine! They are big, bright and colorful. These statues are for a six-year-old girl named Pyper. She loves roosters! Roosters are adult male chickens. Pyper also has autism.

David and Sara LeBlanc are Pyper's parents. They live in Ogunquit, Maine. They also own a restaurant called The Omelette Factory.

The LeBlancs put up a few roosters on their lawn. The statues are about six feet tall. That's about as big as a refrigerator! But then town officials said the roosters had to go. The town said the statues were advertising the restaurant. And they did not have permission to do that.

David LeBlanc disagreed with the town leaders. He said roosters don't lay eggs. The roosters were not related to the restaurant.

It Started With A Beloved Stuffed Rooster

Roosters are Pyper's favorite animal. She had a stuffed rooster as a little girl.

In 2025, she visited a store with her father. There, she saw a large rooster sculpture for sale. She asked her dad about it. He suggested they bring it home.

Eventually, the family had more than 24 roosters. Pyper liked hiding behind one while waiting for the school bus. Her parents said the roosters help her feel better.

The family put a rooster on their restaurant sign. Then, the town said the statues were advertising.

The LeBlancs had to pay some fines. This is a payment you have to make if you break a law. They also had to take down all their rooster statues.

But the LeBlancs did not back down.

The Town Offers A Compromise

A group of town leaders met to talk about the rules. They considered how the roosters help Pyper. The town made a deal. They said the family could keep two roosters on their lawn. But they could not have any more.

Autism spectrum disorder is a complicated condition. It affects people differently. Comfort objects are commonly used to help autistic people. These items can help with strong emotions, such as stress. Beverley Cush Evans is an expert in special education.

"It's part of who they are and what they need," Evans said.

The family had to give some of the roosters away. But now, people are putting up roosters to show support for Pyper. One person even sent in a photo of their rooster in New Zealand. That's near Australia!
