levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Giant metal roosters spread autism acceptance in Maine after town zoning spat
levels.body:
OGUNQUIT, Maine— Giant metal roosters are popping up on lawns in and around a community in southern Maine and as far away as New Zealand in support of a 6-year-old autistic girl and her love of the colorful creations.

David and Sara LeBlanc had a rotating display of the roughly 6-foot-tall (1.8-meter-tall) ornaments decorating their Ogunquit lawn until officials in the small coastal town deemed them to be impermissible advertising for their attached restaurant, The Omelette Factory.

The couple initially resisted the town's removal order, insisting the roosters were meant to comfort their daughter Pyper, not advertise their business.

"Roosters don't lay eggs," David LeBlanc told The Associated Press on Wednesday.

But they eventually came to an agreement with the town allowing them to keep two of the roosters in front of their home.

As for what to do with the others? That's where friends, neighbors and complete strangers came in.

It Started With A Beloved Stuffed Rooster

The LeBlancs took in Pyper as a foster child and later adopted her. She arrived with a stuffed rooster, and roosters became her favorite animal, her parents said. When her father took her to a Tractor Supply Store to play with baby chicks last year, she noticed a large rooster sculpture for sale and asked her dad what it was saying.

"I think he wants to come home," David LeBlanc said he told her.

Eventually, their collection grew to more than two dozen roosters, which they set up in batches for seasonal and holiday displays. Pyper took to hiding behind one each morning while waiting for the school bus, which her parents said helps her regulate her emotions and navigate transitions.

But the couple ruffled feathers when they added a rooster to their restaurant's logo, which is featured on its shirts and other merchandise. Although the LeBlancs said they view the rooster as a "family crest," the town saw their lawn statues as advertising.

A code enforcement officer, Tyler McOsker, issued the LeBlancs $450 in fines and ordered them in April to "remove all unpermitted signage, including but not limited to rooster statues."

McOsker didn't respond to an email requesting comment. But he told the Zoning Board of Appeals in June that he had no idea the roosters were connected to Pyper's autism diagnosis until the couple appealed the fines. He also pointed to a May 2025 article in a local weekly newspaper that described the roosters as a "fun and unconventional way to announce that The Omelette Factory is officially open for business."

"That, to me, is the definition of a sign. You're announcing you're opening," McOsker told the board.

David LeBlanc said the reporter misinterpreted a customer's joke about the roosters serving as an "Open" sign.

"We never said that," he said.

The Town Offers A Compromise

The zoning board discussed the issue in June. At one point, board member Jay Smith voiced frustration at the lack of medical proof that the roosters were necessary.

"I'm inclined to think there may be some merit to a comfort animal on the front lawn … but the point is, how many does it take?" he said.

Autism spectrum disorder is a complex developmental condition that affects different people in different ways, and comfort objects are frequently incorporated into therapy for autistic children to help manage transitions, support emotional regulation and provide a sense of familiarity, Beverley Cush Evans, a professor of special education at Lesley University, told the AP.

"It's part of who they are and what they need," she said.

Eventually, the board decided it lacked the authority to rescind the fines but tried to accommodate the family by granting a disability variance that essentially deemed two roosters necessary for Pyper's access to the home.

"I want to emphasize we're talking about two roosters. If they have babies or multiply in the night — no," another board member said.

The variance requires the roosters to be part of a railing, however, and for now, they are just bolted to the steps. The couple has been fined another $500 for noncompliance.

A Show Of Support

David LeBlanc said he is moving on from the dispute and is focusing on the good that has come from it. The family has given roosters to others to "foster" and show their support for autism acceptance, starting with a man named Sam who lives up the road. Though Pyper was sad to see them go, she understands the adage about making lemonade, LeBlanc said.

"She understands that the roosters being taken away were the lemons, and Sam and his friends, fostering them, are the lemonade," he said. "It's a beautiful thing."

Thanks to news coverage and a Roosters of Ogunquit Facebook page, the story has spread far and wide. One supporter wrote in from New Zealand sharing pictures of his children with a rooster statue in their yard.

Hetal Patel, who owns a motel in nearby Wells and has a relative with autism, wanted to buy a rooster after hearing about Pyper. They were sold out in the Ogunquit area, though, so she and her son went to New Hampshire to get one.

"We found the last one," she said. "We couldn't wait to put it out. People were so supportive, they were honking. It was so nice to see all the love for Pyper."

cover.caption: After only playing three rounds of golf, golfer Bayleigh Teepa-Tarau wins the nine-hole title at the Zespri AIMS Games in Tauranga, New Zealand. His teacher, Whetu Wiremu (right), introduced Bayleigh to the sport.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Twelve-year-old becomes national golf champ after playing only three full rounds
levels.body:
Twelve-year-old Bayleigh Teepa-Tarau won a major New Zealand golf contest. Bayleigh has autism. His autism means he sometimes has trouble communicating with others. But it doesn't stop him from being good at golf. In fact, it may even help. Before winning the contest, Bayleigh had only played three full rounds of golf in his life.

Bayleigh played in the Association of Intermediate and Middle Schools (AIMS) Games. The AIMS Games are New Zealand's biggest sporting event for 11- to 13-year-olds. Bayleigh won the gold medal in nine-hole golf. He played with borrowed clubs. He doesn't even own a set of clubs.

Bayleigh didn't just win a gold medal. He also helped his school win the team title. His performance was incredible. It was particularly incredible for someone who has been playing for such a short time.

"Bayleigh is just unbelievable and has natural talent," said Mickey Huriwaka. He is a longtime golfer. He said watching Bayleigh was like watching a pro golfer. "That was how good he was."

Borrowed Clubs And Three Rounds Of Practice

Whetu Wiremu is Bayleigh's golf coach. He is a teacher's aide at the Tāneatua School. He recently started a golf team at the school. Someone told him Bayleigh used to carry around a golf stick. So, Wiremu asked the quiet boy if he wanted to join the team.

Bayleigh said, "OK."

The children took group lessons for six months, Wiremu said. But they weren't able to learn much. He said the boys never got "one-on-one kind of help."

The school didn't have enough money to buy golf clubs for Bayleigh and his teammates. Instead, Wiremu had to borrow clubs. He drove the kids to a nearby golf course. They played three full rounds of practice. Each round lasted around three hours.

"He doesn't worry about if he's done a bad shot or a good shot," Wiremu said of Bayleigh. "He just loves the sport." It's that love that makes him so good, Wiremu added.

"I Want To Be Like Tiger Woods"

Wiremu believes Bayleigh's autism helped him during the contest. It helped him focus on the game.

"He doesn't really get nervous for anything that he does," Wiremu said. "He kind of just does it to have fun."

Bayleigh has become a star after the AIMS win. A business said it would buy golf clubs for Bayleigh and his teammates. Golf New Zealand has also offered to help the team.

To celebrate their win, Wiremu took Bayleigh and his teammates to have sushi. That's Bayleigh's favorite food. After that, Bayleigh suggested that they go play more golf.

"I like playing golf, and I'm always going to play golf," Bayleigh said. "I want to be like Tiger Woods."

Bayleigh Teepa-Tarau participated in the AIMS Games, showing a high skill level in the sport.

title: What to know about the latest Israel-Hamas conflict
zhTitle: 以色列与哈马斯冲突：背景说明
reason: 封锁、控制权与历次战争，读懂新闻标题需要的那条时间线。

At right, Israeli police officers evacuate a family from a site in Ashkelon that was hit by a rocket fired from the Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: What to know about the latest Israel-Hamas conflict
levels.body:
October 7, 2023, was a major Jewish holiday. On that day, Hamas militants from Gaza made a surprise attack on Israel. The militants killed and kidnapped many people. In response, Israel launched rockets into Gaza. Israel's Prime Minister said the country is now at war with Hamas.

Hamas has been in power in Gaza for 16 years. The U.S. State Department considers Hamas to be a terrorist group. The European Union and other Western countries also consider it a terrorist organization.

Hamas attacked as many as 22 locations in Israel. They gunned down civilians and soldiers.

Israel's military said on October 10 that it had regained control over its border with the Gaza Strip. Its government vowed to hunt down the militants.

The conflict already has killed people on both sides. More than 1,000 people have died in Israel, and 830 people have been killed in Gaza and the West Bank.

More than 150 people were kidnapped by Hamas. The hostages are Israeli soldiers, women, children, and the elderly. Some of the hostages are from other countries. Hamas says it will kill a hostage every time Israel's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza is just 25 miles long and six miles wide. At 139 square miles, it's about the same size as Detroit, Michigan.

Over 2 million Palestinians live in Gaza. It is part of a region called the Southern Levant. The area has been called many names, including Palestine, Israel, and Canaan. Both Jews and Arabs, many of whom are Muslim, have historical and indigenous ties to the region.

In 1948, the area was under British control. The United Nations decided that the territory would be split into two countries. Palestine would be Arab, while Israel would be Jewish. Israel declared its independence and Arab countries invaded, starting the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

Many Palestinians fled or were forced to leave. Egypt captured Gaza during the fighting. Jordan took control of two other Palestinian areas — East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In 1967, Israel and its neighbors went to war again. This time, Israel captured Gaza, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, began in Gaza in 1987. It later spread to the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Hamas emerged in Gaza during this time. In the 1990s an agreement with Israel created a Palestinian government called the Palestinian Authority, which was given partial control over Gaza and the West Bank.

The Hamas Takeover

A second intifada happened in 2005. Israel withdrew from Gaza.

In 2006, Hamas won the Palestinian elections. Hamas clashed with the Palestinian Authority, and then took control of Gaza.

In 2007, Egypt and Israel closed their borders with Gaza. This blockade has lasted 16 years.

The Blockade

Israel says the blockade keeps Hamas and other militant groups from importing weapons. Egypt says it wants to stop the conflict from spilling over into its borders. Rights groups say the blockade punishes all Gazans.

Gaza is a hard place to live. About half of the Gazans don't have jobs, electricity goes out frequently and the tap water is polluted.

Palestinians in Gaza cannot leave the territory without permission. This makes it extremely difficult to leave the country to work, study or visit family.

The Wars

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles.

In 2021, an 11-day war between Israel and Hamas began after a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, a site sacred to both Jews and Muslims.

Israel's military has destroyed Gazan neighborhoods, forcing thousands to makeshift shelters.

Hamas has fired thousands of rockets into Israel, creating widespread fear. Their range has steadily increased in recent years.

Why Now?

In recent years, Israel has made peace deals with Arab countries. In the past, Arab countries didn't want to make peace with Israel. The U.S. has recently been trying to make a deal between Israel and Saudi Arabia. Hamas receives support from Iran. Iran is Saudi Arabia's enemy.

Meanwhile, Israel has a new far-right government. Its politicians support Israeli settlements in the Palestinian West Bank. Palestinians and the United Nations consider those settlements to be illegal.

Israeli religious nationalists have also increased their visits to the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Recently, hundreds of ultra-Orthodox Jews and Israeli activists visited the site. This angered Hamas. For decades there had been an agreement. Muslims were allowed to pray there, but not Jews.

Hamas leaders say there are several reasons for the attack. They include an Israeli crackdown on militants in the West Bank and the settlements. They also cite thousands of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Israel's blockade of Gaza.

At right, Israeli police officers evacuate a family from a site in Ashkelon that was hit by a rocket fired from the Gaza Strip on October 7, 2023.
figures.credit: Photos: Fatima Shbair and Tsafrir Abayov/AP

figures.caption: Since Hamas militants attacked locations in Israel near the Gaza border on October 7, 2023, Israeli airstrikes have rained down across Gaza. Hamas has also continued to fire rockets into Israel.

levels.body:
During the major Jewish holiday of Simchat Torah on October 7, 2023, Hamas militants from Gaza fired a barrage of rockets and stormed into Israeli towns. The militants killed dozens and abducted others in an unprecedented surprise attack. Israel launched retaliatory airstrikes in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country is now at war with Hamas.

Hamas has been in power in Gaza since 2007. The U.S. State Department designated Hamas a terrorist group in 1997. The European Union and other Western countries also consider it a terrorist organization.

Hamas gunmen attacked as many as 22 locations outside of the Gaza border, reaching as far as 15 miles (24 kilometers) inside of Israel. In some places, they gunned down civilians and soldiers.

Israel's military said on October 10, 2023, that it had regained control over the border with the Gaza Strip.

The Israeli government vowed to hunt down the militants and intensify an assault on Gaza, the Palestinian territory ruled by Hamas and home to 2 million people.

The conflict already has killed hundreds on both sides, with more than 1,000 people dying in Israel since the incursion on October 7. In Gaza and the West Bank, 830 people have been killed.

Israel says it takes pains to avoid civilian casualties as it targets Hamas sites in Gaza, which is heavily built up and has few open spaces. But Hamas militants also fire rockets and operate in civilian areas, using civilians for cover while drawing return fire to houses, offices and mosques.

In Israel and beyond, the families of more than 150 people kidnapped by Hamas feared for the lives of their loved ones. Among the hostages are Israeli soldiers, women, children, and the elderly, along with dozens of foreigners. Hamas has warned it will kill one of the hostages every time Israel's military bombs civilian targets in Gaza without warning.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza is a Palestinian territory sandwiched between Israel and Egypt. It is just 25 miles long and six miles wide. At 139 square miles, it's about the same size as Detroit, Michigan.

Gaza is home to over 2 million Palestinians. Gaza is part of the Southern Levant, a region that has had many names throughout history, including Palestine, Israel and Canaan. Both Jews and Arabs, many of whom are Muslim, have historical and indigenous ties to the region.

The United Nations (U.N.) decided in 1948 that the territory of Palestine, which was controlled by Britain at the time, would be split into two countries: Israel and Palestine. Palestine would be majority Arab, while Israel would be a Jewish state, based on a U.N. plan to divide the area. Nearby Arab countries did not agree with this. Israel declared its independence and Arab countries invaded, starting what is now known as the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.

Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fled the fighting or were forced to leave their homes. After the war, Egypt took control of Gaza and Jordan took control of two other Palestinian areas — East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

Israel captured Gaza, along with the West Bank and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories to form their future state.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, erupted in Gaza in 1987 — the same year Hamas was founded — and later spread to the other occupied territories of the West Bank and East Jerusalem. The Oslo peace process in the 1990s established the Palestinian Authority and gave it limited autonomy in Gaza and parts of the occupied West Bank.

The Hamas Takeover

Israel withdrew its troops and Jewish settlements from Gaza in 2005, after a second and far more violent intifada.

The following year, Hamas won a landslide victory in Palestinian elections. That triggered a power struggle with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and his Fatah party, which rule the West Bank. A week of clashes in 2007 left Hamas in control of Gaza.

Hamas — and Gaza — is more religiously conservative than the West Bank and the Palestinian Authority. Hamas has been known to arrest political opponents and violently suppress protests against its rule.

In 2007, Egypt and Israel closed their borders with Gaza, and the blockade has now lasted 16 years.

The Blockade

Israel says the blockade is needed to keep Hamas and other militant groups from importing arms, whereas Egypt maintains the blockade to prevent Hamas-related conflict from spilling over into its borders. Human rights groups say the blockade is a form of collective punishment.

The closures, along with years of Hamas' misrule and long-running feud with the Palestinian Authority, have devastated Gaza's economy. Unemployment is around 50 percent, power outages are frequent and the tap water is badly polluted.

Palestinians in Gaza face heavy restrictions from both Egypt and Israel that make it difficult to travel abroad for work, study or to visit family. They often refer to Gaza as the world's largest open-air prison.

The Wars

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles. The worst so far was the 2014 war, which lasted for 50 days and killed 2,200 Palestinians, more than half of them civilians. Seventy-three Israelis were killed.

Then in 2021, a bloody 11-day war between Israel and Hamas was sparked after a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, a site sacred to both Jews and Muslims.

Israel's airstrikes and incursions into Gaza have destroyed entire neighborhoods, forcing thousands to shelter in U.N. schools and other facilities.

Palestinian militants have fired thousands of rockets into Israel. While most are intercepted by Israeli missile defenses or land in open areas, they sow widespread fear and can bring life to a standstill. Their range has steadily increased in recent years, with some striking as far as the major cities of Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.

Why Now?

In recent years, Israel has made peace deals with Arab countries without having to make concessions in its conflict with the Palestinians. The U.S. has been trying to broker a deal between Israel and Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia is a bitter rival of Iran, which provides support to Hamas.

Meanwhile, Israel has a new far-right government, which supports the continuation of Israeli settlements in the Palestinian West Bank. Palestinians and the United Nations consider those settlements to be illegal.

In recent years, Israeli religious nationalists have increased their visits to the Temple Mount compound in Jerusalem. Recently, during the Jewish harvest festival of Sukkot, hundreds of ultra- Orthodox Jews and Israeli activists visited the site. This prompted accusations that Jews were praying there in violation of an agreement where Muslims pray at the Al-Aqsa Mosque and non- Muslims can visit — but not pray.

In some places, they gunned down civilians and soldiers as Israel's military scrambled to muster a response.

Israel's military said on October 10 that it had regained effective control over its south and the border with the Gaza Strip.

The declaration came as the Israeli Defense Forces sought to make good on the government's vow to hunt down the militants and to intensify an assault on densely populated Gaza, the Palestinian territory ruled by Hamas and home to 2 million people.

The latest eruption of violence raised the specter of another devastating war and once again drew international attention to the impoverished, densely populated strip.

Here's a look at the Gaza Strip and its place in the Middle East conflict.

A Narrow Coastal Strip

Gaza, sandwiched between Israel and Egypt, is just 25 miles (40 kilometers) long and 6 miles (10 kilometers) wide. It was part of the British-ruled Palestine Mandate before the 1948 Arab- Israeli War. After the war, Gaza came under Egypt's control.

Large numbers of Palestinians who fled or were driven from what is now Israel during that war ended up in Gaza, and the refugees and their descendants now number 1.4 million, accounting for more than half of Gaza's population.

Israel captured Gaza, along with the West Bank and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war. The Palestinians want all three territories to form their future state.

The first Palestinian intifada, or uprising, erupted in Gaza in 1987 — the same year Hamas was founded — and later spread to the other occupied territories. The Oslo peace process in the 1990s established the Palestinian Authority and gave it limited autonomy in Gaza and parts of the occupied West Bank.

The following year, Hamas won a landslide victory in the Palestinian elections. That triggered a power struggle with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' Fatah party, culminating in a week of clashes in 2007 that left Hamas in control of Gaza.

Hamas has done little in the way of imposing Islamic law on Gaza, which was already very conservative. But it has shown no tolerance for dissent, arresting political opponents and violently suppressing rare protests against its rule.

The militant group has remained firmly in power through three wars and a 16-year blockade.

The Blockade

Israel and Egypt imposed the crippling blockade after the Hamas takeover. Israel says it's needed to keep Hamas and other militant groups from importing arms. Rights groups say the blockade is a form of collective punishment.

The closures, along with years of misrule and Hamas' long-running feud with the Palestinian Authority, have devastated Gaza's economy. Unemployment hovers at around 50 percent, power outages are frequent and the tap water is badly polluted.

Palestinians face heavy movement restrictions that make it difficult to travel abroad for work, study or to visit family, and often refer to Gaza as the world's largest open-air prison.

Hamas and Israel have fought three wars and several smaller battles. The worst so far was the 2014 war, which lasted for 50 days and killed some 2,200 Palestinians, more than half of them civilians. Seventy-three people were killed on the Israeli side.

Then in 2021, a dispute at the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, sacred to both Muslims and Jews, and which includes the Al-Aqsa Mosque, spilled over into a bloody 11-day war between Israel and Hamas.

Its leaders say hundreds of its 40,000 fighters took part in the assault. Israel says the group has about 30,000 fighters and an arsenal of rockets, including some with a range of about 250 kilometers (155 miles), and unmanned drones.

title: Hawaii is turning fishnets and other plastic trash into roads
zhTitle: 夏威夷用废渔网铺路
reason: 海洋垃圾进入沥青的实验，已处理的吨数，以及这条路能走多远。

cover.caption: Plastic waste from the ocean, like fishnets, has been used to pave roads in the state of Hawaii.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Hawaii is turning fishnets and other plastic trash into roads
levels.body:
In Hawaii, ocean trash is being recycled to cover roads. The is an experiment. But it could be a way to deal with a growing cause of pollution: plastic.

Paving roads with plastic is being done in other states too, including in Missouri and Texas. But Hawaii is the first state to try adding trash from the ocean, including old fishing nets. The Hawaiian islands face a unique plastic trash problem. A lot of fishing gear gets thrown into the water. There is also a lot of waste from tourists. There's even some plastic released from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. That is a giant collection of ocean trash in the North Pacific Ocean.

"We're extremely concerned about the shedding of plastics or other chemicals into the environment," says Jennifer Lynch. She is a scientist at Hawaii Pacific University in Honolulu.

Tiny bits of plastic are in the trash. They release chemicals, which are harmful to humans.

Plastic For Pavement

Lynch runs a program where researchers collect and sort plastic and other trash from beaches. They then pick out waste made with the type of strong plastic found in milk jugs and fishing nets. They send the waste and nets to the U.S. mainland. There the waste gets shredded and ground up. The materials are then sent back to Hawaii. There they are mixed with other ingredients to make asphalt. That is the black, gooey stuff made that's often used to pave roads.

Three experimental strips went down in 2022. One had a section of asphalt mixed with a rubber. That makes the road stronger and more flexible. Ground-up ocean trash and the rubber were added to a second batch. A third batch had the ocean trash and asphalt, but no rubber.

Eleven months later, researchers tested how much plastic was released. They found that the pavement with ocean trash released similar amounts of tiny plastic pieces as the pavement with no plastic.

Road Recipes

Phase two of this program started in 2024. It tested five types of pavement, including combos with and without rubber and plastic. Some has ground-up fishing nets. Others had other plastic trash. Data on which pavement performed best should be available soon.

Bill Buttlar is a scientist at the University of Missouri. He is impressed with the program. But he notes that Hawaii is different from the U.S. mainland. Hawaii get a lot of rain. Plus volcanos make the ground move a lot. That can cause cracks in roads. "The main challenge to scaling this is getting the recipe right," Buttlar says. "What works in Hawaii may be a little different than what works in the U.S. Midwest."

Phase two of this program launched in 2024, and it tested five types of pavement, including combos with and without rubber and plastic. Some contained ground-up fishing nets, while others contained other plastic trash, and data on which performed best should be available soon.

Bill Buttlar directs the Mizzou Asphalt Pavement and Innovation Lab, which is at the University of Missouri in Columbia. He's impressed with the program, but still, he notes that Hawaii's roads face different challenges than those on the U.S. mainland. Hawaii's tropical climate brings heavy rains, and volcanic activity there causes the ground to constantly shift, which can crack roads. "The main challenge to scaling this is getting the recipe right," Buttlar says. "What works in Hawaii may be a little different than what works in the U.S. Midwest."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Here's what happened when sixth-graders designed their dream school
levels.body:
A group of sixth-grade students in Arizona designed the schools of their dreams. Some had rooftop gardens. Others had fancy bathrooms.

Knox Gifted Academy is a school in Chandler, Arizona. The project let students build small models of their dream schools.

Tara Menghini and Krista Wilkewitz are technology teachers at the Academy. They led the dream school project together. They wanted students to use digital tools to be creative.

The sixth-graders used coding skills, conducted research, and worked together. They also used their imaginations.

Students Explored Possibilities

The project started with asking kids about their school experience.

"It's a question I don't think kids get asked enough," Menghini said. "What is the purpose of school? Why are you even here? What do you want to get out of school? And then we say, 'what could school look like?'"

Next, the students talked to experts in school design. They talked with a principal whose school was under construction. They interviewed a school architect. An architect is someone who designs buildings.

The class learned about real schools doing unique things. They watched a video about schools that use artificial intelligence. They heard about a school focused on project-based learning.

Menghini used to teach in Japan. She said that students there help with cleaning and serving lunch. She shared that with the students, too.

Virtual And Low-Tech Models

Teams of students brainstormed their dream school. They made a list of must-have features.

Next, they made a model of their school on the computer. This helped students think through their planning, Wilkewitz said.

"They knew, OK, this might work, this might not work," she said.

Kids then made blueprints. Blueprints are special drawings that show details about a building. Next, they made miniature models. They used materials like cardboard, popsicle sticks, and tissue paper.

Projects Show Kids Want Choice

The project helped teachers understand their students.

"They want choice," Menghini said. "They want to know that what they're learning means something."

One student created a kitchen for kids to learn about math. Students might practice fractions while making cupcakes.

Menghini said some students added details for teachers. One group made covered parking spots and charging stations for electric cars.

"They thought of us!" she said.

The school invited families to see the students' final designs.

Wilkewitz said the kids' excitement was the best part.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Here's what happened when 6th-graders designed their dream school
levels.body:
ORLANDO, Florida — Rooftop terraces brimming with gardens. A glamorous school bathroom with lights around the mirrors, like those you'd find in a movie star's makeup room. An air- conditioned indoor recess room, complete with soft, twinkly lights and a sketching and drawing nook.

Those are some of the architectural features and amenities that 6th graders at Knox Gifted Academy, a public magnet school in Chandler, Arizona, incorporated into their dream school facilities, which they brought to life both in virtual and real-life 3D models.

The project was part of a push by technology teachers Tara Menghini and Krista Wilkewitz to prod their students to use digital tools to fuel creativity, not passively consume content.

It also gave students a chance to deploy their coding skills, conduct research, collaborate, and, especially, use their imaginations.

The teachers kicked off the project — which took up about an academic quarter during the students' twice-weekly technology classes — by asking kids about their school experience.

"It's a question I don't think kids get asked enough, or at least are not asked their feedback about: What is the purpose of school? Why are you even here?" Menghini said. "What do you want to get out of school? And then we say, 'what could school look like?'"

The students then met with experts in school design.

They interviewed an experienced local school architect on Zoom, who could tell from the wall behind the students that their school had been built in the 1970s.

They FaceTimed with the principal of a nearby campus under construction as he walked through the site wearing his hard hat.

The class also researched real-world — but outside-the-box — possibilities. They watched a news video about Alpha Schools, a network of private schools that rely heavily on artificial intelligence to provide instruction for part of each day. They learned about Design 39 in San Diego, a public pre-K-8 school dedicated to project-based learning.

And Menghini talked to the students about her experience teaching in Japan, where students play an active role in running the school — including cleaning the building and serving lunch.

The students then brainstormed their dream school in teams and decided on its nonnegotiable features.

Next, they created digital versions of their schools — or classrooms — that they could explore in virtual reality, specifically using Delightex, a 3D-immersive platform. (Knox Academy has a paid version, but there is also a free version. Minecraft Education is another option, Menghini suggested.)

The digital aspect of the project helped students more completely think through their planning, Wilkewitz said.

It allowed for "modeling and working out the kinks, so that when they got to their physical build, they knew, OK, this might work, this might not work," she said.

Kids then used their math skills to sketch out blueprints. Next, they made real-life models of their dream schools using decidedly low-tech materials: matboard or cardboard, popsicle sticks, fake foliage, wood cubes, fabric, tissue paper, dowel rods, toothpicks, pompoms, and more. (For this, Wilkewitz and Menghini visited a 4,000-square-foot recycling center and carted away donated junk for free.)

The teachers also prepped students with training on some potentially dangerous tools — including hot glue guns and X-Acto knives.

The project gave the teachers some insight into what their students think and worry about.

One student created a test kitchen where kids could learn about math concepts, like fractions, while baking cupcakes, making pizzas, or decorating cinnamon buns.

"The things that the kids wanted to change have to do with agency," Menghini said. "They want choice, they want to know that what they're learning means something."

Menghini was also touched that one group's model included covered parking spots so teachers' cars wouldn't overheat in the Arizona sun, complete with solar panels to power electric vehicle charging stations.

"They thought of us!" she said.

At the project's conclusion, the school invited parents to visit for a glimpse inside the students' fantasy facilities.

"I feel like it's the most important part," Wilkewitz said, "…kids getting to show and be excited about what they did."

title: High schooler's coloring book tells story of Ohio immigrants
zhTitle: 高中生画的移民故事涂色书
reason: 从涂色书学英语，到自己出三本书，一名辛辛那提学生把经历做成了作品。

cover.caption: Asifiwe Shema, a rising junior at Aiken New Tech High School, shows fourth-graders at Roselawn Condon School pictures he included in his memoir.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: High schooler's coloring book tells story of Ohio immigrants
levels.body:
Asifiwe Shema is a student in Cincinnati, Ohio. His family arrived from Africa when Shema was younger. He did not speak English when he arrived.

Then, he learned English words from coloring books.

The coloring books had words and pictures. He used them to learn English.

Shema is 17. And now he has written his own coloring book for others.

Learning English In The Garage

Shema and his family are from Burundi. Burundi is a country in Africa. They moved to the U.S. as refugees. A refugee is a person who has to leave their country because it is not safe. People might have to leave their countries for many reasons. One example could be a large flood.

Shema started school in Cincinnati in 2019. He made friends who spoke many languages.

Then the world changed in 2020. There was a virus that made everyone stay inside. It was COVID-19. Shema had to go to school from his family's garage.

Online school was not easy. But Shema learned English by using coloring books. He matched words with pictures.

"English started to click for me," he said. "Every single day I improved."

From Memoirs to Coloring Books

Shema's first book is about his family's move from Africa. The second book is about his time at school. He worked with a group that helps immigrants share their stories.

An Ohio group asked Shema to make a coloring book. The people in the group support immigrants. The book is called "Ohio Is My Second Country."

Shema got ideas from his family and friends.

Figures From Around The World

The pages in the coloring book show people from many places. The book has words in 15 languages.

The Ohio Immigrant Alliance paid Shema $1,000 for the project. He saved $700. He gave $150 to his mom.

Shema said he learned that showing care is like planting flowers. It makes something beautiful.

At first, Shema read coloring books. Then he learned English and wrote two books about his life. He made a coloring book. Now he shares his voice with others. From something small came something big.

levels.title: High schooler's coloring book tells story of Ohio immigrants
levels.body:
Asifiwe Shema is not the average high school student. He has published three books and designed a T-shirt for the United Nations. He's a leader in the school's Future Farmers of America club. This fall, he's entering 11th grade at Aiken New Tech High School in Cincinnati, Ohio. He's already thinking about college. He is thinking of studying business or art.

He said it all started with coloring books. His 4th-grade teachers gave them out to students when COVID-19 began in 2020.

"Those coloring books had words beside the pictures," he told a group of fourth-graders at his old school. "And as I colored, I learned English slowly but surely."

Shema is now 17. He came to the United States speaking Swahili and French, but not English. But it was coloring books that helped him learn the new language.

And now, a coloring book is one of his three books.

Learning English In The Garage

Shema and his family came from Burundi, a country in Africa, in 2019. They came to the United States through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program. This helps refugees, or people who cannot return to their home country because of different reasons. People can become refugees for many reasons. One reason could be environmental disasters, such as floods.

In fall of 2019, Shema started school in Cincinnati. He made many friends who spoke lots of different languages.

When COVID-19 made everyone stay home, "everything changed," he said. "My teachers became faces on a screen, and my friends turned into small boxes on a computer."

Every day, Shema attended school from his home's garage. He learned English by using coloring books to match words with pictures.

"English started to click for me," he said. "Every single day I improved."

From Memoirs To Coloring Books

Shema has two memoirs. These are autobiographies that focus on a certain time in a person's life. Shema's first memoir, "Unexpected Change," is about his family's move from Africa. The second memoir, "Unexpected Growth," is about his time at school and during the lockdown. He published the books with a group that helps immigrant students share their stories.

"I wrote every day, using words I learned from coloring books and turning them into poems," he said. One of his poems is called "Seed by Seed, I Grow."

The Ohio Immigrant Alliance heard about Shema's memoir, "Unexpected Growth." Then the group asked Shema to make a coloring book. His new book is called "Ohio Is My Second Country."

"Many migrants carry the feeling of being from two places for the rest of their lives, and love both," the group said.

Shema said family and school friends inspired some of the 19 illustrations in the book. "I have a diverse group of friends," he said.

Figures From Across The Globe

One "Ohio Is My Second Country" page shows a man and woman from Guatemala with a bird native to their country. Guatemala is in Central America. Another shows women from Burundi in special clothes. (His mother coached him on that one.) A third pictures a soccer player who could be from many countries. The book's cover shows people from Cincinnati who come from many different countries.

The book has captions in 15 languages with the black-and-white pictures.

The Ohio Immigrant Alliance paid him $1,000 for the project. He put $700 in the bank and gave $150 to his mother.

"Every seed begins small," Shema told a group of 4th graders, reading from his memoir poem. He said he learned that caring (about others, life, and himself) is like planting flowers. It makes something beautiful.

At first, Shema read coloring books. Then he learned English and wrote two memoirs. He got the chance to make a coloring book of his own. Now he is sharing his voice with others. From something small came something big.

Aiken New Tech High School student Asifiwe Shema has published three books and designed a T- shirt for a United Nations group. He's a leader in the school's Future Farmers of America club who is featured in a new documentary. A junior this fall, he's gunning for college, maybe for business, maybe for art.

It's all been possible, he said, because of coloring books his fourth-grade teachers gave him at the start of COVID-19.

"Those coloring books had words beside the pictures, and as I colored, I learned English slowly but surely," he told current fourth-graders during a recent visit to Roselawn Condon, the school that helped launch him.

Shema, now 17, had come to the United States speaking Swahili and French, but not English.

A coloring book is now one of his three published titles.

Learning English In The Garage

Shema, his parents and his eight siblings arrived from the central African country of Burundi in mid-2019 under the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program.

That fall, teachers welcomed Shema to Roselawn Condon, a pre-kindergarten to eighth-grade Cincinnati Public School, and he found friends who spoke a variety of other languages.

When COVID-19 sent him home, "everything changed," he said in one of his memoirs.

"My teachers became faces on a screen, and my friends turned into small boxes on a computer."

Day by day – working from a makeshift classroom in the garage of his family's Delhi Township home – Shema expanded his English skills by connecting words and pictures in coloring books.

"English started to click for me," he said. "Every single day I improved."

Shema's first memoir, "Unexpected Change," explains his family's journey from Africa. The second, "Unexpected Growth," focuses on his time at Roselawn Condon and the lockdown months. He published them with Maketank Inc, a nonprofit that publishes memoirs of immigrant and refugee students.

"I wrote every day, using words I learned from coloring books and turning them into poems," he said in the second title, introducing a poem he called "Seed by Seed, I Grow."

"Many migrants carry the feeling of being from two places for the rest of their lives, and love both," the Columbus-based immigrant advocacy group said in promoting the book.

cover.caption: NASA astronaut José Hernández waits to enter the space shuttle discovery at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida on August 7, 2009. Since he was a young child, he set the goal of becoming an astronaut.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: "A Million Miles Away" tells story of Latino migrant worker turned NASA astronaut
levels.body:
José Hernández grew up working in the California fields. He was a migrant farmworker with his family. When he was 10 years old he realized he wanted to be an astronaut.

In 1972, Hernández was watching the last Apollo mission on television. He remembers watching men walk on the moon in black-and-white. He went outside and looked up at the moon. That's when he knew he wanted to be an astronaut.

Hernández made that dream come true. He became a NASA astronaut. He is also an engineer. An engineer is a person who invents, designs, tests, and builds systems, processes, and products to solve problems.

A movie about Hernández is now streaming on Amazon Prime. It is called "A Million Miles Away." It follows Hernández and his family. They traveled from a rural village in Mexico to the fields of California. The movie then follows Hernández's journey all the way to the International Space Station (ISS). The ISS is a laboratory that circles the Earth. It is where astronauts from around the world live and learn about space.

A Family Effort

Hernández said he did not go from being a migrant farmworker to being an astronaut on his own. He had a lot of help. He said the movie did a good job showing this.

Everyone pitched in. His parents stopped moving from field to field. They put their dream of building a home back in Mexico on the back burner. Hernández's wife also put her dream of opening a restaurant on hold. She did this so Hernández could focus on NASA.

Hard Work Pays Off

NASA picked Hernández for astronaut training in May 2004. He had been turned down 11 times before that.

"I felt I had done the work and the preparation,'" Hernández said. But he knew he might not get picked. Around 12,000 people applied for 15 spots.

"But I still thought, 'It's about time.' Because I felt so ready many cycles before," he said.

He completed training in 2006. His mission launched into orbit in 2009.

Hernández doesn't just want viewers to feel inspired. He wants to help them put their dreams into action.

"It's worth dreaming big, as long as you're willing to put in the work and effort," Hernández said. "There's a recipe there, sprinkled throughout the movie. It's an inspirational movie but you also have some tools to take home with you."

Directed and co-written by Mexican filmmaker Alejandra Márquez Abella, whose credits include "Northern Skies Over Empty Space" and "The Good Girls," the film did a "masterful job at representing my story and ensuring that it wasn't just a story about one individual rising as a migrant farmworker to become a U.S. NASA astronaut but rather a community effort," Hernández adds.

title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
zhTitle: 旧货店里认出的失踪画作
reason: 一次辨认怎样被证实，艺术品鉴定要走的几道程序。

cover.caption: A woman bought this painting for $4 at a thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. It turned out to be a valuable work of art by the painter N.C. Wyeth.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
Earlier this year, a woman went shopping for a picture frame. She came out of the store with buried treasure.

The woman went to the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. She dug in a pile of frames and pulled a painting. She bought it for just $4.

Art experts think the painting was created by N.C. Wyeth. He is an American painter. N.C. Wyeth is famous for his portraits and landscapes. He also made paintings to go in the book "Treasure Island."

This discovery is probably his painting "Ramona." It shows a daughter and her foster mother. It is part of a series that went with a book that was also called "Ramona." The book was written in 1884 by Helen Hunt Jackson.

The drawings or paintings that go with a book are called illustrations. The illustrated version of "Ramona" came out in 1939. Wyeth made four paintings to go with the book. Two of the others are still lost.

Many of Wyeth's paintings have sold for a lot of money. Some have even sold for millions of dollars. In September 2023, the woman sold the painting for $191,000.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

After woman first bought the painting, she hung it in her home. One day, she posted a picture of it on Facebook. People online were excited. They told her that it might be painted by a famous artist.

The woman went to the Brandywine Museum of Art. They have the largest collection of Wyeth paintings. She also met with Lauren Lewis. Lewis is an expert on Wyeth's work in particular. Lewis thought the painting could be real.

Bonhams Skinner is the company that sold the painting. Experts at Bonhams Skinner examined the painting. They said that it was real, too. It had the same kind of frame and backing that Wyeth used to use.

Nobody knows how the painting ended up in a thrift store. Bonhams Skinner workers have a theory. Maybe someone connected to the book version of "Ramona" received it as a gift. It might also have been given to Helen Hunt Jackson.

Kathleen Leland works at Bonhams Skinner. She says that discoveries like this one are rare. You probably won't find a rare painting the next time you go to the thrift store. So don't be too hard on yourself!

levels.name: 基础
levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
Earlier this year, a woman was shopping for a picture frame at the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. But, she did not find one.

The painting she pulled out of a mismatched pile of frames at a New Hampshire thrift store turned out to be a long-lost 1930s work by American painter N.C. Wyeth of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania.

The woman bought what is now believed to be N.C. Wyeth's work "Ramona"from Savers for a mere $4. It sold for $191,000 at an auction run by the company Bonhams Skinner.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

The woman remembers how she felt when she pulled it out of the pile of frames. In that moment, she joked that she had maybe found something valuable. Bonhams spokeswoman Sheri Middleton said that the woman's discovery has been "a bit overwhelming for her." She also said that the woman prefers not to have her name released to the media.

The woman decided to hang the painting in her home. She never thought that it was the work of one of America's best painters. When she searched for it on the Internet, she didn't find anything resembling the painting.

N.C. Wyeth's works are distinctive. The works he created from his Chadds Ford studio were known all over the world. He also famously illustrated an edition of the novel "Treasure Island." He lived between 1882 and 1945 and was the father of American master painter Andrew Wyeth.

This piece is one of four Wyeth created for Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 book "Ramona." The book was released with the paintings in 1939. In it, a determined orphan faces her unforgiving foster mother.

The painting stayed in the woman's home for years until she decided to post it on a Facebook group called "Things found in Walls." That's when things got interesting.

Strangers Told Her She Might Have Treasure

Some commenters in the Facebook group recognized the painting as a possible N.C. Wyeth. They sent the woman to the Brandywine Museum of Art in Chadds Ford. They also connected her to a former Wyeth curator in Maine named Lauren Lewis.

Lewis drove three hours to meet the woman, who noticed how excited Lewis was. That was the first time the woman began to realize that the painting might be real.

Painting Fetches Hundreds Of Thousands At Auction

Bonhams Skinner is the company that sold the painting. It was sold at an auction, where people competed to take home the painting by offering the highest price. Some of Wyeth's more famous workshave sold for millions of dollars. Bonhams predicted that the painting would fetch between $150,000 and $250,000. It sold for $191,000.

One of Bonhams Skinner's employees told the woman that the painting was likely real. How did they know? First, it matched Wyeth's signature style. Also, it was placed in a simple frame with a red panel in the back. Both of these were details common to Wyeth's work.

The largest known collection of N.C. Wyeth works is held by the Brandywine Museum of Art. It also offers tours of the artist's Chadds Ford home and studio. Only one of the other three illustrations from the "Ramona" book is known to have been recovered.

It's still not known how the painting ended up in a thrift store. Bonhams Skinner has one theory. They suspect that book publisher Little, Brown and Company gifted it. It might have gone to one of "Ramona'"s editors or ended up with the author's belongings after she died.

Thrift-store lovers shouldn't get their hopes up they'll find lost paintings, said Leland. She said that discoveries like this one are uncommon.

levels.title: Thrift store shopper discovers lost painting by N.C. Wyeth
levels.body:
The woman wasn't shopping for fine art at the Savers thrift store in Manchester, New Hampshire. She was looking for a nice frame that she could put a different picture in.

Instead, she made a life-changing discovery: The painting she pulled out of a mismatched pile of frames at a New Hampshire thrift store turned out to be a long-lost 1930s work by American master N.C. Wyeth of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania.

The woman bought what is now believed to be N.C. Wyeth's work "Ramona" from Savers for a mere $4. It sold for $191,000 at a September 19, 2023, auction run by the company Bonhams Skinner.

"Lost" Painting Hung In Private Home For Years

The woman remembered joking that she had maybe found something valuable when she pulled it out of the pile of frames. Bonhams spokeswoman Sheri Middleton said that the woman's discovery has been "a bit overwhelming for her." She also said that the woman prefers not to have her name released to the media.

The woman decided to hang it in her home, never suspecting it was the work of a well-known American painter. When she searched for it on the Internet, she didn't find anything resembling the painting.

N.C. Wyeth's works are quite distinctive. The works he created from his Chadds Ford studio a were known around the world. He also famously illustrated an edition of the novel "Treasure Island." He lived between 1882 and 1945 and was the father of American master painter Andrew Wyeth.

This piece is one of four Wyeth created for a 1939 edition of Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 book "Ramona." It depicts the tense relationship between an orphan and her unforgiving foster mother. The painting stayed in the woman's home for years until she decided to post it on a Facebook group called "Things found in Walls." That's when things got interesting.

Strangers Told Her She Might Have Treasure

Some commenters in the Facebook group recognized the painting as a possible N.C. Wyeth. They sent the woman to the Brandywine Museum of Art in Chadds Ford. They also connected her to a former Wyeth curator in Maine named Lauren Lewis.

Lewis drove three hours to meet the woman, who noticed how excited Lewis was. That was the first time when the woman began to realize that the painting might be real.

Experts at auction house Bonhams Skinner confirmed that the painting was likely an original. First, it matched Wyeth's signature style. It also was placed in the practical frame and backing panel that Wyeth was known to use.

"Beginning in the mid-1930s, Wyeth used a particular type of artist board: Weber 'Renaissance' panels, distinctive for their red backs and elaborate labels. And this was the case for this painting," auction house expert Kathleen Leland told art blog Hyperallergic this month.

Painting Fetches Hundreds Of Thousands At Auction

Some of Wyeth's better-known works, such as "Portrait of a Farmer,"have sold for millions of dollars at auction. The company had expected the painting to fetch anywhere between $150,000 and $250,000. It ended up selling for $191,000.

The largest known collection of N.C. Wyeth works is held by the Brandywine Museum of Art, which also offers tours of the artist's Chadds Ford home and studio. Only one of the other three illustrations from the "Ramona" book is known to have been recovered.

The question of how the painting ended up in a thrift store has yet to be answered, but the auction house does have one theory. They suspect that book publisher Little, Brown and Company had offered the "Ramona" painting as a gift. It might have been given to either a book editor or to the book author's estate.

Leland said that discoveries such as this are rare. Thrift-store hounds shouldn't get their hopes up that they will find similar lost paintings. "It is difficult for anyone other than an expert in antiques or fine art to be able to recognize the significance of what they have found."

cover.caption: The World Dog Surfing Championships took place in Pacifica, California on August 1, 2026.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Meet the pups who ruled the 2026 world dog surfing championships
levels.body:
Some of the best surfers in the world gathered at a California beach on August 1. But these weren't ordinary surfers. They were dogs! They showed off their talents in the World Dog Surfing Championships. This is the 10th year of the event.

Top Dog of the Day

The top dog of the day was Rippin' Rosie. She is a Labrador retriever from Santa Cruz. Rosie won in the large and extra-large dog category. She also won the stand-up paddleboard contest with her owner, Steve Drottar. And she received the Spirit of Dog Surfing award.

Drottar has surfed for 40 years. He called Rosie his "dream dog." She jumped onto a paddleboard at a lake when she was only 7 months old. Soon after, she was riding ocean waves. Now, they surf four or five days a week.

"As long as I don't mess up," Drottar said. "Rosie's going to do great."

Iza is a French bulldog. She had a bright pink fin on her life jacket. She won first in the medium dog category. She came in second place overall. She also teamed up with Rusty the Surfing MinPin for the dog-dog tandem contest. This is when two dogs ride the same surfboard. Iza and Rusty won this event.

Pups Teaching Pups

Bradley "Shortboard" Cooper won first place in the small dog group. Carson Surf Dog and Rusty came next. Tina Musto and Jill Nakano are Carson and Bradley's owners. Nakano helps the dogs start. Musto helps them finish.

Their surf-dog family began with a dog they rescued from Hawaii. Their dog, Kihei, learned to surf with Nakano. Kihei later helped teach Carson to surf. Carson then helped Bradley learn. "Dogs kind of mimic each other," Musto said. "They want to do what the big brother's doing."

Now, the dogs surf mostly for fun. The family travels to competitions along the California coast.

Rusty had the best style of the event. The miniature pinscher surfs with leopard- or tiger-patterned fur. He also wears goggles with "angry eyes" and a dinosaur-style fin. His owner, Sophia Sadlowski, said Rusty began surfing at 4 months old. He inspired her to learn at age 59.

"He just honestly trained me," Sadlowski said.

Many dog owners have become good friends through surfing. They meet at beaches and cheer for each other's dogs. They help each other with their dogs.

"Everybody loves their dogs," Drottar said. "They love doing something with their dogs."

levels.title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx probe successfully delivers asteroid Bennu samples to Earth
levels.body:
NASA collected samples from an asteroid. NASA is the U.S. space agency. An asteroid is a small rocky object. Asteroids orbit the sun like planets do, though asteroids are much smaller.

Those samples finally landed on Earth. The space capsule landed on September 24. Teams from NASA and the U.S. Air Force collected the capsule. It landed in the Utah desert.

This is the first time NASA has taken an asteroid sample. And it is the first time NASA got the sample back from space.

The Mission

The asteroid is called Bennu. The mission took seven years to complete.

OSIRIS-REx is the spacecraft that collected the samples. It launched from Earth in 2016. The spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018. There, scientists learned the asteroid looked like a pile of gravel and rubble. They thought it would look like solid rock. The scientists had to make a new plan.

OSIRIS-REx had a new landing site. It was much smaller than the first one. But the spacecraft landed. The craft collected samples in 2020. Then, OSIRIS-REx left Bennu in 2021.

The trip was more than 4 billion miles. That's about 6.2 billion kilometers. That is a long long trip to Bennu and back to Earth.

The Capsule

OSIRIS-REx did not land on Earth. It stayed above Earth. It let go of the capsule that held the samples. The capsule fell 63,000 miles. That's about 101,000 kilometers above Earth. The fall took less than 10 minutes in total.

Once on the ground, teams collected the capsule. They checked for damage. But the capsule looked whole. It was not broken. They hooked the capsule up to a helicopter. They took it to a temporary clean room.

Scientists then opened the capsule. Inside was a canister. It held the actual asteroid samples. Teams prepared the sample. They took it to Houston, Texas. That's where NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) is.

What Will Come Of The Samples?

NASA now has 8.8 ounces of material from Bennu. That's about 250 grams. Scientists plan to study the samples. They have many questions. They want to learn about Earth. And they want to learn about the solar system.

NASA will keep most of the sample. It will keep about 70 percent. The rest of the asteroid will be shared with other scientists. About 200 scientists will share 25 percent of the sample. The Canadian Space Agency will get 4 percent. The space agency in Japan will get the smallest amount.

The space capsule with samples landed in the Utah desert. Teams with NASA and the U.S Air Force recovered the capsule.

"Touchdown for science!" said Jim Garvin, chief scientist of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. "For the first time in history, we brought goodies back home from this kind of object. This is so huge and we're all breathing a big sigh of relief."

The Mission

The successful landing and recovery of the asteroid Bennu samples marks the end of a seven-year mission.

OSIRIS-REx, the space craft that collected the samples, launched from Earth in 2016. The spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018. There, it found an asteroid resembling more of a pile of gravel and rubble than a solid rock. Scientists with the mission then had to rethink the plan for the probe's landing. Instead, the spacecraft had to land in an area less than one-quarter of the size of its original intended landing site. The craft collected samples in 2020, and then left Bennu in 2021.

The entire trip was over 4 billion miles (6.2 billion kilometers) to reach Bennu and then make the journey home.

OSIRIS-REx probe released its sample return capsule on September 24. The spacecraft was about 63,000 miles (101,000 kilometers) above Earth. The capsule contains some 8.8 ounces (250 grams) of rocks and other material from Bennu. These materials could help answer some of scientists' most burning questions about the origins of life on Earth and the early days of our solar system.

The OSIRIS-REx capsule reached speeds of up to 27,000 miles per hour (43,450 kilometers per hour) as it descended through Earth's atmosphere. This is the layer of gases that surrounds the planet. The capsule's heat shield experienced temperatures as high as 5,300 degrees Fahrenheit (2,900 Celsius).

The capsule deployed its main parachute at an altitude of about 20,000 feet (6,100 meters). This was four times higher than expected at 5,000 feet (1,500 meters). The capsule appeared to land safely.

The Capsule

As the sample return capsule floated down to the desert floor, the capsule cooled down enough so that U.S. Air Force personnel could approach after locating it. The descent from the edge of the atmosphere to the desert sands took under 10 minutes in total.

"Boy, did we stick the landing," said Dante Lauretta, principal investigator of the OSIRIS-REx mission.

Once on the ground, the surrounding area was examined to make sure it was safe for OSIRIS-REx team members and recovery personnel to approach. Recovery teams found that the capsule was intact. From there, the capsule was hooked up to a helicopter and airlifted to a temporary cleanroom set up at the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground.

Once secured inside the facility, the capsule was opened. The canister inside that contains the sample of asteroid Bennu will be prepared for transport once again. The asteroid material will next be loaded onto an aircraft and flown to NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas. There awaits a newly built facility for studying the samples. It is called the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division.

What Will Come Of The Samples?

"Congratulations to the entire OSIRIS-REx team. You did it!" NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said in a video during live commentary. "This mission proves that NASA does big things. Things that inspire us, things that unite us, things that show that nothing is beyond our reach."

The sample will be divided among different scientific institutions and world space agencies. NASA will keep 70 percent of the sample at JSC. There, scientists will analyze it for years to come. Twenty-five percent will be shared between over 200 scientists at 35 different facilities. Four percent will be given to the Canadian Space Agency, and 0.5 percent will be given to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

OSIRIS-REx is NASA's first to collect an asteroid sample. JAXA has two such missions under its belt. That agency's Hayabusa 1 collected materials from asteroid Itokawa and returned them in 2010. Hayabusa 2 returned samples from asteroid Ryugu in 2020.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx probe successfully delivers asteroid Bennu samples to Earth
levels.body:
DUGWAY PROVING GROUND, Utah — NASA's first-ever samples of an asteroid in deep space have landed safely on Earth in a historic first for the United States.

In a midmorning operation at the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground in the arid Utah desert, teams with NASA and the U.S. Air Force successfully recovered a space capsule with samples of asteroid Bennu taken by the agency's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft in 2020. The mission marks the first time that NASA has taken a sample of an asteroid, not to mention successfully recovering it.

After traveling for over 4 billion miles (6.2 billion kilometers) to reach Bennu and then make the journey home, the OSIRIS-REx probe released its sample return capsule on September 24, while it was about 63,000 miles (101,000 kilometers) above Earth. The capsule contains some 250 grams (8.8 ounces) of rocks and other material from Bennu, material that could help answer some of scientists' most burning questions about the origins of life on Earth and the early days of our solar system.

"Touchdown for science!" Jim Garvin, chief scientist of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said from the landing site during a live broadcast. "For the first time in history, we brought goodies back home from this kind of object. This is so huge and we're all breathing a big sigh of relief."

The OSIRIS-REx capsule reached speeds of up to 27,000 miles per hour (43,450 kilometers per hour) and its heatshield experienced temperatures as high as 5,300 degrees Fahrenheit (2,900 Celsius) as it descended through Earth's atmosphere.

The capsule deployed its main parachute at an altitude of about 20,000 feet, four times higher than expected at 5,000 feet, but it appeared to land safely. Officials with NASA and Lockheed Martin Space Systems, which built OSIRIS-REx, told reporters in the post-landing conference that the drogue chute likely deployed, but was just not seen on cameras monitoring the descent.

"The bottom line is we landed. When the main parachute came out, that was the moment I was waiting for," Mike Moreau, OSIRIS-REx recovery team lead at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said in the briefing. "The drogue's on top of the main parachute, so it all had to come out," he added.

As the sample return capsule floated down to the desert floor of the U.S. Department of Defense's Utah Test and Training Range, the capsule cooled down enough so that U.S. Air Force personnel could approach after locating it.

The descent from the edge of the atmosphere to the desert sands took under 10 minutes in total to end a 4 billion-mile journey. The $1 billion OSIRIS-REx mission launched in 2016, arrived at Bennu in 2018 and collected samples of the asteroid in 2020.

"Boy, did we stick the landing," Dante Lauretta, principal investigator of the OSIRIS-REx mission, said in a post-landing briefing.

Once on the ground, the capsule and surrounding area was examined to make sure it was safe for OSIRIS-REx team members and recovery personnel to approach and examine the capsule. An early examination by recovery teams found that the capsule was intact and suffered no breaches during landing.

From there, the capsule was hooked up to a helicopter via a longline and airlifted to a temporary cleanroom set up at the U.S. Army's Dugway Proving Ground.

Once secured inside the facility, the capsule was opened, and the canister inside that contains the precious sample of asteroid Bennu will be prepared for transport once again. The asteroid material will next be loaded onto an aircraft and flown to NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas, where a newly built facility is waiting for it, the agency's Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division.

"Congratulations to the entire OSIRIS-REx team. You did it!" NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said in a video during live commentary. "This mission proves that NASA does big things. Things that inspire us, things that unite us, things that show that nothing is beyond our reach."

From there, the sample will be divided among different scientific institutions and world space agencies. NASA will keep 70 percent of the sample at JSC where it will analyze it for years to come. Twenty-five percent will be shared between over 200 scientists at 35 different facilities. Four percent will be given to the Canadian Space Agency, and 0.5 percent will be given to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

OSIRIS-REx is NASA's first to collect an asteroid sample, but JAXA has two such missions under its belt. That agency's Hayabusa 1 collected materials from asteroid Itokawa and returned them in 2010, and Hayabusa 2 returned samples from asteroid Ryugu in 2020.

The successful landing and recovery of the asteroid Bennu samples marks the end of a seven-year mission that saw its share of surprises. When the spacecraft arrived at Bennu in 2018, it found an asteroid resembling more of a pile of gravel and rubble than a solid rock. Scientists with the mission then had to rethink the plan for the probe's landing, which required reprogramming the spacecraft to land in an area less than one-quarter of the size of its original intended landing site.

But the OSIRIS-REx team pulled it off. Lauretta said during a pre-landing media briefing on September 22 that the OSIRIS-REx team has been consistent in its ability to work through the unexpected issues that popped up.

"We've always taken a deliberate, careful, cautious approach," Lauretta said. "And I think that's why this mission has been so successful up to this date."

title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches

cover.caption: Hundreds of seashells are scattered along North Carolina's Cape Hatteras National Seashore after Hurricane Lee passed through the region.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches
levels.body:
A hurricane caused huge waves in North Carolina in September 2023. A hurricane is a big storm. It has very high winds. It can also have rain, thunder and lightning. A hurricane can do a lot of damage. People name storms to keep track of the damage. This hurricane was called Lee.

The winds from Hurricane Lee caused big waves. Hurricane Lee brought lots of seashells onto North Carolina's beaches. That made shell hunters very happy.

Seashells are made by sea animals. Shells are a hard, outer layer. They protect the animal that lives inside. Animals such as clams have shells. So do scallops and sea snails.

North Carolina's beaches were full of whelk shells. Whelks are sea snails. They have beautiful, spiraled shells. There were also smaller shells called olives. They are made by olive sea snails. There were even hard-to-find shells like the Scotch bonnet.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

Laura Castro is a shell collector. She saw a photo of a pickup truck. It amazed her. It was full of whelks! They were found on the Outer Banks. This is a string of islands. They are on the coast of North Carolina.

But Castro found something exciting, too. It was a lion's paw scallop shell. They are rare in North Carolina.

Experts say it is not always a good idea to take shells. It may harm the beaches. Birds use shells for their nests. Fish use shells to hide from enemies. So do small crabs. A shoreline can wear away more quickly without shells.

levels.name: 进阶
levels.title: Shell hunters find treasures that Hurricane Lee left on North Carolina's beaches
levels.body:
Hurricane Lee churned up school-bus-sized waves in North Carolina in September 2023. Hurricanes are large storms with strong winds. Those winds can cause big waves. And those big waves turned several North Carolina beaches into treasure troves for shell hunters. The beaches were full of seashells from the storm.

A seashell is a hard, protective outer layer. Seashells are made by some animals that live in the sea. Every empty shell on a beach was once part of an animal. The shells could have belonged to an animal like a clam, scallop, oyster or snail. When these animals die, their shells are left behind.

North Carolina's beaches were full of whelk shells. Whelks are sea snails. They have beautiful, spiraled shells. There were also smaller shells called olives. Olive snails make shells that are long and smooth. There were even hard-to-find shells like the Scotch bonnet. This is another type of sea snail. But as big hurricanes sometimes do, Hurricane Lee left even rarer shells.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

The storm left large amounts of shells after it passed. In some places, collectors said, it was hard to walk on the sand or wade in the surf. They'd always be hitting a whelk or a piece of driftwood.

Shell collector Laura Castro groaned with envy over a photo. It was of a pickup truck full of whelks gathered on the Outer Banks. This is a string of islands that lie along the coast of North Carolina. The Outer Banks saw the storm's biggest waves.

Still, Castro managed to enlarge her own collection. She found an unbroken lion's paw scallop shell at Bear Island. The shells of these scallops are rarely found on North Carolina beaches. That's because the scallops live in deep, dark water. They often live more than 100 feet down. But the storm brought some shells ashore.

Some experts warn against taking seashells from the beach. They say it could hurt the environment. Seashells are an important part of the coast's ecosystem. An ecosystem is a biological community of plants, animals and tiny living things. Birds use seashells to build their nests. Seagrasses and sponges live on them. Fish and hermit crabs use shells to hide from enemies. Removing shells and shell fragments could also change how quickly a shoreline might wear away.

The Best Beaches To Find Shells

No two hurricanes are exactly alike. One storm can cover one section of beach in shells. At the same time, it can wipe miles of nearby shore clean. Still, the beaches below are recommended for shell hunting in North Carolina.

- Holden Beach is an island in Brunswick County. After Hurricane Lee, it was covered with whelks and olive shells. It also had sea biscuits. These are round-shaped animals that live in the sea. They look like puffy versions of their relative, the sand dollar. The sea biscuits were fossils, which are the remains of plants or animals preserved in rock. The sea biscuit fossils were millions of years old. The strong waves pushed the fossils out on the beach from the deep water.

- Cape Point is part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore. A cape is a narrow piece of land. It stretches out into the ocean. Cape Point had many different types of whelks. Collectors found whale bone fossils. There were even octopi!

- Bear Island can be reached by ferry from Hammocks Beach State Park. The waves brought in shells like the lion's paw scallop that Castro found.

Hurricane season lasts through November.

- Shackleford Banks is part of the Cape Lookout National Seashore. This island is a good place to find big whelks and sand dollars.

Here are some of the lion's paw scallop shells that were found on Sunset Beach in North Carolina.
