The Scotch bonnet is also the official shell of the state of North Carolina. But as big hurricanes sometimes do, Hurricane Lee left even rarer shells. These shells aren't usually found within hundreds of miles of the North Carolina coast.

What Have Shell Hunters Found?

The storm left a huge amount of shells after it passed. In some places, collectors said, it was hard to walk on the sand or wade in the surf. They'd always be hitting a whelk or a piece of driftwood.

Shell collector Laura Castro groaned with envy over a photo. It was of a pickup truck full of whelks gathered from the Outer Banks. This is a string of islands that lie along the coast of North Carolina. They saw the storm's biggest waves.

Still, Castro managed to enlarge her own collection. She found an unbroken lion's paw scallop shell at Bear Island. This is part of Hammocks Beach State Park. The shells of these scallops are rarely found on North Carolina beaches because they live in deep, dark water. They often live more than 100 feet down. But the storm brought some ashore.

Some experts warn against removing seashells. They say it could hurt the environment. Seashells are an important part of the coast's ecosystem. An ecosystem is a biological community of plants, animals and tiny living things. Birds use seashells to build their nests. Seagrasses and sponges live on shells. Fish and hermit crabs use them to hide from enemies. The removal of shells and shell fragments could also change how quickly a shoreline might wear away.

The Best Beaches To Find Shells

No two hurricanes are exactly alike. One storm can cover one section of beach in shells, while at the same time, it can wipe miles of nearby shore clean. Still, the beaches below are recommended for shell hunting in North Carolina.

- Holden Beach is an island in Brunswick County. After Hurricane Lee, Holden Beach was covered with whelks and olive shells. It also had sea biscuits, round-shaped animals that live in the sea. They look like puffy versions of their relative, the sand dollar. But the Holden Beach sea biscuits were fossils, which are the remains of plants or animals preserved in rock. The fossils were millions of years old when sea biscuits still lived in North Carolina. The strong waves pushed the fossils out on the beach from the deep water.

- Cape Point is part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore. A cape is a narrow piece of land that stretches out into the ocean. Cape Point had many different types of whelks. Collectors found whale bone fossils. There were even octopi!

- Bear Island can be reached by ferry from Hammocks Beach State Park. The waves brought in shells like the lion's paw scallop that Castro found. She said her best shell finds were partly buried in the edge of the surf.

Hurricane season lasts through November.

- Shackleford Banks is part of the Cape Lookout National Seashore.

This island is a good place to find big whelks and sand dollars.

But as big hurricanes sometimes do, Hurricane Lee also deposited specimens not typically found within hundreds of miles of the North Carolina coast.

In some places, collectors said, it was hard to walk on the sand or wade in the surf without hitting a whelk or a piece of driftwood a day or two after the storm had passed.

But Castro, who lives on Emerald Isle, managed to expand her own collection, finding an intact lion's paw scallop shell at Bear Island, part of Hammocks Beach State Park. Those are rarely found on North Carolina beaches because they live in deep, dark water, often more than 100 feet down.

While thousands of shells have been harvested by collectors, many of whom posted photos of their hauls on social media, several North Carolina beaches still may yield better-than-average buckets full for the next several days.

No two hurricanes are exactly alike, and beach excursion guide Ray Stallings of Hatteras Island says the same storm can cover one section of beach in shells while leaving miles of adjacent shoreline wiped completely clean.

- Holden Beach, a Brunswick County island where a re-nourishment project delivered tons of fossilized sea biscuits in the spring, was covered again with those, whelks and olive shells following Hurricane Lee.

- Cape Point, part of the Cape Hatteras National Seashore, which juts into the Atlantic like an Outer Banks elbow, received maybe the greatest bounty from Hurricane Lee. The beach, accessible by permitted four-wheel-drive vehicles or by a lengthy walk from Ramps 43 and 44 off of North Carolina Highway 12, had a profusion of whelks of different sizes and types. Collectors also have found fossilized whale vertebrae and driftwood along the beach, as well as a number of octopi.

- In Buxton, also on Hatteras Island, Melinda Meadows said on September 18 that guests at her Cape Hatteras Motel came in over the weekend with buckets of shells.

- Bear Island, accessible by ferry from Hammocks Beach State Park, is a popular destination for shell hunters year-round. Hurricane Lee added to the treasures there, bringing in specimens like the lion's paw scallop shell Castro found. While some of the shells were on the beach, Castro said her best finds from the storm have been partially buried in the edge of the surf.

levels.title: What did they find in the West Point time capsule from 1829?
levels.body:
A time capsule was opened on August 28, 2023. A time capsule is a box that holds items to be found many years later. The items are important to the people who fill the box. The time capsule is often buried or hidden for years.

This box was at the United States Military Academy at West Point in New York. It is a military school. The box was filled in 1829. It was placed inside the bottom of a statue.

The statue was of Thaddeus Kosciuszko. He helped the United States during the Revolutionary War. The war lasted from 1775 to 1783.

The box was found almost 200 years after it was hidden in the statue. That was in May 2023, But what was inside?

At First, Disappointment

An event was planned to open the box. A crowd came to see what was in the time capsule. People were excited before the box was opened.

People were disappointed when the box seemed to have only dirt inside.

But later, a better search through the dirt turned up six silver coins. They were made from 1795 to 1828. A medal to celebrate the Erie Canal was also found in the dirt. The canal is a waterway that was completed in 1825. It connected the Great Lakes to the Atlantic Ocean.

The Mystery Box

Steve Gilland is the leader of the academy. At the start, he said no one knew what was in the box. More than 5,000 people also watched the event online. He said that it would "be better than Geraldo."

He was talking about Geraldo Rivera. He is a journalist. Many people watched on TV in 1986 as Rivera opened a secret space that was owned by a famous lawbreaker. That person was Al Capone. The space was empty.

At first, the box at West Point seemed empty, too.

More Careful Searching

Paul Hudson is an archaeologist at West Point. Archaeologists study human history. They often dig up old sites. When Hudson reached into the box, he found only dust.

At the box opening event, the box did not live up to people's hopes, Hudson said.

But he was not ready to stop looking. Hudson did not think someone would put an empty box in the statue.

So he looked more carefully through the dirt.

His search afterward turned up the coins and medal.

People at the event heard more about Kosciuszko. He was a leader from Poland, a country in Europe.

Kosciuszko was known for fighting for freedom.

levels.title: What did they find in the West Point time capsule from 1829?
levels.body:
In 1829, a metal box was closed and placed into the bottom of a monument at a U.S. military academy. The monument was for Revolutionary War hero Thaddeus Kosciuszko.

The box held items from the 1820s and was meant to be opened later. Almost 200 years passed, and in May 2023, the time capsule box was found.

An event was planned to open the box. A crowd came to see what had been put into the 1829 time capsule at the United States Military Academy at West Point in New York. Excitement was building before the August 28, 2023, reveal.

Cadets at the academy had wondered on social media what might be inside. Would the box hold an American flag, boots, old maps of West Point, or maybe dining hall silverware?

The crowd left disappointed, as the opening of the box showed only silt or dirt deposits.

Coins And A Canal Medal

Later, a closer search through the dust revealed six silver coins dating from 1795 to 1828. Their values ranged from 1 cent to a dollar. An 1826 medal honoring the Erie Canal was also discovered in the dirt. The waterway was completed in 1825, connecting the Great Lakes with the Atlantic Ocean.

"Nobody has any idea what's inside of it," U.S. Military Academy leader Steve Gilland had said at the start of the ceremony, which was also seen by more than 5,000 viewers online. "You all are here and are going to see it with all of us." He also said, "It's going to be better than Geraldo."

"Geraldo" was Geraldo Rivera. In 1986, 30 million viewers watched on TV as he opened a secret space kept by famous lawbreaker Al Capone. The opened space contained only dust.

Another leader at the academy, Shane Reeves, also mentioned Rivera at the event.

Three Box Options

Reeves said there were three options for what might happen as they opened the box. The first was that they would find nothing, similar to Rivera's event.

Reeves said someone told him that if "we had a sense of humor, we would have asked Mr. Rivera to be up here with us. [Maybe] we should have done that.'"

The second option would be finding only dust, Reeves said. A third option, he said, would be to find "amazing, historic" items.

The event was a mix of the first and second possibilities.

Hiding Under The Silt And Rocks

Paul Hudson is an archaeologist at West Point. Archaeologists study human history, often by digging up sites. When Hudson reached into the box, he found only dust and silt, bits of rock and dirt.

Opening the box did not live up to everyone's hopes for it, Hudson said. "There is a layer of silt. That's what we were removing here that settled in the bottom." It appears that water got into the box, he said.

But Hudson was not ready to give up on finding something in the box.

"We don't want to think that they went to all the trouble to put this box in the monument and not put anything in it," he said. "We're going to collect all the silt at a later point. We'll screen it through a fine mesh screen to see if we can find any remains in it."

His work after the event turned up the coins and the medal.

"A Son Of Liberty"

Those who attended heard more about Kosciuszko. He was admired by George Washington and was a friend of Thomas Jefferson. Kosciuszko was a leader from Poland.

Jefferson called him "as pure a son of liberty as I have ever known," Reeves said.

Sam Watson, a professor in the academy's history department, said he thought about why Kosciuszko would get a monument.

"He wasn't an American," Watson said. "They didn't choose George Washington. They didn't choose Thomas Jefferson." People chose someone who could represent the fight for freedom around the world, he said.

Watson said Kosciuszko fought for freedom in Poland, calling him "the George Washington of his country."

"I was told yesterday that if we had a sense of humor, we would have asked Mr. Rivera to be up here with us," Reeves said. "I was like, 'We should have done that.'"

Option 2, Reeves said, would be reaching a hand into the box only to find dust, "very much like Indiana Jones in 'Raiders of the Lost Ark,' except we don't want the Angel of Death to come out and melt our faces off, so we're going to hope for not that."

There was a third option, he said: "There are amazing, historic artifacts, something we didn't even know or think about."

They should have booked Geraldo Rivera for what turned out to be a mix of the first and second possibilities.

"The box didn't quite meet expectations," Hudson said. "There is a layer of silt. That's what we were removing here that settled in the bottom. The bottom had bowed out. It appears to have been from moisture penetration."

Potentially, it was something small and organic that may have come apart over time, but we're just not certain."

"Kosciuszko had fought for freedom against the Russians occupying Poland. He really was not just an engineer, not just a military leader, not just a revolutionary. He's all of those things," Watson said. "He was really the George Washington of his country."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Ancient Indigenous earthworks in Ohio named UNESCO World Heritage sites
levels.body:
A group of old mounds in Ohio is now a World Heritage site. It is the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks. It is protected by a group called UNESCO. The group's name is short for United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. It chooses the sites. They are picked because they are important to culture, history and science.

Many people want to keep the site safe. They include Ohio History Connection and Indigenous tribes. They worked together to make sure the earthworks were recognized. They said the mounds are special.

The earthworks are made up of eight sites. They are in southern Ohio. One is on a golf course. The Hopewell sites are now even more important. Other World Heritage sites include Machu Picchu in Peru and the Great Wall of China.

Skills On Display

Chief Glenna Wallace is from the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. She is very excited about the World Heritage designation.

Wallace said everyone should see the skills of the earthwork builders. She said her ancestors were smart and talented.

The earthworks were made thousands of years ago near the Ohio River. People traveled to them from far away. Archaeologists found things from distant places. Some were from the Rocky Mountains in Colorado.

Recognizing America's Indigenous People

Deb Haaland works for the United States government. She said UNESCO recognizes America's Indigenous people.

Audrey Azoulay is with UNESCO. She said the site is an important part of American history. It is one of the biggest earthwork structures in the world.

It Took Many People And Years

The National Congress of American Indians supported the UNESCO listing. So did the Seneca Nation of New York State. The Inter-Tribal Council represents tribes in Northeast Oklahoma. It backed it, too.

Megan Wood is in charge of Ohio History Connection. She said it took more than ten years to add the site. Tribes and the National Park Service helped.

There are five sites in Chillicothe, Ohio. They are Mound City Group, Hopewell Mound Group, Seip Earthworks, High Bank Earthworks and Hopeton Earthworks. They are part of Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.

Fort Ancient Earthworks and Great Circle Earthworks are two more sites. Octagon Earthworks is the last. It is on a golf course.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine thinks the state's first World Heritage site will bring more visitors. People will see a special part of history.

levels.title: Ancient Indigenous earthworks in Ohio named UNESCO World Heritage sites
levels.body:
A group of ancient Indigenous ceremonial and burial mounds in Ohio was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage sites on September 19, 2023. UNESCO is short for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. A World Heritage site has cultural, historical, scientific or other importance. It is legally protected through UNESCO.

Groups of people want to protect the sites. They include Ohio History Connection and Indigenous tribes with ties to the area. They worked together to get the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks recognized. They said that the earthworks are in good shape and are culturally important. They called them "masterpieces of human genius."

The earthworks are made up of eight sites. They are located across 90 miles (150 kilometers) in southern Ohio. This includes a mound on a private golf course and country club. The designation puts the Hopewell sites in the same group as famous places like Machu Picchu and the Great Wall of China.

Feeling Excited And Thoughtful

Chief Glenna Wallace is from the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. She said that she felt very excited about the World Heritage designation.

Wallace said, "Tears came to my eyes, and exhilaration turned into reflection." She added that it is important for the world to see and recognize the spirituality, artistic skills and architectural knowledge of their ancestors who created the earthworks. She described her ancestors as true geniuses.

The earthworks were built between 2,000 and 1,600 years ago near the Ohio River. People from different parts of the continent came to these sites for ceremonies. Archaeologists found things from as far away as the Rocky Mountains. The Rocky Mountains are in Colorado.

Recognition Of America's Indigenous People

Interior Secretary Deb Haaland said that this is a great recognition of America's Indigenous people.

She said the "designation is an opportunity for the United States to share the whole story of America and the remarkable diversity of our cultural heritage, as well as the beauty of our land."

The eight Hopewell sites are amazing because they are so big. They also line up with stars, planets and patterns in the sky.

UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay said the earthworks will teach people about this important part of American history.

Three months ago, the United States joined UNESCO again. Now, its 25th site is on the World Heritage List. This shows the variety of the country's cultural and natural heritage, Azoulay said. She added that the site's inclusion on the list recognizes the important work of American archaeologists. They found remains here that are 2,000 years old. It is one of the biggest earthwork constructions in the world.

It Took Many People And Years

The National Congress of American Indians and the Seneca Nation of New York State were among the tribes that supported the UNESCO listing. The Inter-Tribal Council, which represents tribes in Northeast Oklahoma, also backed it.

The process was slowed by a court battle to restore public access to one of the earthworks. The Moundbuilders Country Club had leased it for a members-only golf course in Newark, Ohio. In December 2022, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled in favor of Ohio History Connection. It allowed them to take control of the Octagon Earthworks. It is one of the eight sites.

Megan Wood is the head of Ohio History Connection. She said it took over ten years for her organization and its partners to add the site. The partners include tribes and the National Park Service.

Other Ohio sites are Fort Ancient Earthworks in Oregonia and Great Circle Earthworks in Heath. In Chillicothe, there are five sites: Mound City Group, Hopewell Mound Group, Seip Earthworks, High Bank Earthworks and Hopeton Earthworks. They are in the Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine thinks that the state's first World Heritage site will attract more visitors. People will see a special part of Ohio's history.

levels.title: Ancient Indigenous earthworks in Ohio named UNESCO World Heritage sites
levels.body:
A group of ancient Indigenous ceremonial and burial mounds in Ohio, described as "part cathedral, part cemetery and part astronomical observatory," was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage sites on September 19, 2023. UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. A World Heritage site has cultural, historical, scientific or other significance. It is legally protected through UNESCO.

Preservationists, led by the Ohio History Connection and Indigenous tribes, many with ancestral ties to the state, worked to have the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks recognized. They pointed out their good condition, unique style and cultural importance. They described them as "masterpieces of human genius."

At a meeting in Saudi Arabia, the World Heritage Committee of UNESCO approved the application.

The earthworks consist of eight sites. They are spread out over 90 miles (150 kilometers) in southern Ohio. This includes one mound on a private golf course and country club. The designation puts the Hopewell sites in the same category as well-known places like Machu Picchu and the Great Wall of China.

Excitement And Reflection

Chief Glenna Wallace is from the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma. She said that she reacted to the World Heritage designation with "pure excitement and exhilaration."

Wallace said, "Tears came to my eyes, and exhilaration turned into reflection." She added that it is important for the world to see and acknowledge the commitment, spirituality, artistic skills and architectural knowledge of their ancestors who created the impressive earthworks. She described her ancestors as true geniuses.

The earthworks were built between 2,000 and 1,600 years ago along branches of the Ohio River. People from different parts of the continent came to these sites for elaborate ceremonies. There is archaeological evidence of materials from as far west as the Rocky Mountains.

The application said that the sites had hosted large ceremonies connected to the order of the world. It talked about the presence of beautiful objects used in rituals, important religious symbols and special clothes.

Recognition Of America's Indigenous People

According to Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, this is a great recognition of America's Indigenous people.

"World Heritage designation is an opportunity for the United States to share the whole story of America and the remarkable diversity of our cultural heritage, as well as the beauty of our land," she said.

The eight Hopewell sites are impressive because they are large and accurately align with geometric and astronomical patterns. For example, they mark all eight lunar standstills over a cycle of 18.6 years.

UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay said that adding the earthworks to the list will help people around the world learn about this important part of American history.

Three months ago, the United States rejoined UNESCO. Now, its 25th site is on the World Heritage List. This shows "the richness and diversity of the country's cultural and natural heritage," Azoulay said. "This inscription on the World Heritage List highlights the important work of American archaeologists, who discovered here remains dating back 2,000 years, constituting one of the largest earthwork constructions in the world."

Many Groups And Years Involved

The National Congress of American Indians and the Seneca Nation of New York State were among the tribes that backed the UNESCO recognition. The Inter-Tribal Council, which represents tribes in Northeast Oklahoma, also supported it.

The process was slowed by a long court battle to restore public access to one of the earthworks. The Moundbuilders Country Club had leased it for a members-only golf course in Newark, Ohio. In December 2022, the Ohio Supreme Court ruled in favor of Ohio History Connection. It allowed them to take control of the Octagon Earthworks. The Octagon Earthworks is one of the eight recognized sites.

Megan Wood is the executive director of Ohio History Connection. She said that it took more than ten years for her organization and its partners to add the site. Its partners include tribes and the National Park Service.

"We are beyond excited to share these sites with more and more Ohioans, Americans and world travelers," she said.

Other Ohio sites are Fort Ancient Earthworks in Oregonia and Great Circle Earthworks in Heath. In Chillicothe, there are five sites: Mound City Group, Hopewell Mound Group, Seip Earthworks, High Bank Earthworks and Hopeton Earthworks. They are in the Hopewell Culture National Historical Park.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine believes the state's first World Heritage site will draw even more visitors to these amazing places. They will see a special part of Ohio's history.

levels.body:
COLUMBUS, Ohio — A network of ancient Indigenous ceremonial and burial mounds in Ohio, described as "part cathedral, part cemetery and part astronomical observatory," was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage sites on September 19, 2023. UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. A World Heritage site has cultural, historical, scientific or other significance. It is legally protected through UNESCO.

Preservationists, led by the Ohio History Connection, and Indigenous tribes, many with ancestral ties to the state, pushed to recognize the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks. They pointed out their good condition, distinct style and cultural significance. They described them as "masterpieces of human genius."

UNESCO's World Heritage Committee approved the application during a meeting in Saudi Arabia.

The earthworks consist of eight ancient sites. They are spread across 90 miles (150 kilometers) of southern Ohio. This includes one mound on the grounds of a private golf course and country club. The designation puts the Hopewell sites in the same category as the wonders of the world, including Peru's Machu Picchu and the Great Wall of China.

"Pure excitement and exhilaration" was the reaction of Chief Glenna Wallace of the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma.

"Tears came to my eyes, and exhilaration turned into reflection, knowing that the world will now see and recognize the commitment, spirituality, imaginative artistry and knowledge of complex architecture to produce magnificent earthworks," she said in a statement. "Our ancestors were true geniuses."

Constructed between 2,000 and 1,600 years ago along branches of the Ohio River, the earthworks hosted ceremonies that drew people from across the continent. There is archaeological evidence of raw materials from as far west as the Rocky Mountains.

Elaborate ceremonies linked to "the order and rhythms of the cosmos" are seen in the "beautiful ritual objects, spectacular offerings of religious icons and regalia" found at the sites, the application stated.

Interior Secretary Deb Haaland said this is a "tremendous" recognition of America's Indigenous people.

"World Heritage designation is an opportunity for the United States to share the whole story of America and the remarkable diversity of our cultural heritage, as well as the beauty of our land," she said.

The eight Hopewell sites are notable for their enormous scale and geometric and astronomical accuracy. An example is the encoding of all eight lunar standstills over an 18.6-year cycle.

UNESCO Director-General Audrey Azoulay said the earthworks' inclusion on the list "will make this important part of American history known around the world."

"Just three months after rejoining UNESCO, the United States has its 25th site inscribed on the World Heritage List, which illustrates the richness and diversity of the country's cultural and natural heritage," she said. "This inscription on the World Heritage List highlights the important work of American archaeologists, who discovered here remains dating back 2,000 years, constituting one of the largest earthwork constructions in the world."

The National Congress of American Indians and the Seneca Nation of New York State were among the tribes that supported the UNESCO designation. So, too, was the Inter-Tribal Council representing tribes living in Northeast Oklahoma The process was slowed by a long court battle to restore public access to one of the earthworks leased to the Moundbuilders Country Club. Its members-only golf course in Newark, Ohio, sits inside it. A ruling of the Ohio Supreme Court in December 2022 allowed Ohio History Connection, the state's historical society, to proceed with an ongoing effort to gain control of the Octagon Earthworks in Newark. It is one of eight sites recognized.

Ohio History Connection executive director Megan Wood said the addition of the site was the result of more than a decade of work by her organization and its partners. Its partners include tribes and the National Park Service.

"We are beyond excited to share these sites with more and more Ohioans, Americans and world travelers," she said.

Other Ohio sites under the new designation are Fort Ancient Earthworks in Oregonia and Great Circle Earthworks in Heath. There are five sites within the Hopewell Culture National Historical Park in Chillicothe: Mound City Group, Hopewell Mound Group, Seip Earthworks, High Bank Earthworks and Hopeton Earthworks.

title: PRO/CON: Data Centers
zhTitle: 数据中心：正方与反方
reason: 同一件事的两篇社论并排放着，用水、用电与税收在两边各被算成了什么。

cover.caption: A data center and its backup diesel generators built by the Markley Group loom over a ballpark and residential neighborhood in Lowell, Massachusetts, on June 30, 2026.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: PRO/CON: Data Centers
levels.body:
PRO: Data Centers Aren't the Enemy — They're the Future

The Editors, Bloomberg Opinion

They look like plain warehouses. But data centers — big buildings full of computers that store information — have become a hot political topic. Some lawmakers want a moratorium, which means a temporary stop, on building new ones. That would be a mistake.

A Growing Industry

About 4,000 data centers already exist in the U.S. Companies plan to build 3,000 more. In 2024, companies spent more than $450 billion building them worldwide. Data centers help power things people use every day, like video apps and online banking. Also, they power artificial intelligence, or AI. Those are computer programs that can learn and make decisions.

Data centers can help the towns where they are built. They pay a lot in taxes. In one Virginia county, data centers provide almost half of the town's tax money. That money helps pay for schools. Building a data center can also mean better roads and stronger power lines for everyone nearby.

Data centers help the whole country too. In 2023, they added $727 billion to the U.S. economy. Every data center job helps create six and a half other jobs.

Still, data centers have downsides. They can be big, loud, and not pretty to look at. They use a lot of water and electricity. Because of this, some communities are protesting them.

Managing Water Use

One worry is water use. Many data centers use "closed-loop" liquid cooling systems to keep their computers from getting too hot. This can use up water that towns need. But the problem is often smaller than people think. One large data center in Memphis uses about as much water as two and a half fast-food restaurants.

Instead of banning data centers, leaders should ask companies to share how much water they use. Companies should also reuse wastewater instead of wasting it.

Solving the Energy Challenge

Energy use is another real worry. Data centers used 17% more electricity in 2025 than in 2024. This demand could double by 2030.

Still, this doesn't call for panic. It calls for planning. Companies that build data centers should help pay to upgrade the power grid. It should be easier for these companies to make their own electricity.

None of this is simple. But over time, data centers and communities can work together. Data centers aren't the enemy. They're the future.

The Bloomberg Editorial Board publishes the views of the editors across a range of national and global affairs. Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

CON: It's Time to Halt the AI Data Center Attack

Mitch Jones, Food & Water Watch

Gas prices have risen quickly because of the war with Iran. But rising energy prices aren't only caused by events far away. A bigger cause has been much closer to home: AI data centers.

An Alarming Discovery

Companies are racing to build huge data centers. They power artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency, a type of digital money. This building boom is changing communities across the country. And it's changing for the worse.

Last year, our organization, Food & Water Watch, began studying data centers. What we found was alarming.

Energy use from AI data centers in the U.S. is expected to triple between 2020 and 2030. These centers could soon use enough electricity to power more than 55 million homes for a year. The largest data centers could use as much electricity as 2 million homes combined.

This is a serious problem. More than half of the energy used by data centers comes from fossil fuels like coal and natural gas. Burning these fuels adds to climate change, causing stronger storms and rising sea levels.

Data centers also use huge amounts of water to cool their computers. By 2028, U.S. data centers could use enough water to fill more than 1 million Olympic swimming pools every year. Meanwhile, many communities already struggle to get affordable water.

The Cost to American Families

The most direct effect on Americans is cost. Because of rising demand from data centers, power companies asked state governments to collect $31 billion more in customer charges in 2025. That's double what they asked for the year before. Electricity prices have jumped 31% since 2020. Families are feeling the difference in their monthly bills.

Communities Push Back

Because of these problems, people are fighting back. Last October, our organization became the first national group to call for a full moratorium on new AI data center construction. Since then, 250 more groups have joined our call. Senator Bernie Sanders recently introduced a bill in Congress to create a nationwide pause.

Communities across the country are taking action too. Many have already rejected new data center proposals. Others have passed laws to slow down construction.

We need a national pause on AI data center construction now. No one has proven that this industry can operate safely without harming people's health or the environment. Until that question is answered, we shouldn't keep building.

Mitch Jones is the managing director of policy and litigation at Food & Water Watch, a national environmental organization fighting for safe food, clean water and a livable climate. He wrote this for InsideSources.com.

figures.caption: A data center and its backup diesel generators built by the Markley Group loom over a ballpark and residential neighborhood in Lowell, Massachusetts, on June 30, 2026.

An aerial view of a 33 megawatt data center with a closed-loop cooling system, amid warehouses on October 20, 2025, in Vernon, California. A closed-loop cooling system continuously reuses the same water. The water absorbs heat from electronics, is then cooled and recirculated to cool the equipment again. Because the system is sealed, it conserves water. It requires a large volume of water just once to fill the sealed pipes during setup.

Electricity prices have jumped 31% since 2020, compared to just 4% in the five years before that. Families are feeling the difference in their monthly bills.

Communities Push Back

Because of these problems, people are fighting back. Last October, our organization became the first national group to call for a full moratorium on new AI data center construction. Since then, 250 more organizations have joined our call. Senator Bernie Sanders recently introduced a bill in Congress to create a similar nationwide pause.

Communities across the country are taking action too. Many have already rejected new data center proposals and passed local rules to slow down construction.

We need a national pause on AI data center construction now. No one has proven that this industry can operate safely without harming people's health, finances or environment. Until that question is answered, we shouldn't keep building.

levels.body:
PRO: Data Centers Aren't the Enemy — They're the Future

By The Editors, Bloomberg Opinion

They look like plain warehouses. But data centers — large buildings full of computer servers and equipment — have become a heated political issue. Politicians from both parties want laws to restrict them. Some even want a moratorium, or temporary ban, on building any new ones. That would be a serious mistake.

A Growing Industry

About 4,000 data centers already exist across the U.S., according to one estimate, with 3,000 more on the way. In 2024, companies worldwide spent more than $450 billion building these facilities. Data centers support much of modern life: cloud computing for communication, banking and health care; services like YouTube, TikTok and Zoom; and, increasingly, artificial intelligence, or AI.

For the communities that host them, data centers can bring real benefits. For one thing, they generate substantial tax revenue. In Loudoun County, Virginia, data centers provide nearly half of the county's total tax money, helping fund schools and other public needs. To support these facilities, power companies often expand their equipment and build new internet infrastructure, which benefits everyone nearby. Construction can be disruptive, but it often leaves behind better roads and stronger power systems.

More importantly, data centers boost economic growth across the whole country. One study found that they added $727 billion to the U.S. economy in 2023. And, every data center job supports six and a half other jobs elsewhere. Data centers will only become more important as AI continues to advance.

That said, data centers do have drawbacks. They can be large, loud and unattractive. They can use a lot of water and electricity. They've also become a symbol of broader fears about AI. As a result, many data centers are facing protests or lawsuits, and about a dozen states are considering laws to restrict them. According to one estimate, this opposition has already blocked more than $150 billion in potential investment.

So what should be done? First, do no harm. A national moratorium would only slow growth, block innovation and cause America to fall behind in the global race to develop AI technology. It's better to enjoy the benefits of data centers while working to reduce their downsides.

Managing Water Use

Consider water use. Many data centers use "closed loop" liquid cooling systems to manage the intense heat produced by powerful computer chips. In some areas, this could strain water supplies. But the problem shouldn't be exaggerated. One analysis found that the water used by a major data center in Memphis — one of the largest in the world — is about equal to the water used by two and a half fast-food restaurants.

The goal shouldn't be to block data centers entirely. Instead, lawmakers should require companies to be transparent about their water use. At the same time, they should encourage them to recycle wastewater and to build systems that reuse water rather than waste it. Lawmakers should also invest in infrastructure and water replenishment programs to help make up for what data centers use.

Solving the Energy Challenge

Another reasonable concern is energy use. Global electricity demand from data centers rose 17% in 2025. And AI-focused centers grew fastest of all. This demand could double by 2030.

Still, this doesn't call for panic — it calls for planning. Companies that build data centers should help pay for the power upgrades to the electricity grids their facilities require. It should also be easier for these companies to generate more of their own electricity. Lawmakers should speed up the approval process for new energy projects as well. Faster approval would benefit the economy.

None of this is simple, of course. But over time, as the goals of tech companies and communities line up more closely, more people should recognize the obvious: data centers aren't the enemy. They're the future.

The Bloomberg Editorial Board publishes the views of the editors across a range of national and global affairs. Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

CON: It's Time to Halt the AI Data Center Attack

Mitch Jones, Food & Water Watch

Gasoline prices have risen sharply as the war with Iran continues. Yet energy prices in many parts of the country were already skyrocketing long before this latest conflict began. The real driver of these rising electric bills hasn't been events overseas or big oil companies. It's been AI data centers and Big Tech.

An Alarming Discovery

Companies are racing to build massive data centers to power the artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency industries. This construction boom is reshaping communities across the country and straining Americans' budgets — and not for the better.

Last year, as a sudden wave of large-scale AI data center construction began overwhelming local leaders in dozens of states, our organization, Food & Water Watch, started closely examining the effects of these massive industrial facilities. What we found was alarming.

Energy demand from AI data centers in the U.S. is expected to triple, between 2020 and 2030. Our analysis found that these facilities could consume up to 580 terawatt-hours of energy every year — a unit used to measure huge amounts of electricity. That's roughly equal to the amount used by more than 55 million households. The largest of these facilities, which may house 5,000 or more servers spread across millions of square feet, could use as much power as 2 million households combined.

This extreme surge in energy demand is unsustainable, and it's already having serious effects on the environment, the climate and countless families' finances. More than half of the energy used by AI data centers comes from fossil fuels, such as coal and natural gas, which are deepening the climate crisis and fueling stronger storms and rising sea levels.

Large-scale data centers also require enormous amounts of water to operate. By 2028, U.S. data centers could use as many as 720 billion gallons of water each year just to cool their servers. That's equal to more than 1 million Olympic-size swimming pools, or enough water to meet the everyday needs of 18.5 million American households. Meanwhile, many communities already struggle to get affordable water.

The Cost to American Families

Speaking of affordability, the most direct effect of the AI data center boom is on Americans' wallets. Driven largely by new data centers, rising power demand pushed U.S. electric and gas companies to ask state governments if they could request $31 billion in rate increases from customers in 2025 — double what they requested the year before. Average residential electricity rates have jumped 31% since 2020, compared to just 4% in the five years before that.

Communities Push Back

It should come as no surprise that people and communities are fighting back. Last October, Food & Water Watch became the first national organization to call for a complete nationwide moratorium on new AI data center construction. We cited the growing burden these facilities place on electricity and water resources. Months later, 250 local, state and national groups joined our call. In response to this growing public outcry, Senator Bernie Sanders recently introduced a bill in Congress to enact a nationwide pause.

Meanwhile, community leaders across the country are taking matters into their own hands. They've rejected dozens of new AI data center proposals and are pursuing multi-year local and statewide halts to the industry's expansion.

Simply put, we need a nationwide pause on the explosive growth of new AI data center construction right now. It hasn't even been determined whether — not just how — this industry can ever operate in a way that adequately protects people and communities from the many hazards and harms that data centers bring wherever they appear.

Mitch Jones is the managing director of policy and litigation at Food & Water Watch, a national environmental organization fighting for safe food, clean water and a livable climate. He wrote this for InsideSources.com.

title: Record low levels on the Danube river affect energy use in Eastern Europe

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Record low levels on the Danube river affect energy use in Eastern Europe
levels.body:
It is very hot in Europe this summer. Temperatures over 104 degrees are common. Not everyone is Europe has air conditioning. But those that do are using them a lot. Now many governments are trying to save electricity to stop an energy crisis.

High temperatures and little rain is causing other problems too. The Danube River, one of Europe's biggest rivers, has very little water. A lot of electricity in Europe comes from nuclear power plants. These are big factories that make electricity. But the plants need water from the river. Without enough water, these plants can't make electricity.

Atoms are the tiny invisible building blocks of everything around us. When an atom is split in the power plant, it gives off a lot of heat and energy. That heat makes steam that spins a turbine to make electricity. But the system needs a lot of water. Water is boiled to make the steam. Cool water is used to turn that steam back into liquid water so it can be used again.

Nuclear Power Plant In Hungary

In Budapest, Hungary's capital, the water in the Danube River was only 4 inches on August 4. That is a new record. At the same time, people were using more electricity and water because of the hot weather.

Hungary's only nuclear power plant at Paks was almost shut down because of the low river water. The plant uses water from the Danube to stay cool. On August 3, the plant was making only 240 megawatts of power instead of 2,000. A watt is a unit of electricity. A megawatt is a million watts. Most home lightbulbs use just 40 or 60 watts.

On August 4 the plant's last working turbine was still running. The plant provides nearly half of Hungary's electricity. Hungary also gets electricity from nearby regions and from renewable energy sources.

Hungary's government has put in place big energy saving plans for factories, businesses and homes. This has saved a lot of energy.

Low Water Flow

Power plants in nearby countries are also making much less electricity.

On August 3, water was moved from the Danube's Bala Canal in Romania to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant. The Danube's water flow in Romania is now less than a third of what it usually is. One reactor at the plant was already shut down. It is working at about half its normal power.

Acting Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan announced a state of alert in the energy sector on July 31. He warned that the Danube's low water levels could cause the shutdown of Cernavoda's second reactor. He asked people to save electricity.

On August 3, Bolojan said two car factories had stopped making cars until August 19. Other companies agreed to use less energy in the evening.

In Serbia, the country's main hydroelectric plant is only working at 20 percent of its capacity because of the low river water levels. These plants turn the energy of moving water into electricity.

Serbian Prime Minister Djuro Macut asked people to use less electricity at home. He said the situation is "serious and demanding."

levels.title: Record low levels on the Danube river affect energy use in Eastern Europe
levels.body:
Europe has seen record-breaking heat this summer. Temperatures above 104 degrees have become the norm. In many European countries, air conditioning is not as widespread as in the U.S. and yet, the relentless heat is pushing the power plants to the edge as people who have access to air conditioning seek relief. Many governments across Central and Eastern Europe are taking steps to conserve electricity and prevent an energy crisis.

As all this unfolds, one of Europe's largest rivers, the Danube, is seeing record-low water levels. And this has forced power plants to the brink of shutting down. About a quarter of the electricity in European Union countries comes from nuclear power plants, which rely on water to cool their reactors. Much of that water comes from the Danube River.

Nuclear power plants contain nuclear reactors that produce energy. Inside, nuclear reactions occur that produce heat through a process called fission. Fission splits an atom's center (nucleus) into smaller parts, which causes a lot of heat and energy to be given off. That heat makes steam that spins a turbine to create electricity. But the system requires water— a lot of water. Water is boiled to make the steam, and large amounts of cool water are used to change that steam back into liquid water so it can be used again.

Nuclear Power Plant In Hungary

Persistent drought and multiple extreme heat waves have pushed the Danube River's levels in Hungary's capital, Budapest, to around 4 inches on August 3. That is much lower than the previous record low of 13 inches set in 2018. Water levels are not expected to rise soon because no significant rain is forecasted. Meanwhile, electricity and water use are on the rise as another extreme heat wave hits the region.

The Danube's very low levels have brought Hungary's only nuclear power plant at Paks close to shutting down for the first time in its 44 years of operation. The Paks plant uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors. On August 3, it was producing only 240 megawatts of power instead of the usual 2,000. A watt is a unit of electricity—a megawatt is a million watts. Most home lightbulbs are 40 or 60 watts, for example. That means the bulb consumes electricity at the rate of 40 or 60 watts per second.

In a video posted to Facebook on August 3, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said the plant's last working turbine was temporarily running. This prevented a shutdown that had been expected over the weekend. As of August 4, the one turbine was still working.

The Paks plant is about 55 miles south of Budapest. It provides nearly half of Hungary's electricity and about a third of its consumption. Hungary also depends on electricity imports from nearby regions and renewable energy sources.

On August 1, Hungary's government required large industrial or commercial users to cut their electricity use. It also asked households to save energy, especially during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m.

The government also announced that electric-powered freight trains would not be allowed to run during peak hours starting on August 3 to save more energy.

On August 3, the government said that these efforts to save energy had resulted in 700 fewer megawatts of electricity being used the previous day.

Low Water Flow

Meanwhile, power plants in nearby countries have also seen big drops in power generation.

On August 3, water was redirected from the Danube's Bala Canal in Romania toward the Cernavoda nuclear power plant. The Danube's water flow in Romania has dropped to 1,500 cubic meters per second—less than a third of its usual flow in July. Authorities have already shut down one reactor unit at the Cernavoda plant, which is working at about half its normal capacity.

Acting Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan announced a nationwide state of alert in the energy sector on July 31. He warned that the Danube's low water levels could cause the shutdown of Cernavoda's second reactor. He asked people to voluntarily limit electricity use during peak evening hours.

On August 3, Bolojan said carmakers Dacia and Ford had stopped production until August 19. Other companies agreed to use less energy during peak hours.

In Serbia, record-low Danube levels have pushed the country's main hydroelectric plant to work at only 20 percent of its capacity. These plants turn the energy of moving water into electricity. Water flows through a pipe, spins the blades of a turbine, and turns a generator to make electricity.

Serbian Prime Minister Djuro Macut asked residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners." He said the situation was "serious and demanding."

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Everything you need to know about North America's "ring of fire" eclipse
levels.body:
Something rare is happening in the sky soon: a solar eclipse. This happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth. The eclipse is happening on October 14.

Sometimes during an eclipse, the moon completely blocks the sun. That is a total eclipse.

The eclipse on October 14 will not be a total eclipse. It will be an annular solar eclipse. The moon will not completely cover the sun. It will make a "ring of fire."

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

The moon is not always the same distance from us. The moon orbits around the Earth. An orbit is a regular, repeating path. The moon has an elliptical orbit. This means it is shaped like an oval.

Sometimes, the moon is at its farthest distance from Earth. This makes the moon appear smaller. At other times, the moon is at its closest distance to Earth. This makes the moon appear larger.

The October 14 eclipse will be visible in North America. It will also be visible in Central and South America. Not everyone will see a ring of fire, though. Most will see a partial solar eclipse. The sun, moon and Earth will not line up perfectly. Only part of the sun will disappear. It will look like a crescent.

Some people will be able to see the annular solar eclipse. This means that they will see the ring of fire. It will only be visible in a certain path. This path is 118 to 137 miles wide. That is 190 to 220 kilometers wide. It will stretch from Oregon through California. The path will also cover parts of Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. It will then move over Mexico. Next, it will move over parts of Central America and South America.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

Most people in the Americas will not see a ring of fire. They will experience a partial solar eclipse. This means they will see the sun as a crescent shape. Here is how much of the sun will be covered in the 10 biggest cities. It also includes the times when you can see the partial eclipse.

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

- Chicago, Illinois: 43 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Houston, Texas: 85 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Phoenix, Arizona: 79 percent at 9:31 a.m. MST

- Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: 25 percent at 1:21 p.m. EDT

- San Antonio, Texas: ring of fire at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Diego, California: 68 percent at 9:26 a.m. PDT

- Dallas, Texas: 80 percent at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Jose, California: 75 percent at 9:20 a.m. PDT

How To Safely View The Partial And Annular Solar Eclipse

The sun can burn your eyes. This is still true during an eclipse. Wear solar eclipse glasses. They will protect you. Be careful with cameras, telescopes and binoculars. They need special lens filters.

From left to right, a total solar eclipse, annular solar eclipse, and partial solar eclipse. A hybrid eclipse appears as either a total or an annular eclipse (the left and middle images), depending on the observer's location.

A solar eclipse is coming soon. On October 14, people in North America will be able to view it. A solar eclipse happens when, at just the right moment, the moon passes between the sun and Earth. During a total solar eclipse, the moon completely blocks the sun's light.

The eclipse on October 14 will not be a total eclipse. It will be something called an annular solar eclipse. This happens when the moon does not completely cover the sun. So it makes a thin outer "ring of fire."

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

This eclipse won't darken skies. That's because it won't fully cover the disk of the sun.

Whether the moon can completely cover the sun depends on the moon's distance from Earth. The moon has a slightly elliptical orbit around Earth. An orbit is a regular, repeating path that one object in space takes around another one. An elliptical orbit is shaped like an oval.

This means that at one point during each month, the moon is at its farthest distance from Earth. This makes it appear slightly smaller than usual. At another point each month, the moon is at its closest distance to Earth. This makes it appear slightly larger than usual.

On October 14, all of North America and Central America will experience a partial solar eclipse. Most of South America will experience one, too. A partial solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth. But the sun, moon and Earth are not perfectly lined up. Only part of the sun will appear to be covered. This gives it a crescent shape.

The annular solar eclipse, or ring of fire, will not be visible everywhere. It will only be visible in a certain path. This path is 118 to 137 miles wide. That is 190 to 220 kilometers wide. It will stretch from Oregon through California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico. Next, it will move over parts of Central America and South America.

On October 14, everyone in the United States will experience a partial solar eclipse. This means that people will see the sun in a crescent shape. Here is how much of the sun will be covered in the 10 biggest cities. It also includes the times when you can see the partial eclipse.

levels.title: Everything you need to know about North America's "ring of fire" solar eclipse
levels.body:
On October 14, 2023, an annular solar eclipse will come to North America.

Roughly 11 years after the same type of solar eclipse crossed the U.S. Southwest on May 20, 2012, this one will be visible from a similar region, crossing eight U.S. states from Oregon to Texas, according to NASA.

During an annular solar eclipse, the moon appears slightly smaller than the sun, so it can't block the entire disk. The result is a beautiful "ring of fire." Here's everything you need to know about this rare event.

What Is An Annular Solar Eclipse?

This eclipse won't darken skies the way the total solar eclipse of August 21, 2017, did. A solar eclipse occurs when a new moon is positioned precisely between Earth and the sun and casts its shadow on Earth.

An annular solar eclipse happens when the moon appears relatively small in the sky so it does not fully cover the disk of the sun, leaving a thin outer ring often called a "ring of fire."

Whether the moon can completely cover the sun's disk depends on the moon's distance from Earth. The moon has a slightly elliptical orbit around Earth, so at two points each month, it is farthest from (apogee) and closest to (perigee) Earth, making the moon appear slightly smaller and slightly larger than average in our sky.

On October 14, 2023, the new moon will look relatively small and, therefore, cover only 91 percent of the sun's disk as viewed from the narrow path of annularity that stretches from Oregon through Texas and beyond.

On October 14, 2023, all of North America and Central America, and most of South America will experience a solar eclipse. For all of that region, the spectacle will be a partial solar eclipse of varying obscuration. Only within the path of annularity, which is 118 to 137 miles (190 to 220 kilometers) wide, will the ring of fire be visible. That path will stretch from Oregon through Northern California, northeast Nevada, central Utah, northeast Arizona, southwest Colorado, central New Mexico and southern Texas. It will then move across the Gulf of Mexico and over Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia and Brazil.

The point of greatest eclipse — where viewers could see a ring of fire lasting 5 minutes, 17 seconds — will occur off the coast of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.

The most scenic places to see the ring of fire are in the U.S. Southwest and at the Mayan temple at Edzná on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

Why Will The 2023 Annular Solar Eclipse Be So Special?

Although it's largely being seen as a warm-up for the 2024 total solar eclipse, the 2023 annular solar eclipse is a great excuse to travel. For eclipse chasers who have yet to see an annular solar eclipse, it's a great opportunity.

As with all eclipses, it's important to be in the center of the path of the moon's shadow if you want to experience as long a spectacle as possible. That means putting yourself on or near the centerline. However, experienced eclipse chasers will head to the northern edge of the path — at locations such as Dolores, Colorado, and Santa Fe, New Mexico — to experience a much shorter, but arguably more dramatic, spectacle.

Viewers in these locations will see a ring of fire for perhaps just a few seconds. But it will be less circular, and one part of the edge of the moon will appear to almost block out the sun. This may make it possible to glimpse the "Baily's beads" ring around the moon during the annularity phase, just as can be seen during a total solar eclipse.

Where To See The Partial Solar Eclipse

Although the ring of fire will get a lot of attention, few people make much effort to travel to see an annular solar eclipse. After all, these events don't quite compare to total solar eclipses. On October 14, 2023, most of the Americas will experience a big partial solar eclipse. Here is what the 10 biggest cities in the U.S. will experience that day; only one will see the ring of fire:

- New York, New York: 23 percent at 1:22 p.m. EDT

- Los Angeles, California: 71 percent at 9:24 a.m. PDT

- Chicago, Illinois: 43 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Houston, Texas: 85 percent at 11:58 a.m. CDT

- Phoenix, Arizona: 79 percent at 9:31 a.m. MST

- Philadelphia, Pennsylvania: 25 percent at 1:21 p.m. EDT

- San Antonio, Texas: ring of fire at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Diego, California: 68 percent at 9:26 a.m.PDT

- Dallas, Texas: 80 percent at 11:52 a.m. CDT

- San Jose, California: 75 percent at 9:20 a.m. PDT

How To Safely View The Partial And Annular Solar Eclipse

To safely view this event, you must use solar filters at all times. Whether your location will experience a partial solar eclipse or an annular solar eclipse, the dangers are the same. In fact, a ring of fire is technically nothing more than a particularly pretty partial solar eclipse. At no point will more than 91 percent of the sun's disk be covered by the new moon. Observers will need to wear solar eclipse glasses, and cameras, telescopes and binoculars must have solar filters placed in front of their lenses at all times.

When Is The Next Annular Solar Eclipse Ring Of Fire?

After the annular solar eclipse on October 14, 2023, the next annular solar eclipse will occur on October 2, 2024, when a ring of fire will be visible from the Pacific Ocean, southern Chile and southern Argentina. At the point of greatest eclipse in the ocean, the ring of fire will last 7 minutes and 25 seconds, but the best spot will be Easter Island (Rapa Nui), located about 2,000 miles (3,200 kilometers) off the western coast of Chile. There, it will be possible to stand among the remote volcanic island's many carved moai statues and see a ring of fire for up to 6 minutes and 9 seconds.

title: Scientist deliberately subjects himself to the world's most painful stingers

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Scientist deliberately subjects himself to the world's most painful stingers
levels.body:
Insect stings can really hurt. Most people try to avoid them.

But Sam Robinson gets stung on purpose. He is a molecular biologist. Molecular biology is a branch of biology. It is the study of the molecules that make up living things.

Robinson wants to understand pain. He wants to find the chemicals that cause it. A chemical is a substance. It has a defined composition and properties used to identify it. Chemicals can occur naturally. They can also be made in a lab.

"I'm genuinely interested," he says. "I wonder, 'What does that sting feel like?' and there's often no information on that."

Research May Lead To New Drugs

Robinson rates each sting. He uses a pain scale developed by Justin Schmidt. Schmidt is an entomologist. Entomologists are scientists who study insects.

Schmidt did not get stung on purpose. But he could not avoid it.

"He worked with these insects for 40 years," says Robinson. "There's no way around it!"

Robinson writes down the intensity of the pain. He writes down how long it lasts. He describes the pain. He notes other symptoms like inflammation. Inflammation is the immune system's response to an irritant. Irritants could include a stinger.

Robinson hopes his research is helpful to other scientists. He hopes it can help them find new pain medications.

First, Robinson must figure out what makes a sting painful. He has to find the neurons that sense the pain. A neuron is a type of cell. It sends and receives messages from the body to the brain and back. Then, scientists can develop drugs that target those neurons.

New medications may be a while off. But Robinson has already had scientific breakthroughs.

In May, Robinson and his team revealed that ants produce neurotoxins. Neurotoxins are poisonous substances. They act on the victim's nervous system. They disrupt the normal function of neurons.

Most Painful Stings

Schmidt rated the bullet ant as having the most painful sting. Robinson agrees. Bullet ants live in Central and South America.

"Apparently it feels like being shot," says Robinson. That is where its name comes from. "Its bite is a really unique pain," he says. It can last for 12 hours.

Robinson says all the stings are worth it. He says people are scared of stings. But most of the time, they do not injure you. They just hurt.

"These things, they're not going to kill you," he says. And the pain eventually goes away.

figures.caption: Tarantula hawk wasps have one of the most painful stings. In the name of science, a scientist allowed himself to be stung by insects.
Some insects can extend and retract their stingers.
After a sting, toxins in the venom cause our bodies to react with pain and swelling.
The Schmidt pain index has a scale of 1 to 4. Coming in at 4, the tarantula hawk wasp and the bullet ant have one of the most painful stings.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Scientist deliberately subjects himself to the world's most painful stingers
levels.body:
Meet the man putting his body on the line — all in the name of science.

"I'm interested in what the chemicals are behind pain and how they interact with our bodies to create that pain," Sam Robinson explains to me in a casual, nonchalant tone.

But there's nothing nonchalant about the way Robinson explores his interest.

A molecular biologist at the University of Queensland's Institute for Molecular Bioscience, he has earned himself quite a reputation for his unconventional research methods, namely, for being stung by the world's most painful insects and plants, on purpose.

"I'm genuinely interested," he tells me. "I find something and I wonder 'what does that sting feel like?' and there's often no information on that, or no good quality information."

Robinson rates each sting using a pain scale developed by the late American entomologist Justin Schmidt, who was famous for his studies of stinging insects.

While Schmidt's stings weren't intentional, they were inevitable in his line of work.

"He worked with these insects for 40 years," says Robinson. "So if you're working with them for that amount of time, you get stung, there's no way around it!

"He was the first one to start recording the different experiences and he made this key observation early on that not all stings are equal. So he developed this pain scale called the Schmidt Sting Pain Index."

While the science behind each sting is complex, Robinson's methods for recording his (painful) experiences are a humble notebook and stopwatch.

"Obviously I'm writing down the intensity of the pain and how long it lasts, but also the type of pain and other symptoms, like inflammation."

Not only is Robinson documenting the effects of different stings on the human body for scientific record, but his observations have the potential to lead to significant biomedical applications.

"One of the cool things it can do is by finding new things and new targets in our own bodies, in terms of our pain-sensing neurons, we can potentially develop a new class of drugs to target that," Robinson says.

"If you can understand, at a molecular level, why something stings when it hurts, then you can potentially come up with a more rational treatment for that.

"A new class of painkillers would be the ultimate health outcome."

But while new medications may be a while off, Robinson and his colleagues have already had myriad scientific breakthroughs.

"The progress has been unbelievable actually. We've had some really amazing outcomes over the last five years or so."

In May 2023, Robinson and his team published a paper in Nature Communications, revealing for the first time that ants inflict pain with neurotoxins.

"I looked into the venom of green ants, along with a bunch of other ants, and found that this particular class of toxin was responsible for the pain," explains Robinson. "And this toxin class was new to science.

"So, for one, we didn't know that's how ants were causing this type of pain, and then, also, no one knew this class of toxin existed!

"We figured out what the toxins target in our nerves and that information is very, very useful to understand how this works at a molecular level and how it's involved in pain."

Another massive breakthrough, published in Nature Communications in 2020, was a discovery about the gympie-gympie (Dendrocnide moroides) plant: What scientists had long thought caused its excruciating sting was incorrect.

"For a long time, people thought that the long-lasting pain was because of the little spines from the leaves or stems stuck in the body — like fibreglass. But we now know that that's not the case because we've figured out what the toxin is in those stinging trees, and how it causes pain," says Robinson.

A common remedy for the infamous gympie-gympie sting is to use sticky tape or wax to remove the tiny stinging hairs from the skin.

"We now know that's completely futile because it's the toxin that's causing this long-lasting pain, it has an irreversible effect on your nerves," Robinson explains.

"It targets something in our nerves that we didn't know was involved in pain and now we know this particular protein is intricately involved in a certain type of pain.

"So that's just two examples of new things we've learned."

Most Painful Stings

The late Justin Schmidt rated the bullet ant (Paraponera clavata) — found in Central and South America — as having the most painful insect sting in the world. Robinson agrees.

"It's called a bullet ant because apparently it feels like being shot," says Robinson. "Now, I don't know what being shot feels like, but its bite is a really unique pain, a very deep, drilling, long-lasting pain. It can last for 12 hours, it's quite amazing.

"It's the most intense pain I've felt from a sting and the length of it just wears you down so that's what gives it this really high rating."

Luckily, we don't have bullet ants in Australia, but Robinson says our green ants (Rhytidoponera metallica) give the bullet ants a run for their money.

"It's a unique sort of pain, that can gradually build and then last quite a long time. It can be quite intense and quite deep."

Also high on Robinson's list of most painful stings is one from, what he calls, the "humungous" tarantula hawk wasp (Pepsis sp.).

"They are just monsters, they can be a couple of inches long, quite frightening, and they have no natural enemies — I think that's because everything knows that when they sting, it just hurts so much!

"When you're stung it's five to 10 minutes of intense pain and swelling."

Like the bullet ant, the tarantula hawk wasp is not found in Australia, but, again, we have an equivalent: the spider-hunting wasp (Heterodontonyx bicolor).

"This sting is right up there with the tarantula hawk wasp," says Robinson.

Chatting to Robinson as he relives these horrid encounters, there's one question I just have to ask: "Is it worth it?"

"Yeah," he says without hesitation.

"These things, they're not going to kill you. People are really worried about stinging things but the reality is, that for 99.9 percent of us, they're just going to cause a bit of transient pain. They're not going to do you any harm beyond that."

title: "Gentle parenting" squirrels: Millions watch TikToker care for animals on his balcony

cover.caption: Derrick Downey Jr. watches Maxine the squirrel play with a retro-style microphone on his balcony in Los Angeles, California.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: "Gentle parenting" squirrels: Millions watch TikToker care for animals on his balcony
levels.body:
Derrick Downey Jr. was relaxing at home in Los Angeles, California. A fox squirrel appeared on his balcony. They stared at each other curiously. Downey then offered the squirrel food. He found some peanuts inside his house. He returned to the balcony and offered the peanuts to the squirrel. Surprisingly, he said the squirrel pulled his hand closer and started eating.

Downey was pleased by this moment. He had been feeling low. The squirrel began visiting him every day. It often brought another squirrel along. Downey named the pair Richard and Maxine.

He posted a video on TikTok. The video showed him with the squirrels. He gave them water and asked them not to fight. His video racked up more than 26 million views. He talks to the squirrels about their feelings.

"You're having a moment — it's OK to have that moment," he said.

The squirrels helped Downey feel better. His followers on TikTok and Instagram loved his squirrel videos. They liked that he recognized the squirrels' feelings. Downey talked about how important mental health is.

A Squirrel House With Furniture And TV

People compared him to a Disney princess. He was being a gentle parent to the squirrels. He posted squirrel videos every day. In a recent video, he tries to teach Maxine how to be patient as he peels her an avocado.

In another video, he shares his wisdom with Maxine as she rests on his shoulder. His followers also took his wisdom. In 2022, he built a squirrel house. His 1 million TikTok followers supported him.

Downey made a squirrel house wish list. Followers sent very small furniture. The website Apartment Therapy posted a story about his squirrel house. He received more packages, and was called the "Squirrel Whisperer."

Fans sent a TV and fireplace front for the squirrels. Downey claimed the squirrels enjoy TV. He feeds them nuts, grapes and avocado. He said he's never been bitten.

"It's bringing people a lot of joy," he said. "I've heard from people all over the world who enjoy watching the videos."

It Started With A Hermit Crab

Downey said he didn't intend to reach so many people. He has always loved animals. When Downey was growing up in Atlanta, Georgia, he always liked watching squirrels run up and down trees.

But he was more taken by the hermit crab that his first-grade teacher kept in her classroom. "I'd stay inside at recess to watch it," he said. "At the end of the school year, my teacher gifted the hermit crab to me. That was my first pet."

He takes video of each squirrel event. He threw a party for Maxine's five kits. Kits are baby squirrels. They lived in a palm tree for about three months until they were old enough to leave the nest.

When Maxine had more kits, Downey helped. The kits were in a tree that was trimmed. This caused their nest to fall. He cared for the fallen kits and returned them to Maxine.

For now, the squirrels scamper back and forth between the squirrel house and trees in the neighborhood. Downey said he sees Richard and Maxine almost every day.

Downey was pleased by this moment. He'd been feeling low. The squirrel started visiting every day, often bringing another squirrel friend. Downey named them Richard and Maxine.

He shared a video on TikTok of him hanging out with the squirrels. The video of him giving the squirrels water and telling them not to fight racked up more than 26 million views.

"You're having a moment — it's OK to have that moment," he said.

As he clicked with the squirrels, he started to feel better himself. His followers loved the squirrel videos. They praised him for validating the squirrels' feelings. Downey pointed out how important mental health is.

"It brought me peace," he said. "I would see Richard walking around, and talking to him made me feel good about the world."

A Two-Story House With Furniture And TV

People compared Downey to a Disney princess for his "gentle parenting" of the squirrels. Downey was encouraged to post daily videos of Richard and Maxine. In one video, he teaches Maxine how to be patient while peeling her an avocado.

In another video, he drops wisdom to Maxine about handling tough days. "You ain't always going to have the best of days," he tells Maxine. "But when life is down and you're going through a moment, just be still, all right? Don't put too much pressure on yourself."

After his breakout video in 2022, he built a two-story squirrel house. His TikTok followers — now more than 1 million — supported this project.

Downey created a wish list for squirrel house furnishings. His followers sent tiny furniture and decorations. After the website Apartment Therapy posted about his squirrel home, he received more packages. His followers called him the "Squirrel Whisperer."

Fans sent a working TV and a fireplace front for the squirrel house. Downey said the squirrels enjoy watching TV. He regularly feeds them nuts, grapes and avocado pieces.

"They really do seem to enjoy watching TV," he said. "But more than anything, I'd have to say they like to eat."

Bringing Joy To A Lot Of People

Downey said the squirrels haven't caused any damage to his home. However, Maxine destroyed a rooftop sofa once and made off with the insides of a pillow. He mentioned scrub-jays sometimes try to steal the nuts left for the squirrels.

Downey had no idea he'd join the others who've created spaces for squirrels. "It's bringing people a lot of joy," he said. "I've heard from people all over the world who enjoy watching the videos."

A fan's family reached out to Downey after she died in hospice. He posted a tearful video saying how lucky he felt to have connected with her. Followers responded.

"You brought her so much kindness, happiness and love!" wrote a follower.

It Started With A Hermit Crab

Downey didn't plan on reaching so many with his squirrel videos. He's always loved animals. As a child growing up in Atlanta, Georgia, he liked watching squirrels run up and down trees.

But he was more taken by the hermit crab that his first-grade teacher kept in her classroom. "I'd stay inside at recess to watch it, and at the end of the school year, my teacher gifted the hermit crab to me," he said. "That was my first pet."

He records each squirrel event. He held a party for Maxine's five kits in January 2023. Kits are baby squirrels. The kits lived in a palm tree for about three months until they were old enough to leave the nest.

When Maxine had another litter, Downey rescued them after their nest fell from a tree that was trimmed. He cared for them and returned them to Maxine.

"Rescuing these baby squirrels and reuniting them with mama Maxine was the greatest feeling ever!" he wrote on his Instagram page.

A follower suggested starting a squirrel shelter. For now, his balcony is that shelter. He said he sees Richard and Maxine almost every day.
