levels.body:
Derrick Downey Jr. was relaxing on his second-story balcony in Los Angeles, California, when a bushy-tailed fox squirrel suddenly appeared.

Downey said they stared at each other for a few seconds, and then he asked the squirrel: "Do you want something to eat?"

"It seemed obvious to me that he did, so I told him, 'Stay here, I'll be right back,'" Downey recalled.

Downey ran into his kitchen and searched in his cupboards until he'd found some peanuts, then he hurried back to the balcony.

"The squirrel was still sitting in the same spot, so I figured, 'OK, he was listening to me,'" he said. "And when I held my hand out with the peanuts, he pulled my hand closer and started eating."

Downey, who had been feeling low, was enchanted by the encounter.

"I was having a rough time, not because of the pandemic, but because of some mental health issues," Downey said.

Since that day in 2020, the squirrel has continued to scamper up to his balcony for treats, often bringing a friend with him, Downey said. He named the affable pair Richard and Maxine for no particular reason other than he liked the sound of it.

He decided to share a video on TikTok of him interacting with the squirrels. The short clip of him giving Richard and Maxine sips of water from a glass and tenderly telling them not to quarrel has racked up more than 26 million views since it was posted last year.

"Don't be fighting! Do you want some water? Come here. I know it's hot — we get agitated, we get aggravated," Downey tells the squirrels in the clip.

"You're having a moment — it's OK to have that moment," he said.

As he bonded with the squirrels, he started to feel better himself.

"Going outside and connecting with nature was my gateway to relief from depression," he said. "It brought me peace. I would see Richard walking around, and talking to him made me feel good about the world."

His TikTok and Instagram followers loved the videos of him getting to know the squirrels and talking to them.

"Validate their moments and emotions. You're the best squirrel dad!" someone commented.

Downey replied: "Mental health is important. Gotta make sure they're good mentally and physically."

Another person commented, "He's gentle parenting the squirrels." And another said, "Bro treats squirrels better than my parents treat me."

Someone compared him to Snow White. "You're literally a Disney princess," another person wrote.

Downey was excited his followers liked the squirrels as much as he did, so he decided to start posting daily videos of Richard and Maxine. In a recent one, he tries to teach Maxine patience as he peels her an avocado.

In another, with a squirrel on his shoulder, he drops wisdom to his furry friend.

"You ain't always going to have the best of days," he tells Maxine. "But when life is down and you're going through a moment, just be still, alright? Don't put too much pressure on yourself."

His followers replied with comments such as, "Thanks so much because that was EXACTLY what I needed to hear right now!!! Grateful."

Shortly after his breakout video in 2022, Downey went to work building a two-story house with a picket fence for the squirrels, and he encouraged his TikTok followers — now numbering more than 1 million — to get involved.

"I created a squirrel wish list so everyone could help me furnish the house and make it cozy," Downey said, noting that it wasn't long before he was swamped with miniature furniture and paintings, a birdbath, holiday decorations and tiny dishes and houseplants.

When Apartment Therapy posted a story about his squirrel-sized home renovations in 2022, packages started to arrive at a faster clip, he said, noting that his followers began to call him the "Squirrel Whisperer."

Fans of Richard and Maxine sent him a tiny working television and a fireplace front. Downey added them to the living room in the wee abode so his little friends could watch the Animal Planet and National Geographic channels in comfort via his streaming service.

"They really do seem to enjoy watching TV," he said. "But more than anything, I'd have to say they like to eat."

Downey leaves out nuts for the squirrels, and he'll occasionally give them grapes and small pieces of avocado. He said he's never been bitten, and his home has never been damaged by the critters, despite some exposed cords on his balcony. Though Newsweek reported earlier this year (2023) that Maxine destroyed a rooftop couch and made off with the insides of a pillow.

"Scrub-jays will show up sometimes and try to steal the nuts," Downey said, referencing the blue jays that live along the Pacific seaboard. "Then it usually gets a little chaotic."

Downey said he never imagined he'd join the ranks of the Texas family that built a squirrel a Whataburger shack, the Mississippi woman who rescued baby squirrels and the woman who opened a chipmunk cafe in Atlanta, Georgia. But he said he's happy to flow with it.

"It's bringing people a lot of joy," he said. "I've heard from people all over the world who enjoy watching the videos."

Now, three years in, his videos attract a community of people who love squirrels, and also are seeking kindness to both animals and humans — just like him.

"This page isn't about the squirrels really, it's about the good vibes," one person wrote on his Instagram.

Last month he heard from the family of a fan of his who died after she spent time in hospice. Downey, who had communicated with her before she died, posted a tearful video saying how lucky he felt to have connected with her. His followers responded in kind with big emotions.

"You brought her so much kindness, happiness and love! Truly to the depths of her soul. She left this plane of existence without fear and with a heart full of squirrels," wrote a follower. "Her transition became even more beautiful because of you, good sir."

Downey said he didn't intend to reach so many people with his squirrel videos, he was just following his instincts. He has always loved animals.

When Downey was growing up in Atlanta, he said he always got a kick out of watching squirrels run up and down trees, but he was more taken by the hermit crab that his first-grade teacher kept in her classroom.

"I'd stay inside at recess to watch it, and at the end of the school year, my teacher gifted the hermit crab to me," he said. "That was my first pet."

He moved to Los Angeles five years ago and works creating social media content, he said.

"I love connecting with people, and now the squirrels have given me a new outlet for that," Downey said, noting that he just finished decorating Richard and Maxine's pad for Halloween.

"Their house is decorated for every holiday — Christmas, Fourth of July, you name it," he said. "They have more decorations than I do."

He records every squirrel milestone — including a gender reveal party he held for laughs in January 2023 for Maxine's new litter of five baby kits — so TikTok viewers can follow the drama unfolding each day on his balcony. The tiny squirrels lived in a palm tree for about three months until they were old enough to leave the nest.

"The gender reveal was mainly for giggles," Downey said, explaining that he didn't know whether her kittens were male or female.

He didn't want to get involved with raising her five young ones.

"I didn't take care of them — I want to keep them wild — but I'm happy if they decide to drop by," Downey said.

"We're not sure who is the father of the babies — people have speculated it's either Richard or Raymond, another squirrel that shows up and takes half the food," he added. "We've nicknamed him Hood Rat Raymond."

Things got more serious in June 2023 when Maxine had another litter, and the kits were in a tree that was trimmed, causing their nest to fall. The workers put the nest in another tree, but Downey thought it wasn't safe. Downey took them in, cared for them, and then returned them to Maxine.

"Rescuing these baby squirrels and reuniting them with mama Maxine, was the greatest feeling ever!" he wrote on his Instagram page.

Someone responded: "Can somebody just donate you a mansion squirrel sanctuary in the woods already. Take Maxine, Richard and all the Grandsquirrels with you."

For now, his balcony residents scamper back and forth between the squirrel house and trees in the neighborhood. He said he sees Richard and Maxine almost every day.

"Maxine will perch on my shoulder, and I'll give her some nuts or avocado and we'll have this perfect little therapeutic moment," Downey said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Synthetic or natural grass? The turf war in a Maryland school district
levels.body:
Montgomery County Public Schools is Maryland's largest school district. It is making a big change to its sports fields. The sports fields that are covered with grass will be covered with turf instead. Turf is made of concrete, plastic and rubber. Some people argue that turf is easier to care for and lasts longer. But others worry that it costs too much. They also worry that turf is not good for the environmental or for students' health.

Pros And Cons

Sidharth Harishanker is a junior at Poolesville High School and co-president of a student-led nonprofit environmental group. He said that artificial fields are too expensive and pose too many risks.

About half of the district's 25 main high school sports fields are turf. The district plans to change the rest to turf, too.

Jeffrey Sullivan is the school district's athletics director. He said the grass fields can't handle the many hours of play the schools need. Turf can handle more hours of play. But it can get dangerously hot in the summer because it traps in more heat.

Grass is cheaper to set up. But turf is cheaper to maintain. Grass needs more upkeep. But doesn't have to be replaced every 10 years.

Calculating Costs

The school district plans on spending $55 million on the turf over the next six years. The district did a study that compared the cost per hour of use for turf and grass fields. Turf fields cost $5.72 an hour. Grass fields cost $23.73 an hour. This does not include the cost to replace the turf.

In 2025 the turf fields were used for 45,816 hours of play. Grass fields were used for 6,885 hours.

Another benefit to turf is that is doesn't absorb water the way grass does. Schools in the district are not allowed to use the grass fields for a day after heavy rain. But there are no rules for turf fields.

Health Concerns

Hannah Donart is a scientist who studies the environment. She is also part of the county council's parent-teacher group. She said the district could save money by taking better care of grass fields. Grass fields could be used as much as turf if they were taken care of better. She added that the county has not budgeted for the cost of replacing the turf.

She is worried about the chemicals used to make turf. She also noted that research shows people get hurt more often on turf.

Turf can also get much hotter than natural grass. The parent-teacher group took some temperature readings. It found that the turf in the county was 65 degrees hotter than nearby grass.

The school district does not allow turf fields to be used when it is very hot out.

Vasilis Vasiliou is a scientist at Yale University. He said that turf fields have burned children who play on them. His research has also found many harmful chemicals in turf. They could go into the air when it is hot. That could be dangerous for people with asthma.

Grace Chi is a junior at Poolesville High. She and other students are worried about the pollution and the turf's high temperatures. But they are also worried about smaller problems.

"Any time I would play on those plastic turfs, I wasn't a big fan of the smell or the little rubber pellets that would get into my shoes," Chi said.

Turf Advocates

Melanie Taylor is the head of the Synthetic Turf Council. It's an association that helps the turf industry. She said that planning, water breaks, shade and safety rules can make turf usable even when it's very hot out.

Taylor said that studies show injury rates are almost the same on turf and grass.

She also noted that both surfaces have environmental trade-offs. Grass needs pesticides. These are chemicals that keep bugs away. The turf industry is working on technology to make the plastic safer, she said.

levels.title: Synthetic or natural grass? The turf war in a Maryland school district
levels.body:
Maryland's largest school district is replacing its grass athletic fields with artificial turf. This decision has sparked a debate between those who favor the convenience of turf and those who worry about the cost and health impacts on students.

The argument about turf versus grass has been ongoing for years among sports and environmental groups. Supporters of turf say it requires less maintenance and lasts longer. However, critics are concerned about its environmental and health effects.

The debate is happening at Montgomery County Public Schools as it prepares to spend $55 million on artificial turf over the next six years. The district plans to spend $15 million through next June on six fields, as well as two or three turf playground installations.

Sidharth Harishanker is a junior at Poolesville High School and co-president of a student-led nonprofit environmental advocacy group. He said that turf fields pose too many risks with too few benefits.

"Why are we spending so much money on this?" he said. "Turf fields are environmentally detrimental, as well as kind of stupid."

The district estimates it will cost $1 million each to replace the existing turf fields at two high schools. Three of the new installations will cost $2.75 million each. A new field at Poolesville High will cost closer to $3.65 million.

Pros And Cons

Jeffrey Sullivan, the district's athletics director, said natural fields can't support the hours of play needed for the district's athletics and physical education programs. This becomes an equity issue for schools without alternatives.

About half of the district's 25 main high school sports fields are artificial. The district plans to change the rest to turf, Sullivan said.

Artificial turf is more than just a sheet of plastic — it's layers of concrete, plastic, and rubber. It can handle more hours of play, but it can get dangerously hot in the summer. Natural grass is cheaper to set up, but artificial turf is cheaper to maintain. Natural grass needs more upkeep, but doesn't have to be replaced every 10 years.

Calculating Costs

The district estimates the cost of setting up natural grass to be $634,000, compared to $2.5 million for an artificial field. Yearly upkeep costs are $100,000 for a grass field and $12,000 for artificial turf. The latter also has an extra $1 million replacement cost every ten years.

In November, the district released a 10-year analysis that compared the cost per hour of use for turf and grass fields. Turf fields cost $5.72 an hour, compared with $23.73 for grass fields. That hourly breakdown does not account for the cost to replace a synthetic field.

The district estimates that in 2025, its synthetic-turf fields supported 45,816 hours of play compared with 6,885 hours on natural-grass fields.

One of the main selling points of artificial turf is the ability to use it quickly after heavy rain, Sullivan said. County-maintained natural-grass fields are off-limits if more than a half-inch of rain falls in 24 hours, but turf fields do not have such restrictions.

Health Concerns

Hannah Donart is an environmental scientist. She is also on the Montgomery County Council of Parent-Teacher Associations. She said the district could save money by investing in well- maintained natural-grass fields. It could use any extra money to help address other needs. She added that the school's cost analysis doesn't account for synthetic turf's replacement cost. Grass fields could also support the same amount of activity as artificial turf if they were better maintained. She is worried about the chemicals used to make turf and noted that research shows people get injured more often on turf.

Turf can also get much hotter than natural grass. The Montgomery Council of PTAs took some temperature readings. It found that, on average, the artificial turf in the county was 65 degrees hotter than nearby natural grass.

The school district does not allow turf fields to be used when temperatures reach 90 degrees, according to the district's athletics handbook.

Yale University scientist Vasilis Vasiliou said the high temperatures of artificial fields have burned children who play on them. His research found many harmful chemicals in turf fill that could be released into the air during high heat. That could make asthma symptoms worse.

Grace Chi is a junior at Poolesville High. Besides the concerns about plastic pollution and high surface temperatures, students are worried about the smaller problems turf fields bring, too.

"Any time I would play on those plastic turfs, I wasn't a big fan of the smell or the little rubber pellets that would get into my shoes," Chi said.

Turf Advocates

Melanie Taylor is the CEO of the Synthetic Turf Council, a national trade association. She explained that artificial turf can become hotter than natural grass. However, with strategic planning, scheduled hydration breaks, shade and heat-safety protocols, it can be used year-round.

Taylor said that studies show no significant difference in injury rates between synthetic turf and natural grass.

She also noted that both surfaces have environmental trade-offs. Natural grass requires pesticides. The artificial turf industry is advancing technology to limit plastic dispersion, which would reduce microplastics in surrounding areas.

"We're very confident in turf as a surface for every level of play. So, it should not keep parents up at night," Taylor said.

Zadok Magruder, Springbrook and Watkins Mill high schools — will cost $2.75 million each. A new field at Poolesville High will cost closer to $3.65 million.

Jeffrey Sullivan, the district's athletics director, said there is no comparison between natural grass and artificial. Natural fields can't support the hours of play needed for the district's robust athletics and physical education programs, Sullivan said, a situation that becomes an equity issue for schools without alternatives.

About half of the district's 25 main high school athletic fields — which are used for sports such as football and soccer — are synthetic. The district is on track to transition the rest to turf, Sullivan said.

Synthetic turf is more than just a sheet of plastic — it's layers of concrete, plastic and rubber. At the base is a gravel or concrete layer installed to support drainage. That is topped with a shock- absorbing pad, then covered with a "grass" carpet made of plastic — typically polypropylene or polyethylene. Finally, infill, most commonly made up of crumb rubber, is dumped on top to fill the gaps.

There are caveats to nearly every argument about whether a natural or synthetic surface is best. Natural grass requires more maintenance, but doesn't have to be replaced every 10 years. Synthetic turf can support more hours of play, but it can get dangerously hot in the summer. Natural grass is cheaper to install, but synthetic turf is cheaper to maintain.

Calculating Costs

The district estimates the cost of natural-grass installation to be $634,000, compared to $2.5 million for a synthetic field. But yearly maintenance costs are $100,000 for a grass field and $12,000 for synthetic turf. The latter also carries an additional $1 million replacement cost every decade.

In November, the district released a 10-year analysis that compared the cost per hour of use for turf and grass fields. By that measure, turf fields cost $5.72 an hour, compared with $23.73 for grass fields. That hourly breakdown does not account for the cost to replace a synthetic field.

Sullivan said artificial-turf fields "save our grass fields" from overuse. The district estimates that in fiscal year 2025, its synthetic-turf fields supported 45,816 hours of play compared with 6,885 hours on natural-grass fields.

One of the main selling points of synthetic turf is the ability to use it quickly after heavy rain, Sullivan said. County-maintained natural-grass fields are off-limits if more than a half-inch of rain falls in 24 hours, according to the county parks department policy. Turf fields have no such restrictions.

Health Concerns

Hannah Donart, vice chair of health and wellness for the Montgomery County Council of Parent- Teacher Associations, said the district could save money by investing in well-maintained natural- grass fields, and use any extra money to help address other needs such as a $740 million backlog in HVAC projects. She said the school's long-term cost analysis is incomplete because it doesn't account for synthetic turf's replacement cost, and that grass fields could support the same amount of activity as synthetic turf if they were better maintained.

Donart, an environmental scientist, called synthetic turf a more expensive and more toxic alternative, noting exposure to chemicals used in manufacturing. She also called turf less safe, pointing to research that shows rates of injuries like Achilles tendon and ACL tears are higher for people who play on the turf.

"Kids and teens are not little adults and are more vulnerable to all these cumulative impacts from these harmful exposures," Donart said.

Synthetic turf can get much hotter than natural grass. The Montgomery council of PTAs took heat readings in early July of three synthetic fields in the county. On average, the synthetic turf was 65 degrees hotter than nearby natural grass, according to documents and photos reviewed by The Washington Post.

The school district restricts the use of turf fields once outdoor temperatures reach 90 degrees, according to the district's athletics handbook.

Yale University epidemiologist Vasilis Vasiliou said the high temperatures of artificial fields have burned children who play on them. His research into turf infill identified the presence of dozens of carcinogens, hormone disrupters and toxic metals that could be released into air during high heat, which, among other things, could aggravate asthma symptoms.

Richard Montgomery High soccer player Margot Ashford, who has sports-induced asthma, said she has a harder time breathing on the main athletic field, which is artificial, than on the practice field, which is natural grass.

"I've definitely seen some of the real negative impacts of synthetic turf," the rising senior said.

Grace Chi, a rising junior at Poolesville High, said that along with the concerns about plastic pollution and high surface temperatures, students are worried about the smaller nuisances turf fields bring, too.

"Any time I would play on those plastic turfs, I wasn't a big fan of the smell or the little rubber pellets that would get into my shoes," Chi said.

Turf Advocates

Melanie Taylor, CEO of the Synthetic Turf Council, a national trade association, said that while synthetic turf does get hotter than natural grass, it can support play year-round with proper planning, hydration breaks, shade and heat-safety policies.

Taylor said there are studies that show no significant difference between injury rates on synthetic turf and those on natural grass. The introduction of shock pads and standard safety testing has also made the surface safer since it was introduced, Taylor said.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: The analog shift in modern communication
levels.body:
People are starting to write notes by hand again. It's not because they want to go back to the past. It's because people use technology all the time. Talking to each other is faster now, so things that take time and effort are more special.

Slower Communication

A note or letter feels different than a text message. We don't see paper communication much in a digital age. Messages on screens are always there. Something on paper is unique.

Businesses are noticing this change. Pinterest is a website where people can search for things they like. The company noticed that more people want handwritten letters and pen-pal ideas. This shows people are taking time for slower communication.

More Effort, More Meaning

Taymoor Atighetchi started a company called Papier. They make cards and journals. He says people like writing notes again because digital messages go away. When someone chooses a card and writes by hand, it takes more effort.

"It says the relationship is worth slowing down for," he says.

Young people like using notecards and writing paper again. They want to take a break from screens.

Skipping Screens

This change is not just about notes and letters. Film cameras, records, and paper items are also getting more popular. Students are choosing paper planners instead of digital ones. They like to decorate them and make them special. They don't want to get notifications.

Atighetchi says writing by hand helps people feel less distracted. It also slows thinking down.

People feel better if they use screens less.

Taking The Time

Time is now seen as something to cherish. People used to think money was the most important thing. But now, taking time to write a note is seen as special.

"The real luxury today isn't money, it's time," Atighetchi notes. "A handwritten note…costs presence. That's why it feels extravagant in the best sense."

Writing a note by hand doesn't cost much money. What matters is the time and care put into it.

Writing By Hand

Fancy pens are still popular. Montegrappa is a luxury pen company. People buy these pens not just because they look nice, but because they help people write thoughtful notes. This idea is spreading. People are writing by hand again to make moments feel important.

Choosing What Matters

This change is not just about going back to old ways. It is about choosing what really matters. Emails and texts are fast and have lots of messages. But handwritten notes are different. They are used for special times that should be remembered.

As communication has become faster and more frequent, gestures that require time, intention and physical presence have more value.

A Lasting Mark

Physical mail affects people more deeply than a digital message. It leaves a lasting mark. This is likely because physical communication is rare in a digital age. Inboxes and messaging platforms are continuous. Something that arrives on paper holds more weight.

Companies are noticing this shift, too. Pinterest is a virtual bulletin board, where people can find, save, and share ideas. Pinterest's 2026 reporting shows that more people are searching for handwritten letters and pen-pal ideas. These are signs of time being set aside for a slower type of communication.

Worth The Effort

Taymoor Atighetchi founded Papier. His company makes items like notecards, planners and journals. He says the return of handwritten notes is a response to the temporary quality of digital things.

"Digital messages disappear… A handwritten note is something you hold, display and rediscover," he explains. "When someone chooses a card, writes by hand and addresses an envelope, the effort communicates something beyond the words. It says the relationship is worth slowing down for."

Notecards and writing paper are becoming popular again with young people. They want to take a break from their phones and computers.

Rejecting Digital Devices

That movement goes beyond notes and letters. Film photography, vinyl records and paper planners are all gaining popularity among a group that has grown up with screens. Students are choosing paper planners for school instead of digital versions. They like being able to add decorations and make them their own. They don't want to be interrupted by notifications.

"Writing by hand…slows thinking, removes distraction and makes you present in a way typing does not," Atighetchi says.

More people want to cut back on technology. They recognize that less screen time makes them feel better.

Time Is More Important

The biggest change is how people think of handwritten communication. With technology, people can be reached quickly and easily. Because of this, taking the time to write has become something rare and valuable.

"The real luxury today isn't money, it's time," Atighetchi notes. "A handwritten note…costs presence. That's why it feels extravagant in the best sense."

The materials used for a handwritten note are not expensive. Instead, what matters is the time and attention that goes into it.

Fancy Pens

The fact that fine writing tools like fancy pens are still in demand shows the same idea. Montegrappa is an Italian company known for luxury pens. Customers buy these expensive pens not just because of how they are made, but because they encourage thoughtful communication. This idea is spreading. People are going back to handwriting to make important moments feel special.

Handwritten Notes Are Better

The rarity of handwritten notes is what gives them power.

"In professional settings, a handwritten note stands out," Atighetchi says.

That explains why businesses are going back to physical communication. A written thank-you is something that digital formats can't compare to.

Making A Choice

This shift isn't just about going back to old ways of doing things. Instead, it's about choosing what's really worth time and attention. Emails and texts are quick and hold lots of messages. But handwritten notes are different. They're used for special moments that matter and deserve to be remembered.

When communication gets faster, handwritten letters become more special. People value them more because they show that someone took time and care. They can help keep important relationships strong.

"In professional settings, a handwritten note stands out in a way nothing else does," Atighetchi says. "It signals that you operate differently and that you value relationships beyond transactions."

That distinction explains why physical correspondence is being reintroduced into business strategies. A written thank-you or follow-up carries memory and differentiation that digital formats struggle to replicate.

More Than A Trend

This isn't simply a return to the past but a fundamental shift in what warrants time and attention. Digital formats are engineered for speed and volume, whereas handwritten notes are reserved for experiences that require full presence and merit preservation. The distinction is intentional.

When communication becomes faster, things that make people pause gain significance. Handwritten correspondence is establishing itself as something indispensable rather than temporary. It fulfills a fundamental human necessity: for permanence, attention, and the kind of continuity that keeps meaningful relationships alive.

Physical mail continues to outperform digital communication on attention and recall, with open rates commonly cited at near-universal levels. The difference reflects rarity as much as format. In environments where inboxes and messaging platforms are continuous, something that arrives on paper carries disproportionate weight.

levels.title: The story behind Chicago's most iconic hot dog
levels.body:
Chicago, Illinois, is famous for its hot dogs. And their hot dogs are special.

The Chicago dog starts with an all-beef frank. The sausage is placed inside a poppy-seed bun. Then, seven toppings are added. Yellow mustard comes first. Then chopped white onions. Then green relish. Then tomato wedges. Then a dill pickle spear. Then pickled sport peppers. Then, finally, celery salt.

One ingredient is not welcome: ketchup. It is too sweet. Its sweetness hides the other flavors.

Origin Of The Chicago Dog

The Chicago hot dog's roots go back to the 1840s. At that time, German immigrants began arriving in Chicago. The new immigrants introduced their sausage-making tradition. Soon, some of them started selling sausages on the streets.

These early sausages were made with pork and beef. They were heavily seasoned. By the 1870s, the sausages were served in a bun.

A few decades later, another wave of immigrants arrived. They reshaped the hot dog.

In the late 1800s, thousands of Eastern European Jews settled in Chicago. Many entered the food business. Jewish dietary laws ban pork. So, the new arrivals took a different approach. They began making all-beef franks.

The Great Depression To The Modern Dog

The Great Depression hit in 1929. Millions of Americans lost their jobs. That meant meals needed to be cheap. The Depression Dog sold for just a nickel. Sellers topped it with mustard, onions, relish and sport peppers.

But the mountain of toppings on today's Chicago dog came later. They were not added until after World War II.

During the war, there were strict limits on food. Once the war ended in 1945, Americans wanted to treat themselves. Hot dog sellers responded. They loaded their franks with extra toppings.

Cooks borrowed ideas from one another and combined them. Chicago's Jewish community contributed three things: the all- beef frank, the dill pickle and the poppy-seed bun. German immigrants introduced the mustard. Jewish, Greek and Italian grocers inspired the fresh tomato wedges. Sport peppers came from the American South. The bright green relish evolved from English piccalilli. Celery salt came from Cincinnati, Ohio.

Chicago dogs are not all the same. Most Chicago stands steam their hot dogs. But The Wieners Circle specializes in charcoal- grilled franks.

Superdawg uses pickled green tomato instead of fresh tomato. Byron's Hot Dogs offers three extra toppings: lettuce, cucumbers and green peppers. Jeff's Red Hots adds sauerkraut.

Despite the differences, these are all Chicago dogs. Their special Chicago character is unmistakable.

levels.title: The story behind Chicago's most iconic hot dog
levels.body:
CHICAGO, Illinois — Summer is a good time for hot dogs, but in Chicago, they are a staple year- round.

While Chicagoans may argue over the Cubs and the White Sox and debate deep-dish versus tavern-style pizza, one thing unites them all: They never put ketchup on a Chicago dog.

Piled high with its signature seven toppings, the Chicago dog is a rite of passage for tourists and a source of hometown pride for locals.

But long before it became the city's signature meal, it was shaped by the people, neighborhoods and traditions that built Chicago.

The standard Chicago dog starts with an all-beef frank nestled inside a poppy-seed bun. It's topped with yellow mustard, chopped white onions, neon green relish, tomato wedges, a dill pickle spear, pickled sport peppers and a dash of celery salt. A sport pepper is a small green chili pepper that is pickled in brine and famous for its bright, vinegary tang and medium-hot kick.

"It's a marriage on a bun," said Tom McGlade, Vienna Beef's senior vice president of marketing. "The ingredients work in harmony."

Though the marriage comes with a strict prenuptial agreement: No ketchup. For many vendors, ketchup's sweetness masks the balance that makes the Chicago dog unique.

"We do make an effort to say that ketchup does not belong on a Chicago-style hot dog unless you're still using training wheels," McGlade said.

Many Chicago stands don't even stock ketchup. Jimmy's Red Hots has long embraced the slogan, "No ketchup, never ever."

At The Wieners Circle, enforcement is more theatrical.

"The children get a pass, and then the rest of them get roasted," said operations manager Emma Kreis.

Origin Of The Chicago Dog

Like Chicago itself, the Chicago dog has no single founder.

Food historian Bruce Kraig, professor emeritus at Roosevelt University, said the city's iconic hot dog emerged through many years of immigration, entrepreneurship and the blending of culinary traditions.

Its roots trace back to the 1840s, when German immigrants arrived in Chicago and introduced their sausage-making traditions. As Chicago grew into a booming industrial city, vendors began selling sausages on the streets, offering workers an inexpensive meal they could eat on the go.

Those early sausages were made with pork and beef, heavily seasoned and stuffed into natural casings that offer the distinct "snap." By the 1870s and 1880s, vendors started serving sausages in a bun for customers to carry through the city's crowded streets.

A few decades later, another wave of immigrants reshaped the hot dog.

In the late 19th century, thousands of Eastern European Jewish immigrants settled around Maxwell Street on the Near West Side. Many entered the food business because it required relatively little money to get started. Since kosher dietary laws prohibit pork, they began making all-beef franks instead.

At the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, Austrian-Hungarian Jewish immigrants Emil Reichel and Samuel Ladany introduced visitors to their all-beef frankfurters. After the fair, they stayed in Chicago and founded what would become Vienna Beef.

"133 years later, here we are, still doing the same thing," McGlade said. "We've honored the original recipe by not changing it at all."

While Chicago was once home to numerous hot dog companies, including Sinai 48, David Berg and Best's Kosher, Vienna Beef has endured as the city's best-known brand. According to McGlade, more Chicagoland hot dog stands serve Vienna Beef than there are Wendy's, Burger King and McDonald's locations in the area combined, most of the stands being independently owned.

"It's a lot of little guys with a lot of little individual entrepreneurial businesses that have leveraged the Vienna name in a way that's meaningful to the public over generations," McGlade said. "We have become part of the fabric of Chicago."

Even Portillo's, one of Chicago's most recognizable restaurant chains, has partnered with Vienna Beef since it opened more than 60 years ago.

The Great Depression To The Modern Dog

When the Great Depression hit in 1929, millions of Americans lost their jobs, and affordable meals became a necessity.

Sold for just a nickel, the Depression Dog became one of Chicago's cheapest and most filling dishes. Vendors topped it with mustard, onions, relish and sport peppers before wrapping it together with a generous handful of fresh-cut fries.

At 35th Street Red Hots and Redhot Ranch locations, owner Jeff Greenfield said the Depression Dog remains the restaurant's signature order.

"Sure it's a Depression Dog, but when you eat it, it makes you happy," Greenfield said.

The mountain of toppings that are on today's Chicago dog weren't added until after World War II.

After years of wartime rationing, Americans craved abundance, and Chicago restaurants answered by piling ingredients onto their food. The era gave rise to iconic dishes such as the Italian beef sandwich and deep-dish pizza.

Hot dog vendors followed suit, loading their franks with extra toppings to stand out from the competition.

At Maxwell Street Market, cooks borrowed flavors from one another to create what eventually became the city's signature "garden on a bun."

According to Kraig, Chicago's Jewish community contributed the all-beef frank, dill pickle and poppy-seed bun. German immigrants brought their tradition of pairing mustard with sausage, while Jewish, Greek and Italian produce merchants likely inspired the addition of fresh tomato wedges. Chopped onions, a staple across countless cuisines, added crunch. Sport peppers came north from the American South, and Kraig said neon green relish likely evolved from English piccalilli. The finishing touch, celery salt, originated in Cincinnati in the 1870s when celery was popular around the country.

"Hot dogs are platforms for culture," Kraig said. "Here in Chicago it's this mixture of ethnicities."

Today, taco stands and food trucks have increasingly replaced hot dog vendors, as Mexican immigration has increased and American tastes have evolved.

Nonetheless, Chicago hot dog culture is sustained by a network of iconic stands, each with its own distinct personality and fiercely loyal following.

While most Chicago stands steam their hot dogs, The Wieners Circle specializes in char-grilled franks, blistered over an open flame.

"We have our charred dogs down to a science," Kreis said. "It's what sets us apart."

The food may draw customers in, but the experience keeps them coming back. The restaurant's famous late-night insults have become as much a part of Chicago as the hot dog itself.

"It's kind of like 'Cheers' where everyone knows your name," Kreis said. "You get people from all walks of life coming into The Wieners Circle and we serve them the same food every day."

For many visitors, however, their first Chicago dog comes from Portillo's.

What began as Dick Portillo's 1963 hot dog trailer has grown into one of the city's best-known restaurant brands, with locations across 11 states.

"Hot dogs are at the heart of Portillo's story," Chief Marketing Officer Denise Lauer said.

The company has introduced variations over the years, including a recently introduced giardiniera and provolone cheese dog in collaboration with Vienna Beef, but the classic remains its signature.

"There's nothing like a great Chicago-style dog," Lauer said.

Other stands have put their own spin on the classic. Superdawg swaps fresh tomato wedges for a pickled green tomato. At Byron's Hot Dogs, ordering your dog with "everything" adds shredded lettuce, sliced cucumbers and green peppers to the traditional seven ingredients. Jeff's Red Hots tops their Chicago dogs with sauerkraut.

Despite those variations, the Chicago dog's identity remains unmistakable.

"This is ours, this is the way we do it, and this defines us," Kraig said. "It's part of our DNA."

levels.body:
The Mielke brothers had a problem, but they did something about it. There are three Mielke brothers. Ethan is 13, Seth is 11, and Jonathan is 8. The brothers live in Rogers City, Michigan. For three years, they sold lemonade. But then something came up that made them stop.

Summer Lemonade Stand

The Mielke brothers had been selling homemade lemonade every summer. They sold it at a farmers market.

Last summer, they received some bad news. The market's new managers told them they would need a permit to sell lemonade. Permits are issued by the district health department. Their mother, Jessica Mielke, contacted the health department. She learned her sons would need a temporary food license. And that license was not free. There was a fee. They would have to pay $57 every two weeks of the summer.

That would total nearly $400. The brothers usually make between $100 and $200 each during the summer. It didn't make sense to continue selling lemonade.

The brothers were very disappointed. But they didn't want to give up.

The Boys Take Action

Their mother suggested they contact their state representative. The boys wrote letters. In January, they took them to Representative Cam Cavitt. He is a member of the Michigan House of Representatives.

Cavitt said he hadn't known about the issue.

"I think it's unfair," he said. "This is a lemonade stand. We all grew up with lemonade stands."

He said running a lemonade stand is a good thing. It can prepare kids to become business owners in the future.

"They're learning the benefits of hard work," he said. "We want to encourage these kinds of things."

Cavitt decided to work on the problem right away.

Help From Michigan Representatives

On June 11, the Mielke brothers spoke at a committee hearing. They described what happened last summer.

On June 25, the Michigan House of Representatives met. The representatives voted 110 to 0 to pass House Bill 6007. The bill would allow children under 18 to run a lemonade stand without permits or fees. The bill is now heading to the state Senate. It should be voted on very soon.

The brothers watched the first vote at home.

"They were pretty excited," their mother said. "It was a pretty neat experience for them." They saw "how the process works when you have an idea or want a law changed."

The brothers hope the new law will pass. They want to get back to selling lemonade.

levels.body:
The Mielke brothers live in Rogers City, Michigan. Ethan is 13, Seth is 11 and Jonathan is 8. Recently, the three of them walked into a community event carrying handwritten letters. The event had been called by their state representative and the brothers were there to let him know about an unfair situation: They had been priced out of selling lemonade.

Summer Lemonade Stand

The Mielke brothers had sold homemade lemonade at a farmers market in rural Michigan for the last three years. They charged 50 cents for adults and 10 cents for kids at the weekly summer stand. Along with the lemonade, they also sold painted rocks and hand-picked produce from their own garden plot. The brothers call their business "Triple M Goods."

A few weeks into last summer's season, the market's new managers told the brothers they would need a permit from the district health department to sell lemonade. Their mother, Jessica Mielke, contacted the health department and learned that if her sons wanted to continue selling lemonade, they would need a temporary food license. The license would cost them $57 every two weeks of the summer.

That would total nearly $400 to sell lemonade at the stand from June through September. The brothers typically make between $100 and $200 each during the summer from the stand, Mielke said. They did the math and decided it didn't make sense to continue.

In an interview with The Washington Post, the brothers said how much they enjoyed making and selling lemonade, and how disappointing it was to stop.

"You can talk to people and get money and things like that," Ethan said.

"I felt bad," Seth said.

"They were really discouraged," Jessica Mielke said.

American children have been running summer lemonade stands since the 1800s, though the rules governing them are very different from state to state. In Michigan, lemonade stands are generally required to have a license. Local health departments are in charge of enforcing the rules, and some require permits and fees.

The Boys Take Action

The Mielke brothers spent the offseason thinking of ways to get back to selling lemonade at their stand. Their mother suggested they take the problem to their state representative. The boys wrote letters and, in January, attended a coffee hour in Alpena, a nearby town, to deliver them to Representative Cam Cavitt.

Cavitt said he hadn't known about the issue until the boys brought it to him.

"I think it's unfair," he said. "This is a lemonade stand. We all grew up with lemonade stands."

He said running a lemonade stand can lay the groundwork for future business owners.

"They're learning the benefits of hard work," he said. "We want to encourage these kinds of things" rather than having kids "staying home and playing video games."

Cavitt said he decided to work on it right away.

Help From Michigan Representatives

On June 11, the Mielke brothers testified at a committee hearing. They drove four hours to Lansing, Michigan, with their parents. The boys prepared a speech together and took turns describing what happened last summer and how it affected them.

"It was a little bit uneasy but after a while we got used to it," Ethan said of his experience at the hearing.

On June 25, the Michigan House of Representatives voted 110 to 0 to pass House Bill 6007. The bill would allow minors to run a lemonade stand without permits or licensing fees — as long as they're selling nonalcoholic drinks that don't require refrigeration, and they make less than $5,000 a year. The bill is now heading to the state Senate, where it could be up for a vote soon.

The brothers watched the vote on a livestream at home and marveled as the vote board lit up, their mother said.

"They were pretty excited," she said. "It was a pretty neat experience for them to see how the process works when you have an idea or want a law changed."

Cavitt said he hopes the bill will move forward and become law — ideally while lemonade stand season is still in full swing. He said he is grateful to the Mielke brothers for raising the issue.

"They petitioned their government and they did this," he said. "If you don't like a law, try to change it."

The brothers said they're proud of the progress they've made and are eager to start selling lemonade again someday soon.

"I just hope that it'll pass," Ethan said.

levels.name: 原文
levels.title: Their lemonade stand faced big fees. So these kids fought back.
levels.body:
Three brothers carrying handwritten letters walked into a community event held by their state representative to air their grievance: They had been priced out of selling lemonade.

Summer Lemonade Stand

The Mielke brothers had sold homemade lemonade at a farmers market in rural Michigan for the last three years. Ethan is 13, Seth is 11 and Jonathan is 8. They charged 50 cents for adults and 10 cents for kids and also sold painted rocks and hand-picked produce from their own garden plot at the weekly summer stand.

A few weeks into last summer's season in Rogers City, Michigan, the brothers were told by the market's management team — which had recently changed — that they would need a permit from the district health department to sell lemonade. Their mother, Jessica Mielke, contacted the health department and learned that if her sons wanted to continue selling the beverages, they would need a temporary food license costing $57 every two weeks of the summer.

That would total nearly $400 to sell lemonade at the stand, which they call "Triple M Goods," from June through September. The brothers typically make between $100 and $200 each during the summer from the stand, Mielke said. They did the calculation and decided it didn't make sense to continue.

In a phone interview with The Washington Post, the brothers said how much they enjoyed making and selling lemonade on Fridays, and how disappointing it was to stop.

"You can talk to people and get money and things like that," Ethan said.

"I felt bad," Seth said.

"They were really discouraged," Jessica Mielke said.

Mielke said that she and her boys had not seen other lemonade stands at the market. The market organizers did not respond to a request for comment from The Post.

Lemonade stands have been a summer staple for American children going back to the 1800s, though rules regulating them vary broadly among states. In Michigan, lemonade stands are generally required to have a license. Enforcement is often left to local health departments — some of which require permits and fees.

Some states across the country allow lemonade stands without permits, as lawmakers have taken up the cause after high- profile cases in which kids have been fined or shut down over missing permits.

The Boys Take Action

The Mielke brothers spent the offseason brainstorming ways to get back to selling lemonade at their stand. Their mother — who followed up with the health department a few months later to see if the rules had changed, and they had not — suggested they take the problem to their state representative, figuring other children were facing the same issue. The boys wrote letters and in January attended a coffee hour in Alpena, a nearby town, to deliver them to Representative Cam Cavitt (R-Cheboygan).

Cavitt said he was struck by the boys the moment they approached him.

"They were very well-mannered and polite, they had firm handshakes and looked me in the eyes," he said.

Cavitt said he hadn't known about the issue until the boys brought it to him.

"I think it's unfair," he said. "This is a lemonade stand. We all grew up with lemonade stands."

He said running a lemonade stand can lay the groundwork for future business owners.

"They're learning the benefits of hard work. ... They're fostering an entrepreneurial spirit," he said. "We want to encourage these kinds of things in our kids rather than staying home and playing video games."

Cavitt said he decided to work on it right away.

Help From Michigan Representatives

On June 11, the Mielke brothers testified at a committee hearing. They drove four hours to Lansing with their parents. The boys prepared a speech together and took turns recounting what happened last summer and how it affected them.

"It was a little bit uneasy but after a while we got used to it," Ethan said of his experience at the hearing.

On June 25, the Michigan House of Representatives voted 110 to 0 to pass House Bill 6007, which would allow minors to run a lemonade stand on private or public property without permits or licensing fees — as long as they're selling nonalcoholic beverages that don't require refrigeration, and they make less than $5,000 a year. The bill is now heading to the state Senate, where it could be up for a vote in as early as a few weeks, Cavitt said.

The brothers — who still sell produce and painted rocks at the farmers market — watched the vote on a livestream at home and marveled as the vote board lit up, their mother said.

"They were pretty excited," she said. "It was a pretty neat experience for them to see how the process works when you have an idea or want a law changed."

Cavitt said he hopes the bill will move forward and become law — ideally while lemonade stand season is still in full swing. He said he is grateful to the Mielke brothers for raising the issue.

"They petitioned their government and they did this," he said. "If you don't like a law, try to change it."

The brothers said they're proud of the progress they've made and are eager to start selling lemonade again someday soon.

"I just hope that it'll pass," Ethan said.

title: Three women's world records set at the annual Lumberjack World Championships in Wisconsin
zhTitle: 伐木世锦赛上的三项女子世界纪录
reason: 锯木、劈柴、滚木、爬杆各自的比赛规则，以及伐木工这个行业的历史。

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Three women's world records set at the annual Lumberjack World Championships in Wisconsin
levels.body:
The Lumberjack World Championships competition was held in July. It was full of sawing, chopping and logrolling. Three new women's world records were set there.

A lumberjack is a worker in the logging business. In past times, lumberjacks cut down trees and transported logs using hand tools. The word "lumberjack" mostly refers to workers in the 1800s and early 1900s. Chainsaws and modern machinery were not yet used. The culture started in Maine. It moved through the Upper Midwest. Eventually, it reached the Pacific Northwest. Lumberjacks lived in camps in the woods. They used big axes and saws. The traditional lifestyle faded after World War II. Motor vehicles and chainsaws modernized the timber industry.

This year, 66 men and 40 women were in the competition. They came from 16 states and nine countries.

Many competitors have custom-built chainsaws. They use carefully sharpened axes and saws.

Karolina Urbanová is from the Czech Republic. She set world records in two events. She earned first place in the Women's Underhand Chop. She also came in first in the Women's Standing Chop.

Meredith Ingbretson of Hayward set a world record in the Women's Boom Run. She ran across the water and back over eight red cedar logs. It took her less than 14 seconds.

Women have been competing since the first competition in 1960. The number of events they are in has grown. They started just competing in logrolling. Now they are in more than 20 timber sports events.

Nancy Zalewski has been a competitor for 27 years. She said when she started, she was chopping with men.

The tradition of competition among lumberjacks began in the 1890s. The competition is held in the Lumberjack Bowl. In the past, the area had been a holding pond for log drives.

A log drive was the old method of moving cut logs from forests to sawmills. Lumberjacks would float logs down rivers and streams. This process used melted snow to carry millions of logs downstream.

The lumberjack theme is everywhere at the festival. There are children in lumberjack socks and flannel shirts. Companies hand out blow-up axes and toy chainsaws. There are wood-carving demonstrations. There is logrolling practice for kids. They also have live music and food trucks. There are axe-themed events. It's fun for all!

Karolina Urbanová, of the Czech Republic, and Stephanie Naud, of Canada, celebrate after Urbanovà broke the world record in the women's underhand chop event during the Lumberjack World Championships, on July 18, 2026, in Hayward, Wisconsin.
Athletes compete in the men's standing chop during the Lumberjack World Championships, on July 18, 2026, in Hayward, Wisconsin.

levels.title: Three women's world records set at the annual Lumberjack World Championships in Wisconsin
levels.body:
The Lumberjack World Championships competition was held in a small Wisconsin community in July. The competition festival was full of high-powered sawing, chopping, logrolling and speed climbing. Three new women's world records were set there.

A lumberjack is a worker in the logging business. In past times, lumberjacks cut down trees and transported logs using hand tools. The word "lumberjack" mostly refers to 19th- and early-20th- century workers. This was before the widespread use of chainsaws and modern machinery. The culture started in Maine. It moved through the Upper Midwest forests and eventually reached the Pacific Northwest. Lumberjacks lived in remote seasonal camps. They used axes and crosscut saws. The traditional lifestyle faded after World War II as motor vehicles and chainsaws modernized the timber industry.

This year, 66 men and 40 women attended the three-day competition. It was held in Hayward, Wisconsin, and ended July 18. They came from 16 states and nine countries.

Competitors take their gear seriously. Many have custom-built chainsaws. They use carefully sharpened axes and single-buck saws that can cost more than $400 just to sharpen. A single- buck saw is more than six feet long. It is a crosscut saw for one person to use alone.

Karolina Urbanová is from the Czech Republic. She set world records in two events. She earned first place in the Women's Underhand Chop. Urbanová cut through 11 inches of white pine in 21.28 seconds. She also came in first in the Women's Standing Chop. She cut through 9 inches of white pine in 19.38 seconds.

Meredith Ingbretson of Hayward set a world record in the Women's Boom Run. She sprinted across the water and back over eight red cedar logs. It only took her 13.78 seconds.

Women have been competing since the first competition in 1960. The number of events they participate in has grown significantly, organizers said. They started just competing in logrolling. Now they participate in more than 20 timber sports events.

Nancy Zalewski has been a competitor for 27 years. She said when she started, she was chopping with men. Zalewski has trained others, including fellow participant Kate Witkowski.

The tradition of competition among lumberjacks began in the 1890s, according to the organization. The competition is held in the Lumberjack Bowl on the shores of Lake Hayward. In the past, the area had been a holding pond for log drives. These log drives were down the Namekagon River.

A log drive was the historical method of moving cut logs from forests to sawmills. Lumberjacks would float logs down rivers and streams. This seasonal process relied on the power of melted snow from winter to carry millions of logs downstream.

The lumberjack theme can be seen throughout the festival. There are children in lumberjack socks, flannels and suspenders. Companies hand out blow-up axes and toy chainsaws. Outside the competition bowl, there are wood-carving demonstrations. There is logrolling practice for kids. They also have live music, food trucks and axe-themed events.

"The culture of it I think is really wonderful," Witkowski said. "I don't know any other sports where the athletes support each other like we do here…." She said the gear is hard to get, and everyone just wants to get better.

levels.title: Three women's world records set at the annual Lumberjack World Championships in Wisconsin
levels.body:
HAYWARD, Wisconsin — Three new women's world records have been set at the Lumberjack World Championships competition held in a small Wisconsin community, full of high-powered sawing, chopping, logrolling, speed climbing and cheers of "Yo-Ho!"

A lumberjack is a worker in the logging industry in North America. Historically, they felled trees and transported timber using manual tools. The term mostly refers to 19th- and early-20th- century laborers before the widespread adoption of chainsaws and modern machinery. The culture started in Maine, moved through the Upper Midwest forests and eventually reached the Pacific Northwest. Lumberjacks lived in remote seasonal camps, using axes and crosscut saws. The traditional lifestyle faded after World War II as motor vehicles and chainsaws modernized the timber industry.

This year, 66 men and 40 women attended the three-day competition in Hayward, Wisconsin, that ended July 18. They represented 16 states and nine countries.

Competitors take their gear seriously with custom-built chainsaws, carefully sharpened axes and single-buck saws that can cost upward of $400 just to sharpen.

Karolina Urbanová from the Czech Republic set world records in two events. She earned first place in the Women's Underhand Chop, cutting through 11 inches of white pine in 21.28 seconds. She also came in first in the Women's Standing Chop, cutting through 9 inches of white pine in 19.38 seconds.

Meredith Ingbretson of Hayward set a world record in the Women's Boom Run, sprinting across the water and back over eight red cedar logs in 13.78 seconds.

While women have been competing since the inaugural competition in 1960, the events they participate in have expanded significantly, organizers said. They started just competing in logrolling, and now they participate in more than 20 timber sports events.

"When I started chopping I was chopping with the men," said Nancy Zalewski, a competitor for 27 years who has trained others, including fellow participant Kate Witkowski.

The tradition of competition among lumberjacks began in the 1890s, according to the organization. The competition is held in the Lumberjack Bowl on the shores of Lake Hayward. In the past, the area had been a holding pond for log drives down the Namekagon River.

A log drive was the historical method of moving harvested timber from forests to sawmills by floating logs down natural waterways. This seasonal process relied on the power of winter snowmelt to carry millions of logs downstream.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: Tunisian beekeepers battle extreme heat to keep the buzz alive
levels.body:
Hela Boubaker is a beekeeper in Tunisia, Africa. This year, she has lost 20 beehives because of heat and wildfires.

Hives are carefully placed in the shade. But at 10 a.m. on a late- August Tuesday, it is already 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius). ""It's not easy," she says. "But at the same time, we are not easy. We won't give up."

Nearly 40 percent of citizens and entire communities rely on farming for their livelihoods. Bees are a big business.

The nation's apiarists must protect their beehives against extreme weather. They are turning to innovative solutions.

Apiarists are beekeepers. Places where they keep beehives are called apiaries.

Extreme Heat And Drought

In recent years, jobs are few and far between. More young Tunisians and many female entrepreneurs are turning to beekeeping. Beekeeping serves as a climate-friendly, sustainable form of self-employment.

Some 13,000 Tunisians work as full-time beekeepers. Thousands more rely on apiary work part-time. Their work produces a combined 280,000 metric tons of honey per year.

For those new to beekeeping in Tunisia, the work has been difficult. Tunisia has faced extreme heat. Temperatures have reached 120 degrees Fahrenheit (49 degrees Celsius). The heat sparked devastating wildfires in 2022 and again in July 2023. This year, the country struggled with a record drought. This is a period of time with less rain than usual. Regions are left without water for weeks at a time.

According to apiarists, the extreme weather has hurt honey production. Bees could produce about 17 pounds (8 kilograms) of honey per hive. In 2023, that's fallen 9 to 11 pounds (4 to 5 kilograms) per hive.

Finding Ways To Keep Bees Alive

Boubaker is an entrepreneur. She is finding ways to keep her bees alive.

She is working with other apiarists. They are adapting to a changing climate. They rent plots of farmers' lands where they place their hives. There, they've added plants that can survive droughts such as lemon trees, thyme and marjoram. This makes sure there is nectar and food sources all year for hives. More delicate flowers and plants wilt in increasingly hot temperatures.

Boubaker moves her hives to different locations, too. In the north, the land is full of pine trees in the mountains. Areas in the south are dry. And the bees also spend time in rich farmlands.

Rotating the hives means they are spread out. Boubaker checks on her 82 colonies every two days. The commute takes six hours and 200 miles (322 kilometers) round trip.

SmartBee App Helps Beekeepers

Innovators are turning to apps to help beekeepers face challenges.

Khaled Bouchoucha is a Tunisian engineer. He has grappled with solving Tunisia's plummeting bee numbers.

"Beekeepers can feel the impact of climate change, but they don't know how to adapt," Bouchoucha said. Climate change is the significant change in the climate of Earth. It happens over a long period of time. Climate change can happen naturally. Today, climate change is largely caused by human activities.

In 2021, Bouchoucha developed and launched SmartBee. This device and app provides beekeepers with real-time data. Keepers can see information about hive temperature, humidity and weight. Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air.

"We give beekeepers real-time information in order to act," he adds. The information is sent to beekeepers' phones. For example, an alert might tell a beekeeper that their hive is overheating. Then, the beekeeper can move the hive to a cooler place. Or the app can tell beekeepers when bees need more food.

SmartBee is also has a GPS locator and warning system. It tells beekeepers if their hives have been moved. This helps beekeepers who keep their hives spread far apart.

SmartBee is now being exported to the Middle East and North African countries. "With North Africa on the front lines of climate change," Bouchoucha said, "we need to be on the front lines of solutions."

figures.credit: Photo: Fethi Belaid/AFP via Getty Images

Hela Boubaker started a honey production business after receiving beekeeping training in 2017. She produces bee venom, in addition to honey, using a device she made. Bee venom can be used in the treatment of some diseases.

Like many apiarists, she rotates her beehives through geographic locations with varying topographies — the mountainous pine-treed north, the more arid south and the rich fertile farmland around Bizerte.

Boubaker's commute to check on her dispersed 82 colonies is a six-hour, 200-mile round trip that she takes every two days.

Yet the geographic dispersal of apiarists' beehives has led to another, emerging threat to Tunisia's honey-makers: crime. Specifically, theft.

Devastated by the sudden loss of entire colonies to heat and fire, and desperate to start over again quickly, some less scrupulous beekeepers have begun stealing the unattended hive boxes of other apiarists.

It is a phenomenon reported on by beekeepers across Tunisia, who have gone to fields to discover that their hive boxes have disappeared.

"Only a beekeeper would have the knowledge and equipment to be able to pick up hives and transport them," says Boubaker, who rents fields in gated farms to minimize theft.

"Unfortunately, people are desperate. When you lose the source of your livelihood, you are desperate to rebuild it. Some may be tempted to steal money. Others steal bees."

SmartBee App Takes Flight

To help Tunisian beekeepers confront 21st century challenges, innovators are putting constantly updated apiary data in an app.

"Beekeepers can feel the impact of climate change, but they don't know how to adapt," says Khaled Bouchoucha, a Tunisian engineer who has grappled with solving Tunisia's plummeting bee numbers. "All the knowledge beekeepers have accumulated for decades and generations is no longer applicable" in a rapidly changing climate.

In 2021, Bouchoucha developed and launched SmartBee, a device and app that provides beekeepers with real-time data on hive temperature, humidity, weight and mortality rates.

"We give beekeepers real-time information in order to act," he adds.

With the data, advance warnings and advice sent to beekeepers' phones, apiarists are informed when to move overheated hives to cooler areas and when isolated hives have become too cold, or they're alerted to provide sugar solutions to boost weak bees — a critical service when hives are often dozens of miles away.

SmartBee is also an anti-theft device. It's GPS locator and warning system sense if boxes are moved. This summer several beekeepers have been able to locate and reclaim stolen hives.

But in the face of global warming, early warning is not enough, beekeepers say.

Bouchoucha's Beekeeper Tech company is using data sets from customers to single out the most productive bee queens in the past few years of higher temperatures and lower food sources, helping beekeepers select the most climate-resilient and adaptable bees for breeding in their specific region.

"Genetics and adaptation are the future of beekeeping," says Bouchoucha, whose SmartBee is now being exported to the Middle East and North African countries, including Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Algeria, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

"With North Africa on the front lines of climate change," he says, "we need to be on the front lines of solutions."

levels.title: UNESCO adds D-Day landing beaches, Mount Olympus, and South Sudan wetlands to World Heritage List
levels.body:
Some very special places just joined a special list. The list is called the World Heritage List. UNESCO takes care of this list. UNESCO is a part of the United Nations. They pick places that are important to people all over the world. These places can be important because of history, culture, or nature. Once a place is on the list, it gets extra help. This help protects the place for the future.

A group of people met in Busan, South Korea, to add new places to the list. Two of the new places are the D-Day beaches in France and Mount Olympus in Greece. There were 25 new places added in total.

The D-Day Beaches

France has five beaches in a region called Normandy. Their names are Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold, and Juno. June 6, 1944, is called D-Day. On that day, more than 150,000 soldiers landed on these beaches. These soldiers were called the Allied troops. The Allies were countries that worked together. They fought against Germany in World War II. The United States, Britain, Canada, and France were all Allies. D-Day helped end the war in Europe.

The beaches still have old signs of the battle. There are old walls, damaged land, and even sunken ships. People say D-Day helped bring peace to Europe. But the beaches need protection. Tourists, weather, and rising water could hurt them.

A historian named David Edgerton said, "It's probably the greatest amphibious landing there's ever been. It ought to be remembered for that alone."

Mount Olympus

Mount Olympus is the tallest mountain in Greece. It is 2,918 meters tall. That is very, very tall!

Long ago, people believed gods lived on Mount Olympus. In Greek mythology, Zeus was the king of the gods. Twelve gods lived on the mountain. Each god had a special job. One god ruled the sea. Another god ruled war. People still tell stories about these gods today.

Mount Olympus also has amazing biodiversity. This means many kinds of plants and animals live there. That is why the mountain was added to the list. It is special for its stories and for its nature.

It took Greece 12 years to get this honor. A town leader named Evangelos Geroliolios said they must work hard now to protect the mountain.

Japan's Ancient Cities

Japan added an old area called Asuka and Fujiwara. Long ago, these were Japan's capital cities. This was over 1,000 years ago!

The area has old palaces, old buildings, and Buddhist temples buried in the ground. Buddhism is a religion. It started in India a long time ago. It spread to many countries, including Japan.

A professor named Yoshiyuki Aihara studies this area. He said if you dig just one meter down, you can find old ruins.

South Sudan's Animal Migration

South Sudan added a place with wetlands and grasslands. Every year, about 6 million animals travel across this land. This is called a mammal migration. That means many animals move together. They travel to find food and water.

The animals include kob, tiang, and gazelles. Elephants, lions, and cheetahs live there too. People have lived in this area for a long time. They farm, fish, and raise animals.

levels.title: UNESCO adds D-Day landing beaches, Mount Olympus, and South Sudan wetlands to World Heritage List
levels.body:
World War II's D-Day landing beaches in France and the famous Mount Olympus in Greece have just been added to the World Heritage List. The list is run by UNESCO, a United Nations agency. UNESCO protects places around the world that matter to all of humanity because of their history, culture, or natural beauty. Once a site is added, it can receive help to protect it for the future. The decision was announced at a meeting in South Korea, where a UN committee reviewed many nominations.

The committee also added ancient Japanese capital cities, along with South Sudan's Boma- Badingilo Migratory Landscape. This site supports one of the largest animal migrations on Earth.

There were 25 new places around the world added in total.

The D-Day Beaches

France's new site includes five beaches in Normandy — Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold, and Juno — plus a nearby cliff called Pointe du Hoc. On June 6, 1944, known as D-Day, more than 150,000 Allied troops landed on these beaches. The Allied powers were the nations — including the United States, Britain, Canada, and France — that fought together against Nazi Germany in World War II. D-Day was a major turning point. It launched the campaign that eventually freed Western Europe from Nazi control.

The International Council on Monuments and Sites reviews historic places. The group said the beaches still hold real evidence of the invasion. This includes old German defenses, bomb-damaged land, harbor remains built by the Allies, and even sunken ships. The council said the sites mark an event that helped restore freedom and peace to Europe. But it also warned that tourism, climate change, rising sea levels, and nearby wind farms could threaten the beaches. Because of this, stronger protection is needed.

Ahlem Gharbi, France's representative to UNESCO, said the Normandy landings marked a turning point away from war and toward peace. She said this recognition matters even more today, since conflicts are happening around the world.

"It's probably the greatest amphibious landing there's ever been. It ought to be remembered for that alone," said historian David Edgerton.

Mount Olympus

Mount Olympus rises 2,918 meters (9,573 feet) above sea level, making it the tallest mountain in Greece. In Greek mythology, the mountain was believed to be the throne of Zeus, king of the gods. It was also home to the twelve Olympian gods. Each god ruled over a different part of life, such as the sea, war, or love. Ancient Greeks told many stories about these gods, and people still read those myths today.

Mount Olympus is also known for its biodiversity. This means it supports many different kinds of plants and animals. For that reason, it was added to the list for two reasons: its cultural and mythological importance, and its natural environment.

It took Greece 12 years to earn this honor. Evangelos Geroliolios is the mayor of a town at the base of the mountain. He said the listing comes with greater responsibility to protect the environment, especially as more tourists are expected.

Georgios Koumoutsakos, Greece's UNESCO delegate, said, "We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to safeguarding Mount Olympus for the benefit of present and future generations. As Greek mythology wisely reminds us, it is always best to remain on good terms with gods."

Japan's Ancient Capitals

The newly listed sites in Japan's Nara region include 19 archaeological locations from the cities of Asuka and Fujiwara. These cities were Japan's capitals from the 6th to the 8th centuries. During this time, Japan built its first centralized government. It based many of its ideas on China's system of government. The sites contain buried remains of royal palaces, government buildings, tombs, and Buddhist temples. Buddhism is a religion that began in ancient India and spread across Asia, including Japan. There, it became closely connected to art, architecture, and government.

Japan's Vice Culture Minister, Shigeki Kobayashi, thanked the committee. He said Japan is committed to protecting these sites for future generations. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who is from Nara, said she hopes the listing will bring more visitors to the region.

Yoshiyuki Aihara is an archaeology professor at Nara University. He says the sites matter because they show how Japan's early government was shaped by China and the Korean Peninsula. "If you dig underneath these rice paddies about 1 meter, you start finding a stretch of ruins in this area, though that's not easy for ordinary visitors to understand," said Aihara, who continues to dig at the site.

South Sudan's Migration Landscape

South Sudan's new site includes wetlands, flood plains, and grasslands. These areas are shaped by seasonal rain and flooding. Each year, an estimated 6 million animals travel across this land. These include white-eared kob, tiang, and Mongalla gazelles. This kind of movement is called a mammal migration. It means a large group of animals moves together to find food, water, or better living conditions as the seasons change. It is considered one of the largest land migrations in the world.

The area is also home to elephants, lions, cheetahs, and other wildlife. It also supports local communities that have depended on herding, farming, and fishing for centuries, according to UNESCO.
