levels.title: UNESCO adds D-Day landing beaches, Mount Olympus, and South Sudan wetlands to World Heritage List
levels.body:
SEOUL, South Korea — World War II's D-Day landing beaches in northern France and the iconic Mount Olympus in Greece were among the sites added to the World Heritage List on Sunday at a U.N. committee meeting in South Korea reviewing dozens of nominations.

The UNESCO committee, which meets in Busan through Wednesday, also inscribed the ancient Japanese capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara and South Sudan's Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape, host to one of the world's largest land mammal migrations and the country's first addition to the World Heritage List.

The French designation covers the five Normandy landing beaches — Omaha, Utah, Sword, Gold and Juno — where more than 150,000 Allied troops came ashore on June 6, 1944, along with the Pointe du Hoc assault site, all central to the campaign to liberate Western Europe from Nazi occupation during World War II.

International Council on Monuments and Sites, which evaluates submissions to the heritage committee, said the sites contain extensive remnants, from German fortifications and bomb- scarred landscapes to Allied harbor structures and sunken vessels, marking an "event widely perceived as having enabled the return of freedom and heralded a lasting peace on the European continent."

ICOMOS also called for stronger monitoring and preservation efforts on the sites, citing potential threats posed by tourism, climate change and rising sea levels, and the development of wind farms near the areas.

Ahlem Gharbi, France's permanent delegate to UNESCO, said the Normandy landings marked a turning point from global conflict toward a postwar order built on peace and security, and that the designation of the sites carries added significance at a time of escalating international crises and wars.

"It's probably the greatest amphibious landing there's ever been. It ought to be remembered for that alone," historian David Edgerton said in a recent interview with The Associated Press.

The World Heritage inscription of Mount Olympus, the mythical home of the 12 Olympian gods, rewarded a 12-year effort by Greece to secure recognition for its tallest mountain as a mixed cultural and natural heritage site. Rising 2,918 meters (9,573 feet) from a base near sea level, the mountain was believed to be the throne of Zeus, king of the gods, while also harboring rich biodiversity.

Evangelos Geroliolios, mayor of Dion-Olympus, a municipality at the foot of the mountain, said in a recent interview with the AP that inclusion on the World Heritage List "places greater obligations on our part to protect this environment," citing the potential impact of increased tourism.

"We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to safeguarding Mount Olympus for the benefit of present and future generations," said Georgios Koumoutsakos, Greece's delegate to UNESCO. "As Greek mythology wisely reminds us, it is always best to remain on good terms with gods."

The designated Japanese locations in the western prefecture of Nara cover 19 archaeological sites from the 6th- to 8th-century capitals of Asuka and Fujiwara, where Japan established its first centralized state modeled after Chinese systems. The sites preserve the largely buried remains of royal palaces, government offices, Buddhist temples and tombs from capitals that influenced the later capitals of Nara and Kyoto.

Japanese Vice Culture Minister Shigeki Kobayashi thanked the committee for inscribing the Asuka-Fujiwara sites and said Japan reaffirms its commitment to "transmitting this valuable property to the future generations." Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a Nara native, wrote on X that she hopes the World Heritage designation will boost tourism to the site.

Yoshiyuki Aihara, a Nara University archaeology professor, told AP the sites are significant because they show how Japan's ancient state was formed through influences from China and the Korean Peninsula.

"If you dig underneath these rice paddies about 1 meter, you start finding a stretch of ruins in this area, though that's not easy for ordinary visitors to understand," said Aihara, who is continuing excavation work at the site.

South Sudan's Boma-Badingilo site encompasses vast wetlands, flood plains and savannas shaped by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics, with an estimated 6 million white-eared kob, tiang and Mongalla gazelles moving across the landscape in response to changing environmental conditions.

It also provides habitat for elephants, lions, cheetahs and other wildlife while supporting various ethnic communities that have lived by herding, farming and fishing for centuries, according to UNESCO.

title: World Cup team bus featured winning art by a 12-year-old soccer fan
zhTitle: 画在世界杯球队大巴上的儿童作品
reason: 十二岁学生的参赛作品被选中印上巴西队大巴，主题是「更好地在一起」。

cover.caption: Twelve-year-old student Leo Silveira from New Bedford, MA, won a global art contest run by FIFA. Here, his winning artwork hangs on the wall next to the cafeteria at his school.

levels.name: 入门
levels.title: World Cup team bus featured winning art by a 12-year-old soccer fan
levels.body:
Leo Silveira is 12 years old. He goes to school in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

Last winter, when Leo was in the sixth grade, he drew a picture at school. He entered it into a worldwide art competition. The competition was run by FIFA. This group runs the World Cup.

Thousands of kids sent in drawings. Leo's artwork won!

As the prize, Leo's drawing was featured during this summer's huge soccer competition. It was displayed on the Brazilian team's official World Cup buses.

Leo was thrilled.

"When they told me, I got really excited," he said. He has been a fan of the Brazil team since 2018.

Better Together

Leo's family is from Brazil, a country in South America. They moved to Massachusetts five years ago. At first, being in a new country was hard. But now, Leo enjoys New Bedford.

Leo's drawing shows a group of fans. They are cheering for the Brazilian national team. The drawing has an important message: We are better together.

The picture features a banner. It translates to "Let's Go Brazil." The other part of the drawing shows a group of kids. One of them is in a wheelchair. Leo says he wanted to "show that we can be different. But when Brazil plays, we all come together."

The drawing took Leo a week to finish. Leo loves art. He also loves playing soccer.

An Amazing Win

Aleisea Guzman is Leo's art teacher. She is proud of what Leo did. Leo tried to show that everyone should be included. "I just thought that was amazing to be a young person and have a voice like that," Guzman said.

Christian Garris is the head of Leo's school. Garris said he was honored to have Leo represent New Bedford at the World Cup.

Leo "is normally a little bit quiet. … But clearly [he] has talents that should be showcased," Garris said. Garris hopes Leo's win will inspire other students. All kids should "use their talents and their voice," he said.

Leo's family is from Brazil, a country in South America. They moved to Massachusetts five years ago, said Christian Garris. He is the head of school at Nativity Preparatory. Leo is the school's only Brazilian student.

Starting out "in a whole different country and whole different language" was hard at first, Leo said. But he has started to enjoy New Bedford since then.

His winning drawing showed fans cheering for Brazil's national team. The drawing's message: we are better together.

"I drew the banner, which translates to 'let's go Brazil,'" he said. The drawing shows young people all cheering for the Brazilian team. Some kids in the picture are standing. One child is in a wheelchair. Leo said he wanted his drawing to show that people can be different. "But when Brazil plays," he said, "we all come together and support them."

The drawing took Leo a week to complete. He loves to make art. He also loves to play soccer with his friends during recess, he said.

As part of the prize, Leo and his father got to see a World Cup game. They went to New Jersey's MetLife Stadium. Brazil played Morocco there on June 13. The game ended in a 1-1 draw. Leo's favorite players are Neymar Jr. and Hyan Carvalho Machado Silva.

An Amazing Win

Leo said his classmates were happy he won. So was his art teacher, Aleisea Guzman. Guzman encouraged her students to enter the competition.

"I tried to get them to know that you won just by submitting," Guzman said. "When he actually got the win, it was incredible."

Guzman is proud of what Leo did. Leo's artwork tries to show that everyone should be included. "I just thought that was amazing to be a young person and have a voice like that," Guzman said.

Garris, the head of Leo's school, said Leo is usually a little bit quiet. "But clearly [he] has talents that should be showcased," Garris said. Garris hopes Leo's win will inspire other students. All kids should "use their talents and their voice," he said.

Leo Silveira, who attended sixth grade at the Nativity Preparatory School in New Bedford last year, entered the competition the day before the late-January deadline.

In mid-April, his parents found out by email that their son's picture of fans cheering on the Brazilian national team had been chosen.

"When they told me, I got really excited," Leo said. "I have been supporting the Brazilian team every single day since the World Cup in 2018."

FIFA congratulated the winning children whose pictures were chosen from thousands of submissions for their favorite teams in a Facebook post on April 14.

Better Together

Silveira's family moved from Brazil to Massachusetts five years ago, head of school Christian Garris said. Leo is the only Brazilian student at the school.

Starting out "in a whole different country and whole different language" was difficult at first, but he has since started to enjoy New Bedford, Leo said. His drawing's message: We are better together.

"I drew the banner, which translates to 'let's go Brazil,' and the other part of my drawing of the kids and the youth in the wheelchair to show that we can be different," he explained. "But when Brazil plays we all come together and support them."

The drawing took Leo a week to complete. Besides his passion for art, he loves to play soccer with his friends during recess, he said.

As part of the prize, he and his father were invited to MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to see Brazil play Morocco on June 13; the teams played to a 1-1 draw. Leo was excited to look for his favorite players, Neymar Jr. and Hyan Carvalho Machado Silva.

An Amazing Win

His classmates were happy to see him win, Leo said. His art teacher, Aleisea Guzman, had encouraged him to enter the competition.

"A few of our students did submit artwork and I tried to get them to know that you won just by submitting," Guzman said. "When he actually got the win, it was incredible. Him considering inclusivity and really connecting back to the soccer culture in his country, I just thought that was amazing to be a young person and have a voice like that."

Guzman has been teaching art to 55 students at the school for two years. Garris said he was honored that one of his students would represent the New Bedford community on an international stage.

"This has taken a kid like Leo, who is normally a little bit quiet, a little bit reserved, but clearly has talents that should be showcased at an international level," he said. "It's about really showing the rest of the kids in the school to use their talents and their voice in whatever way that they can use it best."
